# Entity index

The things of `20-claims/entities.yaml` and every public claim each one is matched in, with the words that matched. It is the review list for the things: the web edition and the agent pack show the same matches as cards.

Version v2.13.0, data through 2026-10-02 (Day 3).

**90 things, 2124 mentions in 1300 of 2228 public claims** (1 pinned by hand). How a claim is matched: `_system/schema/claim.md`, section *Things*.

**How to review.** Read the precision sample below and mark every row where the matched words do not mean the thing (another sense of the word, or a different thing with a similar name): fewer than 5 wrong in 100 is the bar. After each rebuild, `git diff 50-maps/entity-index.md` shows exactly the mentions that came and went. A wrong mention: make the alias a phrase, scope it to topics or `unpin` the claim. A missed one: add an alias or `pin` the claim.

## Precision sample

100 mentions picked by a hash of the claim id and the thing id, so every build picks the same ones while the data stays the same. For each row: do the matched words mean this thing here? Mark a wrong row with an x.

| # | Claim | Thing | Matched words | Claim text or quote | Wrong? |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [`D1-C162`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) | `gemini` | Gemini app | Google said that after the launch of Nano Banana, its image generation model, the Gemini app became the number one app in the app store in 2025. | |
| 2 | [`D1-C018`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) | `ai-mode` | AI Mode | One in six AI Mode searches is multimodal, using voice or images. | |
| 3 | [`D1-C029`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) | `google-search-console` | Search Console | Search Console has a property setting called Search generative AI that gives direct control over AI Overviews and AI Mode without affecting web rankings. Its states are inherit from parent, include and exclude. | |
| 4 | [`D1-C203`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) | `googlebot` | Googlebot | A crawler is software that downloads pages, extracts their links and repeats the process on the links it extracted; Googlebot is the main crawler of Google Search. | |
| 5 | [`D1-C249`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) | `rich-results-test` | Rich Results Test | A community demo showed a script that opens Chrome with a saved session, pastes a URL into Google's Rich Results Test, waits about 15 seconds, then screenshots and saves the result and retries on failure (the demo's recording is largely unintelligible; the tool name is a best reading). | |
| 6 | [`D1-C281`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) | `webmcp` | WebMCP | A community speaker presented WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) as a way for a site to declare the actions it offers to AI agents, for example booking an appointment in a calendar, so an agent does not have to scrape the interface; the speaker called it faster, easier and cheaper. | |
| 7 | [`D1-C342`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) | `google-shopping` | Google Shopping | Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot is today just one user of a centralized crawling platform, and that dozens of other clients, such as Google Shopping and AdSense, send their crawl requests through the same infrastructure under other crawler names, with only the larger ones documented. | |
| 8 | [`D1-C073`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) | `soft-404-error` | soft 404 | A soft 404 is a page that returns a success code while its content looks like an error or an empty page. It is kept out of the index but continues to be crawled, wasting crawl budget. | |
| 9 | [`D1-C353`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) | `http-4xx` | 4xx | 429 Too Many Requests is the exception among 4xx codes: instead of meaning there is nothing at the URL, it tells Google's crawler to slow down, and Google slows its crawling. | |

- [`D1-C022`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: Search Agents in AI Mode let users set standing requests for updates, such as being told when a product goes on sale, a team wins or a price drops below a level.

- [`D1-C030`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: The Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews, AI Mode and generative AI features in Discover. Excluding removes both links to the site and use of its content to ground answers.
- [`D1-C184`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: Google said AI Mode is growing almost exponentially and that people are searching more because of it, not less.
- [`D1-C185`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: Google said a multi-part query, such as a white three-row SUV for two teenagers and a car-sick dog, cannot be satisfied by a list of links because no single article covers every aspect, while AI Overviews and AI Mode can synthesise an answer that helps users decide where to go.
- [`D1-C189`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: AI Overviews and AI Mode work together: a user can start with an AI Overview and continue the conversation in AI Mode.
- [`D1-C192`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: Google said Search agents in AI Mode had launched globally a day or two before 30 September 2026.
- [`D1-C193`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: A search marketing agency reported on 29 September 2026 that Google's VP of Product for Search announced on X, on 28 September 2026, that AI Mode information monitoring was rolling out to everyone globally in the Google app; Google's I/O 2026 post had launched information agents first for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in summer 2026.
- [`D1-C194`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **AI Mode**: A Search agent is set up by typing a natural-language request, which AI Mode interprets to create an alert; Google called this an information agent.
- [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **AI Mode**: AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D1-C208`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **AI Mode**: AI Overviews and AI Mode may have extra processes of their own, like any other search feature, but the bulk of their processing is the same as for normal Search.
- [`D1-C387`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **AI Mode**: An audience member asked, in questions submitted before the event, how often Googlebot should be expected to visit a site now that AI Mode has rolled out, and whether AI means more crawling.
- [`D1-C388`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **AI Mode**: AI Mode is a feature that sits on top of Google's existing crawling infrastructure, so Google does not crawl a site more because of AI Mode.
- [`D1-C409`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) **AI Mode**: A community speaker argued that the change in search behaviour is not only longer AI Mode queries but conversation: a follow-up such as 'compare these two' relies on the context of earlier turns.
- [`D1-C117`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **AI Mode**: With one in six AI Mode searches being multimodal, original images with descriptive file names, alt text and captions feed AI answers as well as image search.

- [`D2-C072`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **AI Mode**: The nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search.

- [`D2-C074`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **AI Mode**: Google's AI features guide says a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, with no additional technical requirements.
- [`D2-C075`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **AI Mode**: Before adding nosnippet or a low max-snippet value, weigh the cost in AI features: both limit how much of the page AI Overviews and AI Mode can use, and John Mueller described those answers as built from snippets.

- [`D2-C103`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **AI Mode**: Setting the Search generative AI control in Search Console to exclude keeps a site's links and content out of Search generative AI features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode, so the site gets no traffic or impressions from them; include is the default.
- [`D2-C116`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **AI Mode**: AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on top of Search results: they are a different experience of the same content Google already has.
- [`D2-C117`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **AI Mode**: AI Overviews and AI Mode typically do not ground their answers by reading pages live, unlike Gemini when a user asks about a specific page, Google said.
- [`D2-C453`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **AI Mode**: AI Overviews and AI Mode launched as fairly text-heavy answers with little image content and few tables, and they have become more structured over time because that is what users want.
- [`D2-C476`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **AI Mode**: The structured data Google processes is not fed very differently to AI Overviews and AI Mode: after cleaning and quality work, the same data goes to both the classic results page and the AI features.
- [`D2-C601`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **AI Mode**: Sites need no extra work to appear in AI Overviews and AI Mode: both work on top of the existing web results, so what works for web results also works for the AI features.

- [`D2-C726`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Mode**: AI Overviews and AI Mode use the same index structures and token-based snippets as classic web results, a point Google called important but not obvious.
- [`D2-C727`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Mode**: Google said that when AI Overviews or AI Mode run a query fan-out, the generated queries are sent to Google's Search index and documents come back with their snippets, which then feed the AI-generated answer (part of this passage is unclear in the recording).
- [`D2-C728`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Mode**: Google's robots meta tag specification says the nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode, and max-snippet also limits how much of it may be used that way.
- [`D2-C729`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Mode**: Google says query fan-out in AI Overviews and AI Mode issues related searches across subtopics and several data sources, which for AI Mode include the Knowledge Graph and shopping data as well as web content (AI Mode launch post, March 2025).
- [`D2-C730`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Mode**: There is no separate AI index to optimise for: when a page never shows up as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode, first check that it is indexed, that no nosnippet rule blocks its snippet and that the site is not excluded in Search Console's generative AI setting, the eligibility conditions Google lists.
- [`D2-C731`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Mode**: Treat nosnippet, data-nosnippet and max-snippet as AI visibility settings too: Google lists them as the controls for content in AI features, and if AI answers are built from index snippets, as Google said on stage, a blocked or shortened snippet leaves AI Overviews and AI Mode less to use.
- [`D2-C750`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **AI Mode**: Google's Trends FAQ says Google Trends filters out searches made by Google products and services, including the internal searches made by AI Mode and AI Overviews.
- [`D3-C056`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **AI Mode**: Google's generative AI features in Search build on the traditional ways of searching, so query understanding also flows into AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D3-C093`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **AI Mode**: Google's Search Console help says AI Mode groups the user's question into subtopics and searches for each one simultaneously, and that a follow-up question in AI Mode is essentially a new query.

- [`D3-C325`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **AI Mode**: AI Mode and AI Overviews are not rich results but standard search features: they need no structured data to function and work with the normal text results from Google's index.
- [`D3-C326`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **AI Mode**: Google's AI features guide says there are no additional requirements, and no special schema.org structured data, needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode; a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet.
- [`D3-C327`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **AI Mode**: Google said that if AI Mode one day showcases images, recipes or similar elements, those parts would need structured data, but in their current form AI Mode and AI Overviews require pretty much nothing extra.

- [`D3-C361`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **AI Mode**: On 11 January 2026 Google announced 'dozens of new data attributes' in Merchant Center for conversational commerce on AI Mode, Gemini and Business Agent, to roll out first with a small group of retailers.
- [`D3-C367`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **AI Mode**: Google's Merchant Center help marks the question_and_answer, document_link, related_product and popularity_rank attributes as primarily intended for conversational experiences such as AI Mode in Google Search.

- [`D2-C075`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **AI Overviews**: Before adding nosnippet or a low max-snippet value, weigh the cost in AI features: both limit how much of the page AI Overviews and AI Mode can use, and John Mueller described those answers as built from snippets.
- [`D2-C083`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **AI Overviews**: John Mueller said, hedging with 'I think', that the max-snippet limit also applies to AI Overviews and AI Mode.

- [`D2-C116`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **AI Overviews**: AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on top of Search results: they are a different experience of the same content Google already has.

- [`D2-C601`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **AI Overviews**: Sites need no extra work to appear in AI Overviews and AI Mode: both work on top of the existing web results, so what works for web results also works for the AI features.
- [`D2-C607`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **AI Overviews**: Check AI Overviews and AI Mode with native-language queries in each target market, not with translated English keywords, and compare with the country breakdown of Search Console's generative AI performance report; topics where competitors are cited and you are not point to missing or weak local content.
- [`D2-C726`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Overviews**: AI Overviews and AI Mode use the same index structures and token-based snippets as classic web results, a point Google called important but not obvious.
- [`D2-C727`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Overviews**: Google said that when AI Overviews or AI Mode run a query fan-out, the generated queries are sent to Google's Search index and documents come back with their snippets, which then feed the AI-generated answer (part of this passage is unclear in the recording).
- [`D2-C728`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Overviews**: Google's robots meta tag specification says the nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode, and max-snippet also limits how much of it may be used that way.

- [`D2-C730`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Overviews**: There is no separate AI index to optimise for: when a page never shows up as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode, first check that it is indexed, that no nosnippet rule blocks its snippet and that the site is not excluded in Search Console's generative AI setting, the eligibility conditions Google lists.
- [`D2-C731`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **AI Overviews**: Treat nosnippet, data-nosnippet and max-snippet as AI visibility settings too: Google lists them as the controls for content in AI features, and if AI answers are built from index snippets, as Google said on stage, a blocked or shortened snippet leaves AI Overviews and AI Mode less to use.
- [`D2-C750`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **AI Overviews**: Google's Trends FAQ says Google Trends filters out searches made by Google products and services, including the internal searches made by AI Mode and AI Overviews.
- [`D3-C056`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **AI Overviews**: Google's generative AI features in Search build on the traditional ways of searching, so query understanding also flows into AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D3-C095`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **AI Overviews**: No Google documentation states that fan-out queries stay out of Search Console, but the docs fit the stage statement: the Performance report counts AI Overviews and AI Mode under the user's own queries, and the Generative AI reports have no query dimension.
- [`D3-C325`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **AI Overviews**: AI Mode and AI Overviews are not rich results but standard search features: they need no structured data to function and work with the normal text results from Google's index.
- [`D3-C326`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **AI Overviews**: Google's AI features guide says there are no additional requirements, and no special schema.org structured data, needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode; a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet.
- [`D3-C327`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **AI Overviews**: Google said that if AI Mode one day showcases images, recipes or similar elements, those parts would need structured data, but in their current form AI Mode and AI Overviews require pretty much nothing extra.
- [`D3-C328`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **AI Overviews**: Day 2 said the structured data Google processes also feeds AI Overviews and AI Mode (D2-C476), while Day 3 said these features do not need structured data to function: markup is not a condition for appearing in AI features, but data taken from it can still reach them.

- [`D3-C498`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **AI Overviews**: Google's AI features guide says traffic from sites appearing in AI features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode is included in the overall search traffic in Search Console and reported in the Performance report within the Web search type.

### Allow (`allow`): 11

- [`D1-C083`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: Under the example file, Googlebot may crawl /, /politics/eu-vote and /sports/live/, and is blocked from /?utm_source=x, /index.html, /politics (no trailing slash), /live/ and /sports/live-score. An 'allow: /$' rule does not cover the homepage with tracking parameters.
- [`D1-C084`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
- [`D1-C516`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: Robots.txt was made extremely simple by design so that anyone could implement and understand it; it was extended as websites grew more complex, but it still has only three rules: user-agent (a named crawler, or * for every crawler), disallow and allow.
- [`D1-C517`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: Everything on a site is implicitly allowed, so an allow rule is only needed to re-open a specific path inside a disallowed one.
- [`D1-C519`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: A user-agent line with its allow and disallow rules forms a user-agent group, and one group can name several crawlers (the talk's example: Googlebot and Bingbot); give named crawlers their own group only when they need rules the * group should not grant to every crawler.
- [`D1-C520`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: In the talk's worked example, disallow /*/live/ blocks /science/live/ and /sports/live/, because * matches any number of characters, and an allow /science/live/ rule re-opens that one path.
- [`D1-C521`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: To let unnamed crawlers fetch only the homepage, use user-agent: *, disallow: / and allow: /$; the $ ends the match, so /$ means only the root path and /cats$ means exactly /cats.
- [`D1-C531`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: In the talk's quiz, the answer for letting Googlebot crawl /staging/preview/ while keeping the rest of /staging/ closed to it was a user-agent: googlebot group with both rules, disallow /staging/ and allow /staging/preview/, rather than an allow in the * group or a Googlebot group with only the allow.
- [`D1-C532`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **allow**: A typo in a rule name is not always ignored by Google: its open-source robots.txt parser deliberately accepts common misspellings of disallow (such as dissallow, dissalow and disalow) and of user-agent (useragent, user agent), but not of allow. Google's spec page does not mention typos, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.
- [`D2-C207`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **allow**: If an API folder must stay blocked in robots.txt, allow the endpoints that rendering needs, for example Disallow: /api/ together with Allow: /api/products/.
- [`D2-C208`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Allow**: A robots.txt carve-out works because Google applies the most specific matching rule, so Allow: /api/products/ beats Disallow: /api/ for product endpoints only; re-test a rendered page after every robots.txt change to script or API paths.

### Canonicalization (`canonicalization`): 69

- [`D1-C207`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **canonical URL**: Google clusters duplicate pages and selects one page per cluster as its representative, the canonical URL, so that users are not shown duplicates.
- [`D1-C421`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) **canonicalization**: Of the two answers a community speaker offered for a request to a URL variant (redirect, or an error page), Google's canonicalization guide favours the redirect: a redirect is a strong signal that its target should become canonical, while an error page throws away any links pointing at the variant.
- [`D1-C128`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **canonicalization**: Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.
- [`D1-C113`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **canonical**: The real cost of duplicates is control and crawling: Google may choose a canonical you did not want, and every copy is still crawled. Copied or scraped content is a separate spam-policy issue.
- [`D2-C031`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **canonical URL**: Google extracts the rel=canonical link, through which site owners state their preferred canonical URL, and uses it in deduplication and in canonical selection.
- [`D2-C310`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **canonicalization**: Google's canonicalization guide says that when Google indexes a page it determines the page's primary content, which it also calls the centerpiece, and clusters pages whose primary content is the same or very similar.
- [`D2-C347`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google's speaker said what SEOs call the canonical is, for Google, the representative of a cluster of duplicate pages: the URL Google would ideally show.
- [`D2-C357`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google's redirects guide says Google keeps track of both the source and the target of a redirect: one becomes the canonical, depending on signals such as whether the redirect is permanent or temporary, and the other becomes an alternate name that may appear in results when a query suggests the user trusts the old URL more. After a move to a new domain, old URLs may still show occasionally; the guide calls this normal.
- [`D2-C359`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonicalization**: Google's duplication talk described three related parts of deduplication: building clusters, localization, and selecting the representative URL, which is the canonicalization site owners see in Search Console.
- [`D2-C362`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Whether a redirect is permanent or temporary matters only for choosing the canonical, not for clustering the URLs together.
- [`D2-C363`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Use permanent redirects (301 or 308) for moves you want reflected in Search: a temporary redirect still groups the URLs, but it changes which URL Google is likely to pick as the canonical.
- [`D2-C368`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google sometimes picks a canonical that looks unrelated because it recognised a URL pattern: if /buy/fax, /buy/typewriter and /office-equipment show the same content, its systems may assume any /buy/ URL, even /buy/seo-service, shows that same office-equipment content without looking at the page.
- [`D2-C372`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Make location and variant pages differ in their main content (local stock, staff, prices, addresses) and return 404 for empty or invalid combinations; otherwise every URL that fits the pattern can be folded into one canonical.
- [`D2-C373`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonicalization**: Google's canonicalization troubleshooting guide says fixing a wrong duplicate cluster comes down to making the clustered pages sufficiently different; pages split out faster when the difference is clear and significant, and Google may keep pages in a duplicate cluster for up to two weeks after a fix.
- [`D2-C379`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: rel=canonical is probably the most common way site owners signal duplicates, but it is very often wrong, for example a tag whose value reads 'canonical target' instead of a real URL (the example is partly unclear in the recording), so Google can only sometimes trust it.
- [`D2-C380`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Many SEOs assume Google must follow their rel=canonical, but because people sometimes get it wrong, Google has to make its own judgment about the canonical.
- [`D2-C385`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google's canonical guide says that for canonicalization Google prefers URLs that are part of hreflang clusters: if German pages for Germany and Switzerland point to each other with hreflang but not to the Austrian page, the German and Swiss pages are preferred as canonicals.
- [`D2-C386`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google picks the canonical from a variety of criteria and uses some kind of machine learning to decide how much weight each criterion gets; the weighting changes from time to time.
- [`D2-C388`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google watches for canonical hijacking, where several domains try to be canonical for the same content, whether accidentally across a site owner's own domains (such as a staging copy) or through third-party domains, maliciously or not, and asks site owners to report cases it gets wrong.
- [`D2-C389`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Whether a page can load is really important for canonical selection: a broken certificate, failing JavaScript or a page that cannot be loaded counts against a URL, and the slide also listed meta refresh and security.
- [`D2-C390`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Clear site-owner signals about which URL should be canonical make a big difference to Google's choice; the speaker named redirects, listing only the preferred URL in sitemaps, and rel=canonical, which the speaker said also helps a bit.
- [`D2-C391`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google's canonical guide ranks the ways to signal a preferred canonical by strength: redirects and rel=canonical annotations are strong signals, sitemap inclusion is a weak signal, and combining methods makes them more effective.
- [`D2-C392`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google's duplication talk described rel=canonical as something that 'also helps a bit', while Google's canonical guide calls it a strong signal alongside redirects and calls sitemap inclusion weak; treat redirects and rel=canonical as the main levers and sitemaps as support.
- [`D2-C393`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonicalization**: Google's speaker said that pointing rel=canonical from the pages of a paginated set to the first page can sometimes make sense depending on the goal, for example to make a category page more visible, but that it affects canonicalization and deduplication.
- [`D2-C394`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google's pagination guide still says not to use page 1 as the canonical of a paginated series, so keep self-referencing canonicals on paginated pages unless you deliberately want later pages folded into page 1 and the items they list are linked from elsewhere.
- [`D2-C396`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Google's closing suggestions on duplication: use redirects for site migrations, use HTTP result codes, don't block agents, check your rel=canonical links, use hreflang links to help Google localize, report weird canonicals in the forums, make secure pages that work, and keep canonical signals clear.
- [`D2-C399`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: When all canonical signals point to the same URL, Google follows what the site owner says; when they point in different directions, Google cannot tell what the owner wants.
- [`D2-C400`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **canonical**: Before a migration or template change, align every canonical signal for the preferred URL (redirects, rel=canonical, internal links, sitemap entries, hreflang and working HTTPS); Google says it follows the site owner only when the signals agree.
- [`D2-C403`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical URLs**: Google's guide to specifying canonical URLs says Google supports explicit rel=canonical link annotations as described in RFC 6596, the canonical link relation specification.
- [`D2-C404`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A broken canonical setup does not fail visibly: pages still load normally while the choice of URL passes to the search engine's own heuristics, so canonical tags need a regular audit with a crawler and the URL Inspection tool.
- [`D2-C406`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: Checking canonicals pairwise (page A has a canonical to page B, page B a self-referencing canonical) is common but, in a community speaker's experience, misses the bigger picture, such as other links pointing to A or B.
- [`D2-C407`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: In a community speaker's terms, a canonical group is the set of all URLs connected through canonical links, and its canonical leader is the page that all the group's canonical links ultimately point to.
- [`D2-C408`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A community speaker advised auditing canonicals as whole canonical groups rather than pair by pair, paying special attention to each group's canonical leader.
- [`D2-C409`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A community speaker said it helps to view small canonical groups as a graph that shows any redirects between members, together with the indexability of each member page.
- [`D2-C410`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A crawler report shown on screen drew one canonical group of five URLs as a link graph with the leader marked by a crown, and listed each member's HTTP status, indexability, document language, leader flag, incoming and outgoing links, and hints.
- [`D2-C411`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: The crawler report shown on screen ran group-level checks on each canonical group: an overall group status, whether the leader has self links, whether languages are consistent across members, and whether the group contains a chain.
- [`D2-C412`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: In the real-world canonical group shown on screen (a German-language travel magazine section, site not named), a feed URL's canonical pointed to a URL on another subdomain that 301-redirected to the leader, a canonical chain through a server-side redirect.
- [`D2-C413`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: The crawler report shown on screen rated a canonical group member that issues a redirect instead of displaying content as an error, and flagged canonical links whose target returns a non-200 status or is itself a redirect.
- [`D2-C414`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical URL**: Google's 2009 Search Central blog post introducing rel=canonical says a canonical URL may be a URL that redirects: Google then processes the redirect as usual.
- [`D2-C417`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: Multiple canonical declarations on one page conflict and are invalid, so the search engine applies its own heuristic and picks the canonical for the site owner; a page should declare only one canonical.
- [`D2-C418`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: Google's 2013 Search Central blog post on rel=canonical mistakes says to specify no more than one rel=canonical per page: when a page has more than one, Google will likely ignore all of them, and any benefit of a legitimate canonical is lost.
- [`D2-C419`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Canonical**: Canonical chains, where a page's canonical target leads on to yet another URL, are named as improper use in the canonical link specification, according to a community speaker.
- [`D2-C420`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: Google's 2009 Search Central blog post introducing rel=canonical says Google's algorithm is lenient and can follow canonical chains, but strongly recommends updating links to point to a single canonical page for optimal canonicalization.
- [`D2-C421`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Canonical**: Canonical chains can run through canonical links alone, through a server-side redirect between members, or through a client-side redirect between members.
- [`D2-C422`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: The crawler report shown on screen flagged a canonical chain as a problem: canonical links that form a chain instead of all pointing directly to the group's canonical leader.
- [`D2-C424`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Canonical**: Canonical loops, such as two HTML pages whose canonical tags point to each other, are a structural conflict: the group has no canonical leader, so its canonical information cannot be used.
- [`D2-C425`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Canonical**: Canonical loops can also run through server-side or client-side redirects, not only through canonical tags.
- [`D2-C426`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A community speaker said that at best a search engine's heuristic would treat a canonical loop through redirects as self-referencing canonicals, and doubted that this is often done when the loop runs through a client-side redirect.
- [`D2-C427`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: When internal links point only to page A and the canonical leader is reached only through A's canonical link, the leader is reachable by machines but not by human visitors, a signal conflict that asks the search engine to index a page users cannot reach.
- [`D2-C428`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: For a canonical leader that users cannot reach through links, a community speaker suggested revisiting the canonical graph and probably making the internally linked page the leader instead.
- [`D2-C429`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A community speaker said pages carry different link equity, and a canonical leader that is not the strongest page in its group is technically valid but most likely suboptimal for ranking, so the strongest page should be the leader.
- [`D2-C430`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical URLs**: Google's guide to specifying canonical URLs says a canonical helps consolidate signals for duplicate pages: links to a duplicate URL are consolidated with links to the preferred URL once the preferred URL becomes canonical.
- [`D2-C431`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A leader reachable only through a canonical and a leader with weak link equity share one fix: point internal links, sitemap entries and redirects at the URL chosen as canonical, so the leader is both reachable for users and the strongest page in its group.
- [`D2-C432`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: The canonical leader of a group should be indexable: it should carry no noindex robots directive, return no error status code and not be blocked in robots.txt.
- [`D2-C433`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: Canonical links between different language versions of a page are a misuse: if a search engine accepted such a canonical group, only one language version would rank.
- [`D2-C435`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical URLs**: Google's guide to specifying canonical URLs says that on pages using hreflang, the canonical should be a page in the same language, or the best possible substitute language if no canonical page exists in the same language.
- [`D2-C436`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: Check that every canonical group contains a single document language: a group spanning languages means canonicals are joining versions that hreflang should connect, and each language version should keep its own self-referencing canonical.
- [`D2-C437`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: In a community speaker's experience, real-world canonical graphs are far more complex than the isolated examples in the talk and commonly mix several canonical problems at once.
- [`D2-C438`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: A community speaker advised fixing canonical chains by cleaning up the canonical graph so that every canonical link points directly to the canonical leader.
- [`D2-C439`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical**: The crawler report shown at the talk rated a redirecting canonical target as an error, while Google's 2009 guidance accepts a canonical URL that redirects and says Google can follow canonical chains; the gap is one of severity, since both recommend pointing every canonical link straight at the final URL.
- [`D2-C440`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonicalization**: Google says canonicalization consolidates link signals from duplicates into the chosen canonical, so a leader with few links of its own is not necessarily weaker once Google accepts it; the practical risk of a weakly linked leader is that Google, treating rel=canonical as a hint, picks a different page as canonical.
- [`D2-C450`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **canonical**: Because Google extracts structured data, images and videos only after deduplication, put markup and media on the URL you want as canonical and keep them identical on its duplicates; markup that exists only on a duplicate that loses canonical selection may never be extracted.
- [`D2-C451`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **canonical**: Google's general structured data guidelines recommend placing the same structured data on all duplicate pages of the same content, not just on the canonical page.
- [`D2-C702`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **canonical**: Google's documentation says a search result usually points to the canonical page, but the other pages in a duplicate cluster are alternate versions that may be served in different contexts, for example a mobile page for a user on a mobile device.
- [`D3-C640`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **canonical URL**: A change of canonical URL usually takes one to three weeks to show, though it can happen in seconds because Google allocates enough resources to canonicalization.
- [`D3-C641`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **canonicalization**: Gary Illyes said he had updated Google's documentation about canonicalization changes about a month before the event (around early September 2026).
- [`D3-C642`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **canonicalization**: Google treats a site move as a complex canonicalization process in which every signal of the old site is recalculated and moved to the new one, and every indexing process has to run.
- [`D3-C669`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **canonicalization**: Google's guide to fixing canonicalization issues says that even after content issues are fixed, Google might hold pages in a duplicate cluster for up to two weeks, and that pages split out faster when they differ clearly and significantly.
- [`D3-C670`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **canonicalization**: The canonicalization documentation update mentioned on stage appears in Google's documentation changelog on 10 July 2026 (re-evaluation time, page last updated 21 August 2026), earlier than 'about a month' before the event; its 'up to two weeks' sits at the short end of the one to three weeks said on stage.

### CDN (`cdn`): 18

- [`D1-C360`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **CDN**: When Search Console reports network errors, the first step Google recommends is to ask the hosting provider, or the CDN, whether they changed anything.
- [`D1-C361`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **CDN**: Network timeouts are usually caused close to the site, very often by a firewall, a CDN, the hosting provider or the DNS provider, and Google has no visibility into them.
- [`D1-C363`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **CDN**: For DNS and network errors caused by a firewall or CDN, Google advises checking whether new firewall rules were set recently and otherwise asking in the CDN's forum, as Google itself cannot see or help with these errors.
- [`D1-C364`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **CDN**: A rise in HTTP errors in crawl reports can come from a CDN throttling crawlers by injecting 429 or 503 responses on the network path between Google's crawler and the site.
- [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **CDN**: CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D1-C371`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **CDN**: Day 1 said a CDN captcha page served with HTTP 200 becomes a soft 404, while Day 2 (D2-C374, D2-C375) said such challenge pages are hard to recognise as errors and can be clustered as duplicates; Google's CDN post describes both outcomes, and in both the real pages drop out of Search.
- [`D1-C088`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **CDN**: Content-Signal lines are now common because a large CDN provider adds them to its managed robots.txt files. Never place any non-standard directive between user-agent lines; put it after a group's rules and test the file with each search engine's tools, such as Bing's robots.txt tester and Google's open-source robots.txt parser.
- [`D1-C529`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **CDNs**: Google said the robots.txt report helps catch CDNs that update a site's robots.txt without the owner's knowledge, and hosts that cloak the robots.txt file, which happens more often than people think.
- [`D1-C376`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **CDN**: Hostload applies per host, not necessarily per site: depending on how a site is configured, its CDN, its app, its subdomains and its main www host may be different hosts.
- [`D1-C077`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **CDN**: This does not mean avoiding HTTP/3, which benefits browsers. The rule is never to run a host that only answers over HTTP/3, and to check that CDN or firewall rules written for HTTP/3 traffic do not break HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.
- [`D2-C105`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **CDN**: Set max-snippet:-1 and max-image-preview:large on every indexable template unless licensing requires otherwise, and check that no CMS, plug-in or CDN setting adds lower snippet or image preview limits by default.
- [`D2-C210`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **CDN**: An API or CDN on its own host needs its own robots.txt check: a blanket Disallow there, or a robots.txt that returns 5xx errors, can stop Google fetching the data a page renders from.
- [`D2-C298`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **CDN**: Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
- [`D2-C374`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **CDN**: A growing cause of wrong clustering is bot protection: when a CDN or another protection system shows Googlebot the same 'you look like a bot, solve this puzzle' page on many unrelated URLs or domains, Google can cluster those pages as duplicates.
- [`D2-C376`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **CDNs**: Google's Search Central post on CDNs says that if Google cannot recognise an error message served with a 200 status as an error, all pages showing the same message may be dropped from the index as duplicates, and recovery can be slow because Google has little incentive to recrawl duplicates. For bot-verification interstitials it recommends sending crawlers a 503 status.
- [`D2-C378`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **CDN**: Check what your CDN or bot protection serves to verified Googlebot and to the AI agents you want to allow; if crawlers must get a challenge page, return it with a 503 status as Google recommends, never as a 200 page across many URLs, which Google may cluster as duplicates.
- [`D2-C920`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **content delivery network**: Serving videos from a content delivery network (CDN) that loads them faster than the site's own server is a win for video SEO, Gary Illyes said.
- [`D2-C593`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **CDNs**: Google's documentation calls a ccTLD a strong signal that a site is meant for a certain country and still lists server location as a possible signal of a site's audience, though not a definitive one because sites use CDNs or are hosted abroad; it does not rank the signals.

### Chrome (`chrome`): 13

- [`D1-C249`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Chrome**: A community demo showed a script that opens Chrome with a saved session, pastes a URL into Google's Rich Results Test, waits about 15 seconds, then screenshots and saves the result and retries on failure (the demo's recording is largely unintelligible; the tool name is a best reading).
- [`D1-C316`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Chrome**: Chrome's WebMCP documentation describes WebMCP as a proposed web standard that site owners can test through an origin trial starting in Chrome 149 or through a Chrome flag for local development.
- [`D1-C460`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Chrome**: Chrome's Lighthouse documentation lists an llms.txt audit among its agentic browsing audits: it flags a server error when llms.txt is fetched and marks the audit not applicable when the file is missing, because providing the file is optional for now.
- [`D2-C094`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Chrome**: John Mueller said notranslate can also be set in a meta tag named google, and that in that form it also turns off Chrome's automatic translation of the page.
- [`D2-C098`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Chrome**: International sites should remove notranslate from their templates unless translation must be prevented: the robots or googlebot form switches off Google Search's translation features, and John Mueller said the form named google also blocks Chrome's translation for visitors who do not read the language.
- [`D2-C126`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Chrome**: Google renders pages with Chromium, the browser technology that also underlies Chrome, Edge and other Chromium-based browsers.
- [`D2-C162`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Chrome**: A community speaker strongly advised SEOs to use Chrome DevTools more often to understand what happens when their pages render.
- [`D2-C180`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Chrome**: If content is missing from the rendered HTML, find the script responsible in Chrome DevTools: open the Network tab, filter by Fetch/XHR and reload the page.
- [`D2-C181`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Chrome**: For each suspect script or API request in Chrome DevTools, check whether it runs, whether something blocks it and whether robots.txt disallows it.
- [`D2-C860`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Chrome**: Besides using Chrome DevTools more often, a community speaker advised checking rendering at scale with a modern crawler.
- [`D2-C465`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Chrome**: Gemini in Chrome relies heavily on the screenshot it takes of a page.
- [`D3-C458`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Chrome**: Multimodal searches reported in Search Console include searches with Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android, images uploaded to Google Search and Chrome's right-click search on an image.
- [`D3-C461`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Chrome**: In a demo, asking Chrome about an image on a web page opened a side panel of visual matches, one of which was on Google's developers site and led on to more information about Search Console; Google described this as the full flow of the multimodal traffic now reported.

### Core updates (`core-updates`): 28

- [`D3-C244`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google's slide said the more people post on the internet, the more saturated topics become and the harder it gets to find the highest quality content, so Google might launch core updates to improve the quality and relevance of search results.
- [`D3-C250`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: Every kind of Search update, whether a feature launch, a core update or a spam update, has the same goal: satisfying users' information needs with better results.
- [`D3-C258`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google stressed that core updates are not punitive: they are not meant to punish any site but to improve how results are surfaced.
- [`D3-C259`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Several times a year Google makes significant, broad changes to its search algorithms and systems, which it calls core updates.
- [`D3-C260`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google announces core updates when they happen by posting them on the Google Search Status Dashboard.
- [`D3-C261`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: As of 3 October 2026, the Ranking history of Google's Search Status Dashboard lists two core updates in 2026 (March and May) and four spam updates (March, June, August and September).
- [`D3-C262`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **Core updates**: Core updates do not target specific sites; they change how Google assesses certain properties of content.
- [`D3-C263`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: A core update may reward pages that were previously under-rewarded, so when some pages go down after a core update, other pages must go up.
- [`D3-C264`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: Pages that perform worse after a core update usually do not violate Google's spam policies; Google has changed, perhaps slightly, how it thinks about quality.
- [`D3-C265`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: Google sometimes couples a core update with an update to its Search Quality Rater Guidelines.
- [`D3-C266`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google's 2019 post on core updates says Google tests any broad core update before it goes live, including feedback from its search quality raters, whose data is not used directly in ranking.
- [`D3-C267`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: The purpose of core updates is to improve the quality and relevance of search results for users.
- [`D3-C268`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: Answering the common question whether to fix individual pages or the whole site after a core update, Google advised taking a close look at the site as a whole and trying to be objective.
- [`D3-C269`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: Because owners struggle to judge their own site objectively, the speaker suggested asking someone else to review the site after a core update drop.
- [`D3-C270`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: To improve a site after a core update, check whether users can complete their information journey on the site and ask users directly, for example with customer satisfaction (CSAT) surveys, then improve based on the answers.
- [`D3-C272`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google's core updates page recommends waiting at least a full week after a core update has finished rolling out before analysing Search Console data, then comparing that week with a week before the update started.
- [`D3-C273`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google's core updates page says a small drop in position after a core update (for example from 2 to 4) needs no drastic action, while a large drop (for example from 4 to 29) calls for a deeper assessment.
- [`D3-C293`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: A ranking drop after a core update is not a penalty, so technically there is no recovery from a core update in the way there is after a spam update.
- [`D3-C294`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: After a core update a site can win back some of its rankings by improving the site as a whole.
- [`D3-C295`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google's core updates page says improvements can take effect in a few days but may take several months for its systems to confirm that the site as a whole produces helpful content, sometimes only at the next core update.
- [`D3-C296`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core updates**: Google's core updates page says Google also makes smaller core updates that are not announced, and these can also lift a site that has improved.
- [`D3-C297`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: A drop after a core update can simply mean that a competitor now does better because Google rethought how it assesses quality as a whole.
- [`D3-C298`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: Google's 'Recoveries' slide advised sites affected by a core update to keep doing a great job, look at what competitors are doing better and learn from sites that are doing better.
- [`D3-C299`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **core update**: After a core update drop, plan a site-wide quality review instead of page-by-page fixes or a technical 'recovery': have someone outside the team assess the site, compare it with the pages that gained, and test whether users can finish their task, for example with short satisfaction surveys.
- [`D3-C661`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **core update**: Google estimated that a core update affects a site within 2 to 4 weeks from the beginning of its rollout.
- [`D3-C662`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **core update**: Recovery after a core update typically takes 3 to 6 months once the site has put in work to regain traffic, and up to 6 months to a year, until the next core update.
- [`D3-C664`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **core update**: Set expectations for recovery work: a manual action can lift within weeks of a real clean-up, but recovery from a core update typically takes 3 to 6 months and may need the next core update, so do not judge quality work within the first weeks.
- [`D3-C705`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **core updates**: Search has changed every year since its start, for example the Florida update in 2003 (before core updates existed), Universal Search and the Knowledge Graph.

### Crawl budget (`crawl-budget-metric`): 39

- [`D1-C073`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **crawl budget**: A soft 404 is a page that returns a success code while its content looks like an error or an empty page. It is kept out of the index but continues to be crawled, wasting crawl budget.
- [`D1-C090`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl budget**: Crawl budget is the combination of crawl rate limit and crawl demand.
- [`D1-C132`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Google's crawl budget guide says each crawler has its own crawl demand, but the crawl capacity limit (hostload) is shared across all crawlers, so high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity left for others.
- [`D1-C096`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl budget**: Crawl budget was described as the attention span Google gives a website, and better performance increases it.
- [`D1-C097`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Google's crawl budget guide is written for sites with over 1 million unique pages that change weekly, over 10,000 pages that change daily, or many URLs reported as 'Discovered – currently not indexed'.
- [`D1-C099`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Three things burn crawl budget: server errors unrelated to server load, useless pages and resources, and infinite URL spaces.
- [`D1-C103`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Four ways to manage crawl budget: use HTTP cache control, have good site navigation, restrict crawlers' access to faceted navigation and action URLs, and improve or remove useless content.
- [`D1-C105`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: URLs disallowed through robots.txt do not affect crawl budget, because they are not fetched.
- [`D1-C106`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: The noindex rule consumes crawl budget, because Google must fetch the page to see it.
- [`D1-C107`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: The nofollow rule can still consume crawl budget: Google does not crawl through the nofollow link itself, but it still crawls the linked page when it finds that page through other links.
- [`D1-C108`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: The non-standard crawl-delay rule is not processed by Googlebot, so it does not save any crawl budget.
- [`D1-C109`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Google advises against using noindex to save crawl budget and against using robots.txt to temporarily reallocate budget. Use robots.txt only for pages you never want crawled, and 404 or 410 for removed pages.
- [`D1-C373`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl budget**: Crawl budget is the finite amount of resources Google allocates to crawling a specific website, and it determines how many of the site's pages are discovered and how often they are revisited.
- [`D1-C378`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Google treats URLs that differ as different URLs and crawls all of them even when they lead to the same content, so infinite URL spaces such as calendars or many versions of a page burn crawl budget.
- [`D1-C379`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: The useless content worth improving or removing to save crawl budget includes very bad or low-quality pages, spam content, duplicate pages and soft error pages.
- [`D1-C380`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: An audience member asked, in a question submitted before the event, whether crawl budget is still an SEO priority in 2026 or only relevant for very large sites.
- [`D1-C381`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Not every site needs to worry about crawl budget, and this has always been so: a site with fewer than a few thousand URLs likely has no crawl budget problem, and a larger site does not necessarily have one either.
- [`D1-C382`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: The stage rule of thumb (under a few thousand URLs crawl budget is unlikely to be a problem) and Google's crawl budget guide (D1-C097: sites with over a million pages that change about weekly, or over 10,000 pages that change daily) leave a middle range where a site should check Search Console's Crawl Stats report before blaming crawl budget for slow indexing.
- [`D1-C383`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: HTTP status codes do not all affect crawl budget in the same way, so knowing what each status code class does is one way to manage crawl budget.
- [`D1-C384`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Every fetch that returns a 2xx success response consumes crawl budget.
- [`D1-C385`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: 4xx responses do not affect a site's crawl budget, because Google expects pages, content and products to come and go as a natural part of the web.
- [`D1-C386`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: The stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget matches Google's documentation that 4xx codes have no effect on crawl rate (D1-C072), with one exception: 429 Too Many Requests counts as a server error and slows crawling like a 5xx (D1-C071, D1-C092).
- [`D1-C393`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: To check whether a site has a crawl budget problem, use Search Console's crawl report (Crawl Stats), which breaks crawl requests down by response and by file type and shows crawl problems Google finds.
- [`D1-C395`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: Google advised checking crawl data in Search Console now and then without obsessing over crawl budget.
- [`D1-C419`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: A 404 fetch is still a fetch: Google's 2017 crawl budget post says generally any URL Googlebot crawls counts towards a site's crawl budget, so the stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget is best read as 'they do not slow crawling, and a 404 tells Google to crawl that URL less over time'.
- [`D1-C420`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl budget**: The stage remark that crawl demand follows the quality of the site as a whole sits beside the same talk's slide (D1-C094), which falls back to the parent path's aggregate only when a URL's own quality is unknown, and Google's crawl budget guide lists page quality among the demand factors; read it as site quality setting the baseline while known URL-level signals still count.
- [`D1-C441`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: An audience member asked how to tell, from log files or by other methods, whether Google is spending crawl budget inefficiently on a site.
- [`D1-C445`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: One fix for parameter variants of a URL is to work out the normalised URL and redirect the variants to it: the redirects cost crawl budget at first, but leave the site with a clean slate.
- [`D1-C465`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: An audience member asked how a large news site can tell whether crawl budget is limiting how fast new articles are discovered (within minutes), and which statistics in Search Console and the logs show this.
- [`D1-C466`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: Gary Illyes said news sites rarely need to worry about crawl budget, because Google crawls them aggressively given their constant flow of new content and new URLs.
- [`D1-C469`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site.
- [`D1-C470`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: Google's crawl budget guide says crawl budget freed by robots.txt blocks is not shifted to other pages unless the site already hits its crawl capacity limit, and advises against robots.txt for temporary reallocation; so block only sections you never want crawled, and expect a shift only on capacity-limited sites.
- [`D1-C545`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem.
- [`D1-C539`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: A Google panelist said useless plugin-generated parameter URLs can be handled at the web server, for example with a rule or a custom module in Apache, which saves crawl budget so that Google may pick up the URLs that matter instead (the exact mechanism is not clear in the recording).
- [`D1-C547`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl budget**: Google's crawl budget guide does not express the crawl capacity limit in requests per second: it limits the total time a server spends holding connections open for Google, counting both the number of parallel connections and their duration. That fits the panel's advice to watch how many connections Googlebot opens (D1-C494): fewer connections is the documented form of a lower capacity limit.
- [`D2-C848`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **crawl budget**: Google said it strongly believes site owners should be able to opt out of crawling and control how their site is crawled, which can matter for legal reasons or for crawl budget.
- [`D2-C886`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **crawl budget**: A community speaker listed the technical SEO goals of a two-site consolidation as lighter pages, faster loading and no crawl budget spent on content that no longer mattered.
- [`D2-C914`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **crawl budget**: Google's crawl budget guide is written for sites with over a million pages changing weekly or over 10,000 pages changing daily, so for a consolidation of about 2,000 URLs the crawl-budget gain is likely minor; the benefit of pruning such a site more plausibly comes from one strong URL per intent and consolidated signals.
- [`D2-C708`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **crawl budget**: The help page explains 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by expected server overload (capacity), while on stage it was explained as Google not wanting the URL yet (demand); the crawl budget guide covers both, so first rule out slow responses and server errors, then treat the status as a quality and demand problem.

### Crawl capacity limit (`crawl-capacity-limit`): 18

- [`D1-C090`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl rate limit**: Crawl budget is the combination of crawl rate limit and crawl demand.
- [`D1-C091`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl rate limit**: Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a host-wide metric shared across all Google crawlers.
- [`D1-C132`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl capacity limit**: Google's crawl budget guide says each crawler has its own crawl demand, but the crawl capacity limit (hostload) is shared across all crawlers, so high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity left for others.
- [`D1-C092`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Hostload**: Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down.
- [`D1-C374`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl rate limit**: Crawl rate limit, or hostload, is a proxy for how many requests per second the connection to a site can handle before Google hits the limit.
- [`D1-C376`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Hostload**: Hostload applies per host, not necessarily per site: depending on how a site is configured, its CDN, its app, its subdomains and its main www host may be different hosts.
- [`D1-C439`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity**: Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites.
- [`D1-C470`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity limit**: Google's crawl budget guide says crawl budget freed by robots.txt blocks is not shifted to other pages unless the site already hits its crawl capacity limit, and advises against robots.txt for temporary reallocation; so block only sections you never want crawled, and expect a shift only on capacity-limited sites.
- [`D1-C545`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity limit**: An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem.
- [`D1-C493`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity limit**: There is no easy way to tell whether a drop in Google's crawling comes from lower crawl demand or a lower crawl capacity limit; most of the time a capacity-limit drop is an abrupt step down.
- [`D1-C494`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity limit**: To check whether Google lowered a site's crawl capacity limit, look at the number of connections Googlebot opens to the site: if it has dropped, the capacity limit changed.
- [`D1-C538`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity**: A Google panelist said crawl demand is not only Search's: when enough of a site's URLs are wanted by Search, Google Ads or another Google product, Google raises the site's crawl demand and crawls up to that level of demand as far as the site's crawl capacity allows.
- [`D1-C546`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity limit**: A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear).
- [`D1-C547`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl capacity limit**: Google's crawl budget guide does not express the crawl capacity limit in requests per second: it limits the total time a server spends holding connections open for Google, counting both the number of parallel connections and their duration. That fits the panel's advice to watch how many connections Googlebot opens (D1-C494): fewer connections is the documented form of a lower capacity limit.
- [`D3-C617`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **crawl capacity**: Google's crawl chart puts a crawl capacity update at seconds when backing off, typically 4 hours or 1-2 weeks, and 1-3 weeks in recovery.
- [`D3-C618`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **crawl capacity**: When a site starts serving 500 errors, Google lowers the crawl capacity allocated to the site within about four hours on average.
- [`D3-C619`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **crawl capacity**: Increases in crawl capacity take longer than decreases, within one to three weeks, because Google first needs to know that the higher demand will last.
- [`D3-C620`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **crawl capacity**: A continuously running process recalculates each site's crawl capacity within a month, so a capacity change takes up to about a month at most.

### Crawl demand (`crawl-demand-metric`): 15

- [`D1-C067`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **crawl demand**: A page with no internal links depends on sitemaps alone to be found, so it is discovered slowly and attracts little crawl demand.
- [`D1-C090`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl demand**: Crawl budget is the combination of crawl rate limit and crawl demand.
- [`D1-C132`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl demand**: Google's crawl budget guide says each crawler has its own crawl demand, but the crawl capacity limit (hostload) is shared across all crawlers, so high demand from one crawler can reduce the capacity left for others.
- [`D1-C093`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl demand**: Crawl demand is driven by the quality of the site, the change frequency of its URLs and their popularity on the internet.
