- [`D1-C095`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl demand**: New content inherits its starting crawl demand from the folder it sits in. Put new high-value content under sections Google already rates well, not under weak ones.
- [`D1-C377`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl demand**: The quality that drives crawl demand is the quality of the site as a whole, not the quality of an individual page.
- [`D1-C420`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **crawl demand**: The stage remark that crawl demand follows the quality of the site as a whole sits beside the same talk's slide (D1-C094), which falls back to the parent path's aggregate only when a URL's own quality is unknown, and Google's crawl budget guide lists page quality among the demand factors; read it as site quality setting the baseline while known URL-level signals still count.
- [`D1-C439`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl demand**: Very large, constantly changing sites get no special handling: when URLs change frequently or are useful to users, Google raises crawl demand and tries to raise its crawl capacity for the site, the same logic it applies to small sites.
- [`D1-C440`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl demand**: If a site's server cannot cope with the extra crawling that higher crawl demand brings, Google reduces its crawling of that site again.
- [`D1-C545`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl demand**: An audience member asked, for very large sites of about 100 million pages, what signs show that a site is limited by crawl budget, and how to tell a crawl capacity limit problem from a crawl demand problem.
- [`D1-C493`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl demand**: There is no easy way to tell whether a drop in Google's crawling comes from lower crawl demand or a lower crawl capacity limit; most of the time a capacity-limit drop is an abrupt step down.
- [`D1-C538`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl demand**: A Google panelist said crawl demand is not only Search's: when enough of a site's URLs are wanted by Search, Google Ads or another Google product, Google raises the site's crawl demand and crawls up to that level of demand as far as the site's crawl capacity allows.
- [`D3-C622`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **crawl demand**: Google estimated that a crawl demand update driven by Search takes about 20 hours on average, with a minimum of minutes and an end point of weeks to months.
- [`D3-C623`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **crawl demand**: When Google notices the web getting excited about a few URLs on a site, it allocates more crawl demand to the whole site so it does not miss content useful to future searchers.
- [`D3-C624`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Crawl demand**: Crawl demand can also come from other Google products, such as Shopping, and the roughly 20-hour estimate covers only demand from Search.

### Crawl stats (`crawl-stats`): 13

- [`D1-C339`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Crawl Stats report**: To debug crawl issues, Google points site owners to the Crawl Stats report in Search Console, found in the Settings page under Crawl stats.
- [`D1-C340`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Crawl Stats report**: Search Console's Crawl Stats report shows how much Google crawls from a site, the errors Google received, and the content types fetched by the different crawlers.
- [`D1-C341`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Crawl Stats report**: Gary Illyes called the Crawl Stats report the most valuable tool for debugging crawl errors, together with server logs, which he called the real thing for those who know how to read them.
- [`D1-C508`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Crawl Stats report**: Google said soft 404s, like some other problem categories, are looked up in Search Console's page indexing report, while other crawl issues are debugged in the Crawl Stats report.
- [`D1-C382`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl Stats report**: The stage rule of thumb (under a few thousand URLs crawl budget is unlikely to be a problem) and Google's crawl budget guide (D1-C097: sites with over a million pages that change about weekly, or over 10,000 pages that change daily) leave a middle range where a site should check Search Console's Crawl Stats report before blaming crawl budget for slow indexing.
- [`D1-C393`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Crawl Stats**: To check whether a site has a crawl budget problem, use Search Console's crawl report (Crawl Stats), which breaks crawl requests down by response and by file type and shows crawl problems Google finds.
- [`D1-C443`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Crawl Stats report**: To judge crawl efficiency, check Search Console's Crawl Stats report: whether total crawling has plateaued over time, and whether the average response time shows the server is fast enough or is limiting Googlebot.
- [`D1-C461`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl stats**: An audience member asked whether and when crawl stats will be added to the Search Console API.
- [`D1-C462`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl stats**: Google said it knew of no plans to add crawl stats to the Search Console API, because that would be a completely new part of the API.
- [`D1-C463`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **crawl stats**: A Google panelist said adding a report that is a variation of the Performance report to the Search Console API would be easier than adding crawl stats, because the Performance report is already in the API.
- [`D1-C492`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Crawl Stats report**: John Mueller said the Crawl Stats report's split of crawling by purpose, discovery versus refresh, gives a rough view of whether discovery crawling is in a reasonable range, though measuring publish-to-first-crawl time is more accurate.
- [`D1-C544`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Crawl Stats report**: John Mueller said that if the Crawl Stats report shows about half of a site's crawling going to discovering new pages, that is a lot of discovery crawling, which suggests that crawling of new pages is not the problem.
- [`D3-C609`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Crawl Stats report**: With a typical refresh of about 30 days and deep or soft-404-like pages recrawled only every few months, link important deep pages from strong hub pages and fix pages that look like errors; then check recrawl intervals by site depth in server logs or the Crawl Stats report.

### data-nosnippet (`data-nosnippet`): 7

- [`D2-C076`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **data-nosnippet**: John Mueller said data-nosnippet is rarely needed but lets a site keep a specific piece of text, such as a business phone number, out of the snippet, so the page can still be found for it while searchers have to visit the page to see it.
- [`D2-C077`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **data-nosnippet**: The data-nosnippet attribute can be used on only a handful of HTML elements.
- [`D2-C078`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **data-nosnippet**: Broken HTML can widen data-nosnippet: if a div marked data-nosnippet is not closed properly, the rest of the page can be blocked from the snippet as well.
- [`D2-C079`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **data-nosnippet**: Google's robots meta tag specification says data-nosnippet may be extracted both before and after rendering, so the attribute should not be added to or removed from existing elements with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C080`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **data-nosnippet**: John Mueller said valid HTML is technically not a ranking factor but does matter for controls such as data-nosnippet.
- [`D2-C081`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **data-nosnippet**: To hide one detail, such as a phone number, a price or a direct answer, instead of the whole snippet, wrap it in data-nosnippet on a span, div or section in the server HTML and validate the HTML so that an unclosed element cannot hide the rest of the page from snippets.
- [`D2-C731`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **data-nosnippet**: Treat nosnippet, data-nosnippet and max-snippet as AI visibility settings too: Google lists them as the controls for content in AI features, and if AI answers are built from index snippets, as Google said on stage, a blocked or shortened snippet leaves AI Overviews and AI Mode less to use.

### Disallow (`disallow`): 18

- [`D1-C084`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
- [`D1-C516`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: Robots.txt was made extremely simple by design so that anyone could implement and understand it; it was extended as websites grew more complex, but it still has only three rules: user-agent (a named crawler, or * for every crawler), disallow and allow.
- [`D1-C519`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: A user-agent line with its allow and disallow rules forms a user-agent group, and one group can name several crawlers (the talk's example: Googlebot and Bingbot); give named crawlers their own group only when they need rules the * group should not grant to every crawler.
- [`D1-C520`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: In the talk's worked example, disallow /*/live/ blocks /science/live/ and /sports/live/, because * matches any number of characters, and an allow /science/live/ rule re-opens that one path.
- [`D1-C521`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: To let unnamed crawlers fetch only the homepage, use user-agent: *, disallow: / and allow: /$; the $ ends the match, so /$ means only the root path and /cats$ means exactly /cats.
- [`D1-C525`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: Google called robots.txt extremely forgiving: a typo in a path only blocks the wrong path, a typo in a rule name such as disallow makes Google ignore that line, and the rest of the file is still used.
- [`D1-C531`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: In the talk's quiz, the answer for letting Googlebot crawl /staging/preview/ while keeping the rest of /staging/ closed to it was a user-agent: googlebot group with both rules, disallow /staging/ and allow /staging/preview/, rather than an allow in the * group or a Googlebot group with only the allow.
- [`D1-C532`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **disallow**: A typo in a rule name is not always ignored by Google: its open-source robots.txt parser deliberately accepts common misspellings of disallow (such as dissallow, dissalow and disalow) and of user-agent (useragent, user agent), but not of allow. Google's spec page does not mention typos, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.
- [`D1-C101`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **disallow**: Google's faceted navigation guide prefers prevention: disallow filter URLs in robots.txt and keep crawlable only item pages plus one unfiltered listing page, or use URL fragments, which Google generally does not crawl. rel=canonical and nofollow are weaker, slower options.
- [`D1-C127`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **disallow**: Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling, not a block: nofollow links will generally not be followed, but the linked pages may still be crawled if Google finds them through sitemaps or other links. To stop Google fetching URLs on your own site, use a robots.txt disallow rule.
- [`D2-C020`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **disallow**: Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
- [`D2-C023`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **disallow**: Explain robots.txt and noindex to developers as two separate controls: robots.txt controls crawling, noindex controls indexing. To keep a page out of Search, let Google crawl it and serve noindex; a robots.txt disallow alone can leave the bare URL in results.
- [`D2-C844`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **disallow**: Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.
- [`D2-C207`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Disallow**: If an API folder must stay blocked in robots.txt, allow the endpoints that rendering needs, for example Disallow: /api/ together with Allow: /api/products/.
- [`D2-C208`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Disallow**: A robots.txt carve-out works because Google applies the most specific matching rule, so Allow: /api/products/ beats Disallow: /api/ for product endpoints only; re-test a rendered page after every robots.txt change to script or API paths.
- [`D2-C210`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Disallow**: An API or CDN on its own host needs its own robots.txt check: a blanket Disallow there, or a robots.txt that returns 5xx errors, can stop Google fetching the data a page renders from.
- [`D2-C298`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Disallow**: Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
- [`D2-C529`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **disallow**: Google's documented ways to keep a site's images out of search results are a robots.txt disallow rule (for example for Googlebot-Image) or a noindex X-Robots-Tag HTTP header, with the Removals tool for emergencies.

### Duplicate content (`duplicate-content-concept`): 28

- [`D1-C039`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **deduping**: Gemini is not part of Search, but it uses crawlers for data, shares some technologies such as tokenization and deduping, and grounds on the Search index.
- [`D1-C212`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **duplicate cluster**: When a page is selected for Google's index, its whole duplicate cluster goes into the index with it.
- [`D1-C397`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) **duplicate content**: A community speaker said similar URLs are an indicator of duplicate content, broken links, unnecessary redirects and other technical issues.
- [`D1-C111`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **duplicate content**: Gary Illyes said there is no such thing as a duplicate content penalty.
- [`D1-C128`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **duplicate content**: Google's canonicalization guide says some duplicate content on a site is normal and not a violation of its spam policies; Google clusters duplicate pages, picks the most representative one as canonical and crawls the duplicates less often.
- [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **deduplication**: A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.
- [`D2-C031`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **deduplication**: Google extracts the rel=canonical link, through which site owners state their preferred canonical URL, and uses it in deduplication and in canonical selection.
- [`D2-C344`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplicates**: Google deduplicates pages because many sites have very many pages and Google's index does not have room for everything.
- [`D2-C345`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: Google's deduplication has three steps: identify and cluster duplicate web pages, pick representative URLs and index the unique pages, and forward signals to the representative URLs.
- [`D2-C346`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: For deduplication, a cluster is a set of pages Google considers essentially equivalent: Google stores one of them in the index and keeps track of the other related URLs.
- [`D2-C348`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **duplicate cluster**: Google forwards the signals attached to every URL in a duplicate cluster, such as links, to the representative URL, so that nothing is lost by showing only one URL.
- [`D2-C349`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplicates**: The first reason Google deduplicates is that users do not want to see the same page repeated in the search results, even if site owners would like it to rank ten times on page one.
- [`D2-C350`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: Storage is a second reason for deduplication: Google's storage has many competing uses and storage prices have risen sharply, so the space for any one use is limited and Google has to draw a line somewhere.
- [`D2-C351`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: Google treats a site migration as deduplication across sites, in which the site owner says the old and the new domain are the same and that Google should pick the new domain, so deduplication also helps Google handle migrations.
- [`D2-C352`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **duplicate cluster**: Google keeps the other URLs of a duplicate cluster as 'alternate names': equivalent URLs with the same content that Google still tracks as alternate versions of the representative URL.
- [`D2-C359`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: Google's duplication talk described three related parts of deduplication: building clusters, localization, and selecting the representative URL, which is the canonicalization site owners see in Search Console.
- [`D2-C360`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **duplicate clusters**: Google builds duplicate clusters from four kinds of input: redirects, content, rel=canonical, and a 'magic bucket' of other things.
- [`D2-C370`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: City pages can trigger the same pattern-based deduplication: for a car dealer brand with branches in several cities and similar stock, Google's systems may decide the city name does not matter and canonicalise to one city's page; the slide asked whether a further city page such as /zurich/services would be treated the same way.
- [`D2-C371`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: To avoid pattern-based deduplication, Google's speaker recommended not having many unrelated, similar-looking URLs that lead to the same content, and returning error pages for URLs that no longer exist so they are clearly unrelated.
- [`D2-C373`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **duplicate cluster**: Google's canonicalization troubleshooting guide says fixing a wrong duplicate cluster comes down to making the clustered pages sufficiently different; pages split out faster when the difference is clear and significant, and Google may keep pages in a duplicate cluster for up to two weeks after a fix.
- [`D2-C381`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: Same-language content for different countries is tricky for Google's deduplication, notably German pages for Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and possibly Spanish-language variants.
- [`D2-C393`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **deduplication**: Google's speaker said that pointing rel=canonical from the pages of a paginated set to the first page can sometimes make sense depending on the goal, for example to make a category page more visible, but that it affects canonicalization and deduplication.
- [`D2-C441`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **deduplication**: Google's indexing pipeline slide put a Processing stage between the crawler and the index and listed HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication and feature extraction above it, with feature extraction highlighted as the step of this talk.
- [`D2-C444`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **deduplication**: Google runs deduplication before feature extraction, so that the expensive extraction work is spent only on a trimmed-down, manageable set of documents.
- [`D2-C450`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **deduplication**: Because Google extracts structured data, images and videos only after deduplication, put markup and media on the URL you want as canonical and keep them identical on its duplicates; markup that exists only on a duplicate that loses canonical selection may never be extracted.
- [`D2-C702`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **duplicate cluster**: Google's documentation says a search result usually points to the canonical page, but the other pages in a duplicate cluster are alternate versions that may be served in different contexts, for example a mobile page for a user on a mobile device.
- [`D3-C133`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **deduplication**: Google's slide said there is not one single ranking system and named spam detection systems, the reviews system, BERT, MUM, RankBrain, freshness systems, deduplication systems, crisis information systems and link analysis systems (PageRank).
- [`D3-C669`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **duplicate cluster**: Google's guide to fixing canonicalization issues says that even after content issues are fixed, Google might hold pages in a duplicate cluster for up to two weeks, and that pages split out faster when they differ clearly and significantly.

### E-E-A-T (`e-e-a-t`): 5

- [`D1-C292`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **E-E-A-T**: A community speaker suggested that LLMs pick up some of Google's years of work on judging honesty and trust (E-E-A-T) by proxy, because they send many queries (probably fan-out queries) to search engines.
- [`D3-C162`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **E-E-A-T**: The rater guidelines' table of contents shown on Google's slide covers page quality rating, YMYL topics, main and supplementary content, website and creator reputation, E-E-A-T and lowest quality pages.
- [`D3-C218`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **E-E-A-T**: Google's Discover slide showed an eligibility gate: content with a policy violation goes to a policy compliance check and low-quality content to an E-E-A-T quality check, and both can end with the content filtered out, while safe and trusted content becomes eligible for Discover.
- [`D3-C222`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **E-E-A-T**: Google's Discover slide defined E-E-A-T: experience means first-hand, personal experience with the topic, expertise the necessary knowledge or skill, and authoritativeness the extent to which the creator or website is known as a go-to source for the topic.
- [`D3-C223`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **E-E-A-T**: Google's Discover slide said trust comes first: untrustworthy pages have low E-E-A-T however experienced, expert or authoritative they seem.

### Faceted navigation (`faceted-navigation-concept`): 5

- [`D1-C101`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **faceted navigation**: Google's faceted navigation guide prefers prevention: disallow filter URLs in robots.txt and keep crawlable only item pages plus one unfiltered listing page, or use URL fragments, which Google generally does not crawl. rel=canonical and nofollow are weaker, slower options.
- [`D1-C102`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **faceted URLs**: If faceted URLs must be crawled, use the standard & separator, keep filters in a consistent order, and return a 404 when a filter combination has no results.
- [`D1-C103`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **faceted navigation**: Four ways to manage crawl budget: use HTTP cache control, have good site navigation, restrict crawlers' access to faceted navigation and action URLs, and improve or remove useless content.
- [`D2-C186`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **faceted navigation**: Non-crawlable link markup, such as onclick links and hash pseudo-links, is common in single-page web apps, and sites that use faceted navigation should check their links for it.
- [`D2-C188`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **faceted navigation**: Hash-fragment links are a problem only where Google should follow them: product, category and language links need a real URL in an `<a href>`, while fragments can deliberately keep filter combinations out of the crawl, as Google's faceted navigation guide allows.

### Gemini (`gemini`): 41

- [`D1-C162`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **Gemini app**: Google said that after the launch of Nano Banana, its image generation model, the Gemini app became the number one app in the app store in 2025.
- [`D1-C163`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **Gemini**: Google described a full-stack approach to AI, from its own TPU chips for AI inference through research and frontier models such as Gemini to its apps.
- [`D1-C172`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **Gemini**: Google said the Gemini model lets Search understand the user's intent, and query fan-out then adds further queries to the first one to enrich the quality of the answer.
- [`D1-C496`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **Gemini**: Google said that last year (2025) it delivered a decade of innovation in 12 months, with its new Gemini model at the top of all the benchmarks.
- [`D1-C039`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Gemini**: Gemini is not part of Search, but it uses crawlers for data, shares some technologies such as tokenization and deduping, and grounds on the Search index.
- [`D1-C335`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Gemini**: Crawling for Gemini may be set to care less about quality and more about the amount of content, because for large language models the number of tokens matters more than quality.
- [`D1-C086`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Gemini models**: Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
- [`D1-C522`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Gemini**: Google said a site can keep a directory or the whole site out of Gemini model training by disallowing it for the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, and that Google respects that policy; the speaker believed Google was the first to offer such an opt-out from model training.
- [`D1-C486`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Gemini**: The panel spoke of blocking Google's 'AI crawling or training' with Google-Extended, but Google documents Google-Extended as a usage token, not a crawler: disallowing it does not stop Googlebot fetching pages and only controls use for Gemini training and grounding.
- [`D2-C067`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Gemini**: nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D2-C117`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Gemini**: AI Overviews and AI Mode typically do not ground their answers by reading pages live, unlike Gemini when a user asks about a specific page, Google said.
- [`D2-C118`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Gemini models**: To train Gemini models, Google renders every page just as it does for Search, so a page that renders correctly for Search also works for Gemini training, provided the site allows its content to be used for training.
- [`D2-C119`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Gemini**: If Gemini training reuses the rendering done for Search, a site needs no separate rendering work for Gemini; whether its rendered content is used for training is decided with the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, not by rendering choices.
- [`D2-C120`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Gemini**: When a Gemini user asks about a specific web page (for example, whether it says anything about the ruby HTML tag), the page is read at that moment rather than during crawling and may be used to ground the answer, which takes extra time.
- [`D2-C121`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Gemini Apps**: Google's crawler documentation defines grounding in Gemini Apps and in Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI as providing content from the Google Search index to the model at prompt time, and sites manage whether their content is used for it with the Google-Extended robots.txt token.
- [`D2-C122`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Gemini**: Google says user-triggered fetchers, which fetch a URL because a user asked for it in a Google product (for example Gemini Notebook fetching URLs users add as sources, or Google-Agent acting on a user's request), generally ignore robots.txt rules.
- [`D2-C123`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Gemini**: Google documents Gemini grounding only as content from the Search index at prompt time; the live read of a specific page at a user's request, described on stage, is not documented, so it is unclear whether it works like a user-triggered fetcher, which generally ignores robots.txt, or follows Google-Extended.
- [`D2-C325`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: Tokenization for AI models such as Gemini, in training and in inference, differs from tokenization for Search, although Gary Illyes qualified this with 'or mostly'.
- [`D2-C329`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: Day 1's slide said Gemini shares technologies such as tokenization with Search, while on Day 2 Gary Illyes showed that the two tokenizers split the same text differently ('or mostly'); read this as a shared processing step with different outputs, so Search's word tokens and Gemini's sub-word tokens are not the same units.
- [`D2-C331`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: Gary Illyes said Gemini's context window, where chunking actually matters, holds millions of tokens.
- [`D2-C332`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: Gemini does not need content cut into small chunks of 100 or 200 words, Gary Illyes said, since a smaller book fits in its context window.
- [`D2-C825`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: Gary Illyes added that, once chunk size is thought of in millions of tokens as Gemini's context window allows, chunking has perhaps lost its meaning anyway.
- [`D2-C333`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: Do not rewrite pages into short, self-contained chunks for AI systems; Google says Gemini reads context windows of millions of tokens, so structure content for readers, with clear headings and complete explanations.
- [`D2-C869`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: Right after saying Gemini's context window holds millions of tokens, Gary Illyes put its size at perhaps 900,000 or even closer to a million, without a unit that the recordings capture.
- [`D2-C872`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Gemini**: The talk gave Gemini's context window both as millions of tokens and as roughly 900,000 to a million; Google's long-context docs say Gemini models have context windows of 1 million or more tokens (about eight average novels per million), so plan with about one million tokens as the documented floor rather than several million.
- [`D2-C465`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Gemini**: Gemini in Chrome relies heavily on the screenshot it takes of a page.
- [`D2-C951`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S14-lightning-session-f-media.md) **Gemini**: A community speaker named the limits of the title-based alt-text script: it rewrites only the hero image, assumes the page title states the user's intent, had been tested in only one language or market, and runs on the free Gemini model.
- [`D2-C669`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **Gemini**: SpamBrain, Google's AI-based spam detection system, is nowadays built on Gemini and fine-tuned specifically for finding spam.
- [`D2-C769`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Gemini**: A Google Trends Explore chart presented on stage put worldwide search interest in Gemini above ChatGPT for the first time ever in September 2025, during a sharp surge for Gemini.
- [`D2-C770`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Gemini**: Google attributed the September 2025 surge in worldwide search interest for Gemini to the viral launch of Nano Banana (the image editing model in the Gemini app), as people searched for both Gemini and Nano Banana.
- [`D2-C771`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Gemini app**: Google announced Nano Banana, a new image editing model from Google DeepMind in the Gemini app, on 26 August 2025.
- [`D2-C772`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Gemini**: On stage the Nano Banana launch was placed in September 2025, but Google announced it on 26 August 2025, so the September 2025 surge in Gemini search interest described in the talk came in the weeks after the launch.

- [`D3-C064`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Gemini**: Individual fan-out queries can be seen in some other places, such as Gemini, some search APIs and other LLM systems.
- [`D3-C066`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Gemini**: Do not build pages for fan-out queries copied from Gemini or other LLM tools: they differ from system to system and Search Console does not report them. Cover a topic's real subquestions on solid pages instead.

- [`D3-C187`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **Gemini**: Google's quality talk showed a surface-level example article (not photographed) that the speaker said Gemini could have generated, while stressing that humans have written such content for a long time too.

- [`D3-C439`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **generative AI report**: Search Console's generative AI report shows impressions broken down by pages, countries and devices.
- [`D3-C440`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **generative AI report**: Google called AI reporting in Search Console an evolving space and expects the generative AI report to get richer, with more information in the future.
- [`D3-C441`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **generative AI performance reports**: Search Console's generative AI performance reports count impressions only, with no clicks and no query dimension (Google documents the Search report for AI Overviews and AI Mode, plus a separate Discover report), so measure visits that follow AI answers with your own analytics.
- [`D3-C465`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **generative AI performance report**: Google's announcement of 24 September 2026 says multimodal search data appears both in the Performance report for Search results and in the generative AI performance report, can be exported, and began rolling out globally that day.
- [`D3-C494`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **generative AI report**: Nik Vujic's agency puts Search Console data, LLM referral traffic from GA4 and the data from Search Console's generative AI report into one LLM prompt to compare a client's performance in classic search and in AI features.
- [`D3-C495`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **generative AI report**: Nik Vujic said he hopes Search Console's generative AI report will get query data.
- [`D3-C542`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Generative AI performance report**: Google's own line on Day 1 was to measure success by metrics that matter to the business, and its Generative AI performance report shows impressions but no clicks; together with the community talk this argues for a report that puts organic next to direct, branded paid search, conversions and revenue.
- [`D3-C596`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) **Generative AI performance report**: Google's finding that AI users visit more brand websites is Google's own research; check it against your own data, such as branded and direct traffic in analytics and the Generative AI performance report in Search Console, before planning on it.

### GEO (`geo`): 7

- [`D1-C059`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **GEO**: The opening keynote closed with the advice to think about UEO, user engine optimisation, next to SEO and GEO: focus on the user and the rest will follow.
- [`D1-C049`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **GEO**: Gary Illyes argued that GEO is a label invented to create a new field and is not needed. Understanding how SEO works is enough.
- [`D1-C050`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **GEO**: Google's answer to 'SEO is dead, long live GEO' is not to worry about the name: good SEO is good GEO and AEO.
- [`D1-C296`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **GEO**: A community speaker argued for adopting the GEO label as the industry's chance to leave behind the bad reputation SEO built, unlike Google's view earlier the same day that the new name is not needed.
- [`D1-C426`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **GEO**: Asked whether optimising for AI search can hurt classic search or the reverse, a Google panelist said yes, pointing to questionable GEO advice published online that he declined to name.
- [`D3-C213`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **GEO**: Tactics sold as AI visibility or GEO, such as hidden text aimed at AI answers, mass-produced pages for fan-out queries or keyword-stuffed passages, are judged under the same spam policies as classic ranking manipulation.
- [`D3-C496`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **GEO**: Nik Vujic said his agency uses the combined data to test whether good SEO is good GEO, and that the answer is 'it depends': for one client it found pages that performed better in generative AI features and LLMs than in standard search.

### Discover (`google-discover`): 28

- [`D1-C148`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **Discover**: The keynote's third driver was that information quality remains a core focus for Google, which wants high-quality sources to serve across Google Search, its AI experiences in Search, YouTube and Discover.
- [`D1-C026`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Discover**: Search profiles launched on 4 June 2026, in the US first, for creators and publishers with a sizable following on at least one major social or video platform. They appear in knowledge panels and Discover.
- [`D1-C030`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Discover**: The Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews, AI Mode and generative AI features in Discover. Excluding removes both links to the site and use of its content to ground answers.
- [`D1-C062`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Discover**: Google's guide for generative AI features recommends the Generative AI performance report in Search Console for measuring how content performs in generative AI features on Google Search and Discover.
- [`D2-C087`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Discover**: The max-image-preview rule sets the maximum size of a page's image previews: none shows no preview, standard a default-sized one and large the largest possible, for example in Discover.
- [`D2-C089`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Discover**: max-image-preview:large matters mainly in Discover, where it allows a large image that draws people's attention, so the rule can make a page more visible than leaving it out, John Mueller said.
- [`D2-C092`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Discover**: John Mueller speculated that the use of max-video-preview may change in future, for example in Discover, where letting people view a full video could make sense.
- [`D2-C525`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **Discover**: An image Google has extracted can appear almost anywhere Google shows results, including Discover, image search, web search and AI features, so its potential reach is immense.
- [`D2-C549`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **Discover**: Videos can appear in the main search results, in video-specific result tabs and in Discover (the tab names are unclear in the recording).
- [`D2-C936`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **Discover**: Setting the max-image-preview robots meta tag to large can make content perform surprisingly well in Discover, Gary Illyes said.
- [`D2-C749`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Discover**: Google Discover is not included in Google Trends, because Discover is a content feed with no search box, while Trends counts only the queries people type into Google Search or YouTube.
- [`D2-C751`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Discover**: Google Trends cannot show demand that reaches people through the Discover feed, so Discover visibility has to be judged from Search Console's Discover performance report rather than from Trends.
- [`D3-C218`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover slide showed an eligibility gate: content with a policy violation goes to a policy compliance check and low-quality content to an E-E-A-T quality check, and both can end with the content filtered out, while safe and trusted content becomes eligible for Discover.
- [`D3-C219`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover documentation says content is automatically eligible for Discover if it is indexed and meets Discover's content policies, needs no special tags or structured data, and is not guaranteed to appear.
- [`D3-C220`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover documentation says Discover uses many of the same signals and systems as Search to determine what is helpful, people-first content.
- [`D3-C221`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover slide said that for eligible content image quality decides click-through: a small thumbnail lowers the click-through rate and a large, high-resolution image raises it.
- [`D3-C222`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover slide defined E-E-A-T: experience means first-hand, personal experience with the topic, expertise the necessary knowledge or skill, and authoritativeness the extent to which the creator or website is known as a go-to source for the topic.
- [`D3-C223`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover slide said trust comes first: untrustworthy pages have low E-E-A-T however experienced, expert or authoritative they seem.
- [`D3-C224`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover slide recommended large images at least 1,200 px wide, with more than 300,000 total pixels and a 16x9 aspect ratio, enabled by the max-image-preview:large setting.
- [`D3-C225`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover slide said to avoid generic images, such as a site logo, and text-heavy images.
- [`D3-C226`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover slide said images are subject to the same policy requirements as the content and that misleading, exaggerated or outrageous images should be avoided.
- [`D3-C227`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover documentation says to specify the large image with schema.org markup or the og:image meta tag, which can influence the thumbnail Discover chooses, and that a vertical image cropped to 16x9 must keep its important details.
- [`D3-C228`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's closing Discover slide pointed to the Discover content policies in Google Search Help and to the Search Central documentation.
- [`D3-C229`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: Google's Discover content policies ask news sources for clear dates and bylines, information about the authors, publication and publisher, and contact information, and say repeated or egregious violations can make a site ineligible for Discover.
- [`D3-C230`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **Discover**: For Discover, set max-image-preview:large on article templates, give every article a relevant image at least 1,200 px wide in og:image or schema.org markup that is neither the site logo nor text-heavy, and show clear bylines and dates.
- [`D3-C435`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Discover**: Review the filters and regexes that Search Console's AI-powered configuration proposes before trusting the numbers: Google's launch post calls the feature experimental, warns that AI can misinterpret requests, and limits it to the Search results Performance report (not Discover or News) and to configuration, not sorting or exporting.
- [`D3-C441`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Discover**: Search Console's generative AI performance reports count impressions only, with no clicks and no query dimension (Google documents the Search report for AI Overviews and AI Mode, plus a separate Discover report), so measure visits that follow AI answers with your own analytics.
- [`D3-C467`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Discover**: Google's help page says platform properties show only how content performs on Google Search, Discover and Google News, not how often it is seen on the social or video platform itself.

### Google-Extended (`google-extended-token`): 12

- [`D1-C032`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Google-Extended**: The control does not affect AI training. Training of the models is limited with Google-Extended instead.
- [`D1-C079`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **google-extended**: The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.
- [`D1-C086`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Google-Extended**: Google-Extended is a control token, not a crawler with its own user agent string. It decides whether crawled content may be used to train future Gemini models and to ground Gemini apps and Vertex AI.
- [`D1-C522`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Google-Extended**: Google said a site can keep a directory or the whole site out of Gemini model training by disallowing it for the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, and that Google respects that policy; the speaker believed Google was the first to offer such an opt-out from model training.
- [`D1-C523`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Google-Extended**: The 'first' needs care: OpenAI documented how to block its GPTBot crawler in robots.txt in August 2023, before Google announced Google-Extended on 28 September 2023. What Google-Extended added was a token that controls AI-training use of pages fetched by Google's existing crawlers, separately from Search; Apple later introduced a similar token, Applebot-Extended.
- [`D1-C485`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Google-Extended**: To opt out of Google's AI training, a site can use the Google-Extended token in robots.txt.
- [`D1-C486`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Google-Extended**: The panel spoke of blocking Google's 'AI crawling or training' with Google-Extended, but Google documents Google-Extended as a usage token, not a crawler: disallowing it does not stop Googlebot fetching pages and only controls use for Gemini training and grounding.
- [`D1-C487`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Google-Extended**: A Google panelist said Apple offers a robots.txt control for Applebot similar to Google-Extended, so a site can allow Applebot for search while opting out of Apple's AI use.
- [`D2-C067`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Google-Extended**: nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D2-C119`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Google-Extended**: If Gemini training reuses the rendering done for Search, a site needs no separate rendering work for Gemini; whether its rendered content is used for training is decided with the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, not by rendering choices.
- [`D2-C121`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Google-Extended**: Google's crawler documentation defines grounding in Gemini Apps and in Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI as providing content from the Google Search index to the model at prompt time, and sites manage whether their content is used for it with the Google-Extended robots.txt token.
- [`D2-C123`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Google-Extended**: Google documents Gemini grounding only as content from the Search index at prompt time; the live read of a specific page at a user's request, described on stage, is not documented, so it is unclear whether it works like a user-triggered fetcher, which generally ignores robots.txt, or follows Google-Extended.

### Google Images (`google-images`): 8

- [`D1-C200`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Google Images**: Visual search predates transformers in Google's own history: its Search timeline dates Google Images to 2001 and Google Lens to 2017, the year Google Research published the Transformer, so read the stage remark as being about today's multimodal AI search.
- [`D2-C538`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **Google Images**: Images that should rank need an img element with a real src; hero or product images set as CSS backgrounds are invisible to Google Images and image features, so keep CSS backgrounds for decorative images you do not need indexed.
- [`D2-C545`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **Google Images**: While the AVIF ingestion hiccup Gary Illyes mentioned lasts, serve AVIF only through source elements inside picture and keep a WebP or JPEG file in the img src, which is the URL Google extracts, even though Google's documentation lists AVIF as supported; then check in Google Images that key images appear.
- [`D2-C554`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **Google Images**: Google's video SEO guide says a video must be embedded on an indexed watch page to be eligible for video features and recommends a dedicated watch page per video where it makes sense for the business; a non-watch page with the video can still appear as a text result or a Google Images result with a video badge.
- [`D2-C943`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **Google Images**: Google's image metadata guide says Google Images supports the IPTC Digital Source Type values for algorithmically created images, such as trainedAlgorithmicMedia, and can show C2PA details in 'About this image', such as whether an image was created or edited with AI tools.
- [`D3-C319`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Google Images**: Image results shown among web results come from Google's image index and are roughly the same images that Google Images shows for the same query.
- [`D3-C345`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Google Images**: Product annotations on Google Images results also come from product structured data and do not need Google Merchant Center.
- [`D3-C351`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Google Images**: For an online shop, Product structured data is enough for product rich results and Google Images product annotations, but the Shopping tab needs a Merchant Center feed too; keep feed and markup values identical, since Google can use the markup to validate the feed.

### Google Lens (`google-lens`): 8

- [`D1-C159`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **Google Lens**: The keynote's personal favourites in the evolution of Search were Google Translate, voice search, the Knowledge Graph (relating entities to give context) and Google Lens.
- [`D1-C188`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Google Lens**: Google said it noticed young users uploading pictures to reverse image search and expecting results that answer something about the picture, and that Google Lens was its answer to that behaviour.
- [`D1-C190`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Google Lens**: Google said Google Lens is used by over 1.5 billion people (figure as said on stage on 30 September 2026; no period was given).
- [`D1-C191`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Google Lens**: Google's May 2025 Search announcement says more than 1.5 billion people use Google Lens to search what they see every month.
- [`D1-C200`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Google Lens**: Visual search predates transformers in Google's own history: its Search timeline dates Google Images to 2001 and Google Lens to 2017, the year Google Research published the Transformer, so read the stage remark as being about today's multimodal AI search.
- [`D3-C458`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Google Lens**: Multimodal searches reported in Search Console include searches with Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android, images uploaded to Google Search and Chrome's right-click search on an image.
- [`D3-C460`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Google Lens**: In a live demo, Google Lens on an Android phone identified a photographed object and listed websites selling it, with deep links that allow buying it online.
- [`D3-C462`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Lens**: Google's Performance report help says the queries dimension is not available for the multimodal search type, because these searches mostly use images, so judge image-led traffic by page, country and device, and make product and article images distinctive enough for Lens to match.

### Search Console (`google-search-console`): 135

- [`D1-C029`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Search Console**: Search Console has a property setting called Search generative AI that gives direct control over AI Overviews and AI Mode without affecting web rankings. Its states are inherit from parent, include and exclude.
- [`D1-C196`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Search Console**: Google said Search Console's generative AI reporting launched alongside the generative AI control, starting with impressions only, and may expand later.
- [`D1-C062`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Search Console**: Google's guide for generative AI features recommends the Generative AI performance report in Search Console for measuring how content performs in generative AI features on Google Search and Discover.
- [`D1-C124`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Search Console**: Google's launch post for the Generative AI performance reports in Search Console (3 June 2026; rolled out to all sites worldwide by 31 August 2026) lists impressions, pages, countries, devices (Search only) and dates, and no click or query metrics.
- [`D1-C239`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Search Console**: A community speaker's example of an LLM error on Search Console data: a chatbot called an average position that went from 8 to 9 an improvement, although position 1 is the top, so the move from 8 to 9 is a decline.
- [`D1-C257`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Search Console**: Before writing code to pull Search Console data for one property, check which data you actually need, what the API can provide and what the API costs, a community speaker advised.
- [`D1-C258`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Search Console**: Pulling Search Console data through the API required setting up a Google Cloud account to get API access, a community speaker said.
- [`D1-C262`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Search Console**: The resulting monthly report showed Search Console data on one side and an AI-written summary of what happened that month on the other; an in-house AI specialist built the dashboard from the SEO manager's code.
- [`D1-C264`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Search Console**: Search Console Help defines position as the position of a link on Google, where 1 is the topmost position, and says the Performance report shows the topmost position a property's link occupied, averaged across all queries.
- [`D1-C265`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Search Console**: Search Console Help separates critical issues, which make a structured-data item invalid and stop it from appearing as a rich result, from non-critical issues, listed under 'Improve item appearance'; the Rich Results Test reports valid items that have warnings.
- [`D1-C266`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **Search Console**: To use the Search Console API you need a Google Account with Search Console permission on the property, a project in the Google API Console and OAuth2 credentials (all Search Console APIs except the Testing Tools API need OAuth2).
- [`D1-C339`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Search Console**: To debug crawl issues, Google points site owners to the Crawl Stats report in Search Console, found in the Settings page under Crawl stats.
- [`D1-C340`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's Crawl Stats report shows how much Google crawls from a site, the errors Google received, and the content types fetched by the different crawlers.
- [`D1-C358`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Search Console**: DNS errors get a site removed from Google Search very aggressively, and Search Console alerts site owners to them.
- [`D1-C360`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Search Console**: When Search Console reports network errors, the first step Google recommends is to ask the hosting provider, or the CDN, whether they changed anything.
- [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Search Console**: CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D1-C368`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's page indexing report breaks down the reasons why pages do or do not show in Search, and its categories help find patterns in how a site's content is crawled and served to Google's crawlers.
- [`D1-C369`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Search Console**: Google's status code page says that with a 204 No Content response Google receives no content and cannot process it, and that a 2xx page whose content is empty or an error message shows as a soft 404 in Search Console.
- [`D1-C508`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Search Console**: Google said soft 404s, like some other problem categories, are looked up in Search Console's page indexing report, while other crawl issues are debugged in the Crawl Stats report.
- [`D1-C140`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
- [`D1-C528`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch.
- [`D1-C535`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **Search Console**: Dave Smart said Search Console reports such a block only on the first URL of the chain, which is confusing: the URL shown as blocked by robots.txt is not itself disallowed.
- [`D1-C537`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **Search Console**: When Search Console says a URL is blocked by robots.txt but the file does not block it, check whether the URL redirects and test every URL in the chain.
- [`D1-C382`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Search Console**: The stage rule of thumb (under a few thousand URLs crawl budget is unlikely to be a problem) and Google's crawl budget guide (D1-C097: sites with over a million pages that change about weekly, or over 10,000 pages that change daily) leave a middle range where a site should check Search Console's Crawl Stats report before blaming crawl budget for slow indexing.
- [`D1-C393`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Search Console**: To check whether a site has a crawl budget problem, use Search Console's crawl report (Crawl Stats), which breaks crawl requests down by response and by file type and shows crawl problems Google finds.
- [`D1-C394`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Search Console**: The file-type breakdown of crawl requests in Search Console is useful for spotting anomalies, such as most crawling going to images on a site that has no images worth crawling.
- [`D1-C395`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Search Console**: Google advised checking crawl data in Search Console now and then without obsessing over crawl budget.
- [`D1-C396`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's crawl data separates discovery (fetches of URLs Google has not seen before) from refresh (fetches of known URLs), and lets you drill down to the problematic URLs.
- [`D1-C443`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Search Console**: To judge crawl efficiency, check Search Console's Crawl Stats report: whether total crawling has plateaued over time, and whether the average response time shows the server is fast enough or is limiting Googlebot.
- [`D1-C448`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Search Console**: An audience member asked what changes to expect in Search Console's reporting on Google's AI features.
- [`D1-C449`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Search Console**: A Google panelist said he expected more AI reporting to launch in Search Console, without a timeline or a promise, because many people at Google care about giving site owners the information to understand and adapt to what happens in Search.
- [`D1-C464`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Relations team talks with the Search Console team about the API more than before, partly because with so many vibe-coded systems around it is very easy to just say 'use the Search Console API to do something', and it is annoying when Search Console has no API for that.
- [`D1-C465`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Search Console**: An audience member asked how a large news site can tell whether crawl budget is limiting how fast new articles are discovered (within minutes), and which statistics in Search Console and the logs show this.
- [`D1-C474`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Search Console**: An audience member asked where the sweet spot is for a sitemap that misses nothing but does not overflow Search Console.
- [`D1-C480`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Search Console**: The consolidation described on stage matches Google's November 2020 move from Google Webmasters to Google Search Central, which moved its main blog, 13 localized blogs and the Search help content of the Search Console Help Center to its developer site: about six years before the event, not the four or five said on stage.
- [`D2-C018`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **Search Console**: Google's Q&A slide said that a sitemap not listed in robots.txt has to be submitted instead, for example in Search Console.
- [`D2-C102`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Search Console**: John Mueller's slide said Search Console has very few indexing-like settings and listed the Search generative AI control as the one control in his talk that is not a meta tag.
- [`D2-C103`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Search Console**: Setting the Search generative AI control in Search Console to exclude keeps a site's links and content out of Search generative AI features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode, so the site gets no traffic or impressions from them; include is the default.
- [`D2-C176`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Search Console**: To check whether JavaScript content is affected, open the URL Inspection tool in Search Console or the Rich Results Test and look for that content in the rendered HTML tab.
- [`D2-C240`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Search Console**: Because Web Fragments monkey-patches core browser APIs such as document, history and location, test pages that use it in Google's rendering (the rendered HTML in Search Console's URL Inspection tool or the Rich Results Test), not only in a normal desktop browser.
- [`D2-C304`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Search Console**: When Search Console reports that content is not rendering, Erin Sparling suggested putting AI agents on the problem, but only after doing your own due diligence.
- [`D2-C306`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Search Console**: To use Search Console to debug what Google can see on a site and why, Erin Sparling said the first step is to get access to the site by verifying ownership (the speaker's words were authorized domains).
- [`D2-C307`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Search Console**: Erin Sparling showed a Search Console result saying a URL would be indexed only under certain conditions, one of which had not been met, and contrasted it with the result for an available URL whose content loads.
- [`D2-C358`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **Search Console**: After a migration, judge success by the new domain's indexing and traffic in Search Console rather than by a site: query on the old domain, and keep the old domain's redirects in place long term so searches for the old brand still reach the new site.
- [`D2-C359`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **Search Console**: Google's duplication talk described three related parts of deduplication: building clusters, localization, and selecting the representative URL, which is the canonicalization site owners see in Search Console.
- [`D2-C884`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Search Console**: The technical steps of a community speaker's domain consolidation included submitting new sitemaps, filing a change of address in Search Console and updating internal links so the new pages did not rely on redirects alone.
- [`D2-C888`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Search Console**: After a domain consolidation went live, a community speaker's team checked Search Console every day, ran full site crawls and compared the numbers with the pre-migration baseline for months.
- [`D2-C912`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Search Console**: Google's site move guide says to submit a Change of Address in Search Console when moving from one domain or subdomain to another, to submit the new sitemap, and to change internal links on the new site from the old URLs to the new ones.
- [`D2-C515`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Search Console**: Google's planned validation workflow has five steps: download the rules from the feature guide, generate the JSON or embedded microdata or RDFa, run the rules against the generated server-side markup as a first check, deploy and test in the Rich Results Test, and monitor ongoing performance in Search Console.
- [`D2-C516`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Search Console**: The SHACL rules are meant to run inside a site's content generation, so markup is sanity-checked before it is published and does not silently regress later, a breakage site owners might otherwise discover only through a Search Console report.
- [`D2-C517`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Search Console**: The SHACL rules will not replace Search Console as the canonical place for structured data reports, because some checks use Google's internal libraries and cannot be expressed in SHACL, but they will catch problems such as a missing required field.
- [`D2-C520`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Search Console**: When the SHACL rules appear, wire them into the build or CMS publishing step as an automated test, so a template change that drops a required property fails before deployment instead of surfacing weeks later in Search Console.
- [`D2-C948`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S14-lightning-session-f-media.md) **Google Search Console**: After shipping LLM-rewritten image alt text on a client's site, a community speaker saw the site's image performance in Google Search Console drop (no figures were given).
- [`D2-C960`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S14-lightning-session-f-media.md) **Search Console**: A community speaker said publishers can also verify their social accounts in Search Console, which makes it easier to track the performance of content repurposed for social platforms.
- [`D2-C607`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **Search Console**: Check AI Overviews and AI Mode with native-language queries in each target market, not with translated English keywords, and compare with the country breakdown of Search Console's generative AI performance report; topics where competitors are cited and you are not point to missing or weak local content.
- [`D2-C975`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S17-poster-session-h-indexing.md) **Search Console**: The Day 2 poster topics included technical SEO testing in CI/CD pipelines, internal links that move rankings, Search Console's URL Inspection tool and API, getting everyone on board during complex site migrations, a CMS migration from WordPress to Contentful, the 'global Spanish' problem and going beyond prompts.
- [`D2-C706`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Search Console**: 'Discovered – currently not indexed' in Search Console is a crawl-scheduling state: Google knows the URL exists but does not want to crawl it yet. Of the two not-indexed statuses discussed, it was called the 'kind of nastier' one.
- [`D2-C711`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Search Console**: 'Crawled – currently not indexed' in Search Console is an index selection decision: Google crawled and processed the page but decided not to keep it in the index.
- [`D2-C717`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's Page indexing report is the place to check for index selection issues, and its not-indexed reasons are useful when testing changes on a site.
- [`D2-C730`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **Search Console**: There is no separate AI index to optimise for: when a page never shows up as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode, first check that it is indexed, that no nosnippet rule blocks its snippet and that the site is not excluded in Search Console's generative AI setting, the eligibility conditions Google lists.
- [`D2-C751`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Search Console**: Google Trends cannot show demand that reaches people through the Discover feed, so Discover visibility has to be judged from Search Console's Discover performance report rather than from Trends.
- [`D2-C788`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Search Console**: A Google Trends line that falls over many years is not proof that a market is shrinking; compare terms against each other in the same chart, and take absolute numbers from keyword tools or Search Console impressions.
- [`D3-C055`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Search Console**: For audiences that type the same words in two scripts or spellings (Hindi in Devanagari and in Latin letters, German with and without umlauts), check which forms appear in Search Console's queries and use those forms in headings and key text.
- [`D3-C063`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Search Console**: Google said fan-out queries are not added to Search Console, because Google considers them part of its infrastructure.
- [`D3-C066`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Search Console**: Do not build pages for fan-out queries copied from Gemini or other LLM tools: they differ from system to system and Search Console does not report them. Cover a topic's real subquestions on solid pages instead.
- [`D3-C093`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Console help says AI Mode groups the user's question into subtopics and searches for each one simultaneously, and that a follow-up question in AI Mode is essentially a new query.
- [`D3-C095`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Search Console**: No Google documentation states that fan-out queries stay out of Search Console, but the docs fit the stage statement: the Performance report counts AI Overviews and AI Mode under the user's own queries, and the Generative AI reports have no query dimension.
- [`D3-C272`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **Search Console**: Google's core updates page recommends waiting at least a full week after a core update has finished rolling out before analysing Search Console data, then comparing that week with a week before the update started.
- [`D3-C412`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Console talk at the Deep Dive covered five Search Console launches of the past year: query groups, AI-powered configuration of the Performance report, generative AI control and reporting, platform properties for social accounts, and multimodal search reporting.
