- [`D3-C413`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's query groups put together queries that express a very similar user intent but are written differently, for example with more or fewer words or with spelling errors, so site owners can see the intent behind their traffic instead of every query string.
- [`D3-C414`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: To show how diverse queries for one intent are, Google's Search Console talk showed a slide titled 'How to spell Britney Spears?' with a long list of spelling variants, citing archive.google/jobs/britney.html.
- [`D3-C415`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Console talk said Google's logs show hundreds of different ways in which people write the query for Britney Spears.
- [`D3-C419`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Query groups can change when the meaning of a query changes over time: a 2023 search for 'Gemini' may have meant the astrological sign, but after Google launched Gemini it means something else, so Search Console may now group it differently.
- [`D3-C421`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Query groups appear in the Search Console Insights report as a table of the top groups, showing the total clicks of all the queries inside each group, with an option to view a larger table.
- [`D3-C422`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Each query group in Search Console is titled with the most prominent query in the group.
- [`D3-C424`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Console team said query groups have been found very useful and that people are using them.
- [`D3-C425`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Console team asks for feedback on every new feature, through the thumbs up and thumbs down buttons or any other feedback feature in Search Console, and said it takes that feedback very seriously.
- [`D3-C429`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's AI-powered configuration is a chat box in which users describe the analysis they want in natural language, and the request is transformed into the Performance report's configuration.
- [`D3-C430`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google said requests to Search Console's AI-powered configuration can be written in any language, not only English.
- [`D3-C431`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's AI-powered configuration lists the changes it will make to the Performance report and applies them only after the user approves.
- [`D3-C432`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's AI-powered configuration is conversational rather than one-shot: a follow-up request adds changes on top of the configuration already applied.
- [`D3-C433`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: An example request for Search Console's AI-powered configuration was to show queries on phone searches containing the word sports in the last six months.
- [`D3-C434`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: In a test by Google's Search Console team, the vague request 'wine-related queries that lead to my site' made Search Console's AI-powered configuration build a regex filter of wine names, such as Merlot, joined by pipe characters, without the user typing the regex.
- [`D3-C435`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Review the filters and regexes that Search Console's AI-powered configuration proposes before trusting the numbers: Google's launch post calls the feature experimental, warns that AI can misinterpret requests, and limits it to the Search results Performance report (not Discover or News) and to configuration, not sorting or exporting.
- [`D3-C436`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console has a tool with which every property owner can tell Google whether the site's content may be used in AI search results, because Google wants content owners to control their content.
- [`D3-C437`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console added reporting of the impressions a site's content gets in the AI surfaces of Google Search, found in the left navigation nested under Search results.
- [`D3-C439`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's generative AI report shows impressions broken down by pages, countries and devices.
- [`D3-C440`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google called AI reporting in Search Console an evolving space and expects the generative AI report to get richer, with more information in the future.
- [`D3-C441`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's generative AI performance reports count impressions only, with no clicks and no query dimension (Google documents the Search report for AI Overviews and AI Mode, plus a separate Discover report), so measure visits that follow AI answers with your own analytics.
- [`D3-C442`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Search Console launched platform properties, which bring social platforms into Search Console, about three or four months before the October 2026 event.
- [`D3-C443`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Platform properties let a user verify ownership of an Instagram, TikTok, X or YouTube account in Search Console and see the traffic Google sends to that account.
- [`D3-C444`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google said it is working on adding more platforms to Search Console's platform properties beyond Instagram, TikTok, X and YouTube.
- [`D3-C445`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google acknowledged that verifying a website in Search Console, by placing a Google token on the homepage or in the DNS setup, is a relatively high bar for some people.
- [`D3-C446`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: A platform property is verified entirely from within Search Console: a pop-up from the platform, for example Instagram, asks the user to grant Google permission to identify the account and its handle, and completing it proves ownership without a token.
- [`D3-C450`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Because platform properties bring many new users to Search Console, Google published documentation and strategy guidance on them, covering how to identify the Search audience, use the 24-hour real-time view, export data and compare platforms such as Instagram and YouTube.
- [`D3-C452`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: In the example YouTube report shown in Google's Search Console talk, long-form videos still got more traffic and more impressions from Google than Shorts; this was one example channel, not a general finding.
- [`D3-C453`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Media teams that publish on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok or X should add each account as a Search Console platform property and compare formats by URL pattern; Google's July 2026 post says an account already used for a Search profile should already give access to its data.
- [`D3-C454`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Console talk presented multimodal search reporting as its fifth and newest launch, under a 'Hot from the oven' badge.
- [`D3-C455`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Multimodal search reporting in Search Console launched about a week and a half before the 2 October 2026 talk.
- [`D3-C458`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Multimodal searches reported in Search Console include searches with Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android, images uploaded to Google Search and Chrome's right-click search on an image.
- [`D3-C461`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: In a demo, asking Chrome about an image on a web page opened a side panel of visual matches, one of which was on Google's developers site and led on to more information about Search Console; Google described this as the full flow of the multimodal traffic now reported.
- [`D3-C464`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google's Search Console help says the experimental AI-powered configuration is visible only to a small percentage of users, allows each user 20 requests per day, keeps existing report filters when it adds new ones, and applies its suggested settings only after the user confirms them.
- [`D3-C468`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search Console**: Google's social and video performance guide says that if you already claimed your Search profile, all of its verified accounts are added automatically as platform properties in Search Console.
- [`D3-C469`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: In a community lightning talk, agency founder Nik Vujic presented how his agency feeds Search Console and GA4 data to an LLM agent to support decisions for its clients.
- [`D3-C470`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Google Search Console**: Nik Vujic called Google Search Console his favourite SEO tool, used alongside GA4, and said third-party SEO tools give only estimates, although they have some use cases.
- [`D3-C471`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic said it is super important to export all of a site's Search Console data, and his agency's workflow starts from Search Console's export to BigQuery.
- [`D3-C472`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: A community slide (Workflow 1) said the first step is to apply the filters you need, even natively in Search Console, for example branded versus non-branded queries, with clicks and impressions.
- [`D3-C473`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Google's launch post for Search Console's branded queries filter (20 November 2025) says the branded versus non-branded split is made by an internal AI-assisted system, not by a regular expression, and that some queries may occasionally be misidentified.
- [`D3-C474`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: A community slide said the Search Console interface export is limited to 1,000 rows.
- [`D3-C475`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: A community slide said the Search Console bulk data export to BigQuery gives the most complete query dataset available, with anonymized queries excluded.
- [`D3-C477`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: The community workflow's third step feeds the exported Search Console dataset into the agency's LLM agent, which queries the dataset and returns the evidence rather than a sample.
- [`D3-C478`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic's slide said no agent is needed to start: pull the Search Console data, import it into any LLM and query it in conversation; his agency built its agent to have everything in one place.
- [`D3-C479`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic recommended Looker Studio as a second way to get past Search Console's data limits.
- [`D3-C480`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: A Search Central blog post on Search Console data limits (October 2022) says the interface exports at most 1,000 rows, while the Search Analytics API and the Looker Studio connector return up to 50,000 rows per day per site per search type.
- [`D3-C481`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Google's blog post on Search Console data limits says anonymized queries are always left out of the report tables but counted in chart totals unless you filter by query, and are left out whenever a filter is applied, so filtered rows do not add up to the chart totals.
- [`D3-C482`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic said his agency uses the Search Console data fed to an LLM in five use cases, the first being cross-comparing and following up different articles.
- [`D3-C483`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic said that after a page is published, the queries it appears for are the first thing to show up in Search Console, while clicks and impressions come much later.
- [`D3-C484`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: A query reaches Search Console's Performance report only through an impression, so queries cannot come before impressions; what rises first after a publish or refresh is the number of queries with a few impressions each, before total impressions and clicks grow noticeably.
- [`D3-C488`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic said analysing Search Console query data with an LLM also helped his agency spot developer mistakes, such as unwanted pages that got indexed, which can also be found in Search Console itself.
- [`D3-C489`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic said some keyword cannibalization is fine because it is logical, but for bad cannibalization his agency groups all of an article's Search Console queries and then decides whether to redirect the pages or rewrite and split the content.
- [`D3-C490`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic advised starting every SEO experiment with a hypothesis, for example a bulk change to one page element across a group of pages, and using an LLM to report the group's Search Console data, for example click-through rate, for the test.
- [`D3-C494`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic's agency puts Search Console data, LLM referral traffic from GA4 and the data from Search Console's generative AI report into one LLM prompt to compare a client's performance in classic search and in AI features.
- [`D3-C495`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Nik Vujic said he hopes Search Console's generative AI report will get query data.
- [`D3-C498`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Google's AI features guide says traffic from sites appearing in AI features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode is included in the overall search traffic in Search Console and reported in the Performance report within the Web search type.
- [`D3-C499`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Search Console's branded queries filter works only for top-level properties, not URL-path or subdomain properties, and only for sites with enough queries and impressions; Google made it available to all eligible sites on 11 March 2026.
- [`D3-C502`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Looker Studio lifts Search Console's 1,000-row interface limit but keeps the connector's cap of 50,000 rows per day per site per search type; only the bulk export to BigQuery is free of the daily row limit, so large sites that need every non-anonymized query should use it.
- [`D3-C535`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **Search Console**: Beyond Search Console, Google's AI features guide suggests tracking conversions and time spent on the site in tools such as Google Analytics to understand the value of traffic from AI features.
- [`D3-C594`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) **Search Console**: Track trust queries about your brand, such as '[brand] legit', '[brand] reviews' or '[brand] seriös', in Search Console and Google Trends for each market, and answer them on the site, for example with a trust or about page, instead of leaving the answer to third-party review sites.
- [`D3-C596`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) **Search Console**: Google's finding that AI users visit more brand websites is Google's own research; check it against your own data, such as branded and direct traffic in analytics and the Generative AI performance report in Search Console, before planning on it.
- [`D3-C615`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Search Console**: A site owner can submit robots.txt in Search Console to force Google to refresh it sooner.
- [`D3-C616`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Search Console**: Plan robots.txt changes a day ahead, because Google may use the old file for about 24 hours; for an urgent change, request a refresh in Search Console instead of waiting.
- [`D3-C651`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Search Console**: Google estimated that a removal requested by the site owner in Search Console takes effect in about 2 hours on average, from minutes up to 24 hours.
- [`D3-C652`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Search Console**: Search Console removals average about 2 hours because Google pushes removals out to its serving system about every 2 hours.
- [`D3-C653`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Search Console**: To hide a URL from Google Search urgently, use the Removals tool in Search Console (about 2 hours) and also add a noindex or a 404, which takes one to three weeks to drop the page from the index.
- [`D3-C667`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **Search Console**: Google's robots.txt guide says its crawlers update their cached copy of a site's robots.txt every 24 hours, and that the Request a recrawl option in Search Console's robots.txt report refreshes it faster.

### Google Shopping (`google-shopping`): 18

- [`D1-C342`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Google Shopping**: Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot is today just one user of a centralized crawling platform, and that dozens of other clients, such as Google Shopping and AdSense, send their crawl requests through the same infrastructure under other crawler names, with only the larger ones documented.
- [`D3-C346`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Shopping tab**: To appear in the Shopping tab of Google Search, a product must be submitted in Google Merchant Center; product structured data alone is not enough.
- [`D3-C347`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Shopping tab**: Google's Merchant Center help says products and details crawled from an online store can show up on Google even when they are not marked up with schema.org or added in Merchant Center, and lists the Shopping tab among the places Merchant Center free listings appear.
- [`D3-C348`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Shopping tab**: Google's free listings help says crawled store products can appear on Google without markup or Merchant Center but does not say whether that includes the Shopping tab; for a shop that wants Shopping tab visibility, the stage rule that Merchant Center is required is the safe working assumption.
- [`D3-C351`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Shopping tab**: For an online shop, Product structured data is enough for product rich results and Google Images product annotations, but the Shopping tab needs a Merchant Center feed too; keep feed and markup values identical, since Google can use the markup to validate the feed.
- [`D3-C353`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Schema.org product markup on websites is another source of billions of product offers for Google Shopping, next to merchant feeds.
- [`D3-C356`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Behind the visible attributes, small pieces of product data such as brand and UPC or other barcodes are very important for Google Shopping's query understanding, retrieval and ranking.
- [`D3-C364`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Google Shopping said highly prescriptive product data is a lot of hard work for merchants and is no longer needed for LLMs.
- [`D3-C378`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Google Shopping called rich data with light structure the AI sweet spot: a little structure that helps the AI system understand the data, not deep, highly nested, complex structures.
- [`D3-C379`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Some structure is much better than none for AI systems, because without structure the model does not really know what is going on, Google Shopping said.
- [`D3-C385`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Google Shopping uses its own crawler, Storebot (Storebot-Google), instead of Googlebot because it needs fresh product information, prices, availability and shipping details and therefore crawls much more often.
- [`D3-C389`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Google's crawler list says robots.txt rules addressed to the Storebot-Google user agent affect all surfaces of Google Shopping, such as the Shopping tab in Google Search.
- [`D3-C395`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Merchant Center's product_detail attribute takes up to 100 specifications, each a section name, attribute name and attribute value, and Google's help says clean key-value specifications improve product details on Google Shopping and AI-driven surfaces.
- [`D3-C402`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Basic, well-specified product attributes such as price, brand and availability remain as important as ever for Google Shopping.
- [`D3-C405`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Web markup is an efficient and unambiguous way for sites to share product data with Google, Google Shopping said, repeating the Day 2 structured data talk.
- [`D3-C406`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Google Shopping named the downside of adding Q&As and documentation to product markup: the page's markup becomes somewhat bigger.
- [`D3-C407`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Google Shopping pointed to a Google holiday shopping blog post with early results from real merchants using the conversational attributes, and to the Merchant Center Help Center and schema.org for the attributes and properties.
- [`D3-C409`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Google Shopping**: Google Shopping described product data for AI as early days in a fast-moving area, with many more changes to come.

### Google Trends (`google-trends`): 57

- [`D2-C637`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **Google Trends**: Re-check regional demand for core product categories at least once a year, for example by comparing regions and seasons in Google Trends, because climate, housing or habits can shift what a market wants.
- [`D2-C747`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends is a free Google tool that gives access to a sample of aggregated, anonymized and categorized searches.
- [`D2-C748`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends data covers searches on Google Search, including web, image, shopping and news search, plus searches on YouTube.
- [`D2-C749`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Discover is not included in Google Trends, because Discover is a content feed with no search box, while Trends counts only the queries people type into Google Search or YouTube.
- [`D2-C750`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Trends**: Google's Trends FAQ says Google Trends filters out searches made by Google products and services, including the internal searches made by AI Mode and AI Overviews.
- [`D2-C751`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends cannot show demand that reaches people through the Discover feed, so Discover visibility has to be judged from Search Console's Discover performance report rather than from Trends.
- [`D2-C755`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends data can be viewed for the whole world, for a single country or for a region within a country, for example Spain or Catalonia.
- [`D2-C756`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google said Google Trends data is almost real time, reaching up to a few minutes before the moment of viewing.
- [`D2-C758`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends offers time ranges from the past hour or the past day back to 2004, so search patterns can be compared across two decades.
- [`D2-C760`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends has two flagship experiences: the Explore page and Trending now.
- [`D2-C761`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Trends**: The Google Trends Explore page, which Google called the heart of Trends, shows search interest in a query or topic and how it changes over time.
- [`D2-C764`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Trends**: Google's Trends Help says Google Trends compares up to 8 groups of terms at once, with up to 50 terms in each group, while Classic explore (the legacy page) supports 5 groups of up to 25 terms.
- [`D2-C765`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Trending now, a tab at the top of Google Trends, shows the topics people are searching for on Google right now.
- [`D2-C766`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Trends**: Google said Trends' Trending now covered 125 countries at the time of the talk (October 2026), plus regions within many of those countries.
- [`D2-C767`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Trends**: Google's August 2024 blog post said Trending now was available in 125 countries, with regional trends in 40 of them; the current Trends Help page says 100+ countries and regions.
- [`D2-C774`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Real-world events such as product launches show up directly in Google Trends search interest graphs.
- [`D2-C775`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: To judge a launch or campaign in Google Trends, compare the brand's baseline search interest before and after the spike, not only the height of the spike, because a lasting baseline lift is the durable gain.
- [`D2-C776`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: A Google Trends chart of worldwide search interest in AI from 2004 to mid-2025 showed a huge rise in the two to three years before mid-2025.
- [`D2-C777`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: An early-2012 worldwide spike in Google Trends search interest for 'ai' was caused by the global hit song 'Ai Se Eu Te Pego', whose title contains the Portuguese word 'ai', not by interest in artificial intelligence.
- [`D2-C778`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: A Google Trends engineer found the cause of the 2012 'ai' spike by zooming in on that time range on the Explore page and reading the related queries.
- [`D2-C779`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google advised being curious and digging deeper when explaining a pattern in Google Trends, because context matters and the obvious explanation is sometimes wrong.
- [`D2-C780`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Trends**: Google's Trends FAQ says Google Trends adds statistical noise to protect privacy, so one-off spikes on queries with low or no search interest may be noise rather than real search activity.
- [`D2-C781`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Before treating a spike in an ambiguous keyword as demand for your topic, zoom in on the period in Google Trends and check the commonly searched queries, since another meaning of the word (as with 'ai' in 2012) may be driving it.
- [`D2-C782`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Worldwide Google Trends search interest for ski since 2004 shows strong seasonality, peaking every winter.
- [`D2-C783`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Worldwide Google Trends search interest for ski also shows a mostly steady decline since 2004, which can be misread as falling search volume.
- [`D2-C784`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends shows search interest, not search volume: each point on its 0 to 100 scale represents the share of searches for the term out of all searches.
- [`D2-C785`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Because total Google searches were far fewer in 2004 than today, a falling search interest share in Google Trends can hide a rising number of searches.
- [`D2-C786`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google said its internal numbers show the actual volume of ski-related searches is going up, even though ski's share of all searches in Google Trends has declined since 2004.
- [`D2-C787`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google stressed that the difference between search interest and search volume matters most when reading very long time ranges in Google Trends.
- [`D2-C788`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: A Google Trends line that falls over many years is not proof that a market is shrinking; compare terms against each other in the same chart, and take absolute numbers from keyword tools or Search Console impressions.
- [`D2-C789`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google presented three uses of Google Trends for content creation, marketing and SEO: keyword selection, scheduling and ideation.
- [`D2-C791`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google recommended using the keywords with higher search interest in Google Trends in page titles and marketing campaigns.
- [`D2-C792`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google's Search Central guide to Google Trends says to use Trends to inform a content strategy only where a topic fits the business and its users, and to focus on terms where the site has expertise and experience.
- [`D2-C793`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Compare candidate keywords in Google Trends for the exact country or region where the page should rank, because the higher-interest wording can differ between markets that share a language.
- [`D2-C795`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends' commonly searched queries come as top queries, with the highest search interest or volume, and rising queries, with the largest increase from the previous time frame to the current one.
- [`D2-C796`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google recommended checking both the top and the rising commonly searched queries in Google Trends when selecting keywords.
- [`D2-C797`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: In Google Trends' commonly searched queries, rising queries point to emerging sub-topics worth a new page or section, while top queries show the established wording to reuse in titles and headings.
- [`D2-C799`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Where a topic is seasonal in Google Trends, Google said the pattern predicts the next wave of search interest, which is the time to run a marketing campaign or have content ready.
- [`D2-C800`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: A Google Trends chart of US search interest over five years showed umbrella and sunscreen correlated, both peaking in June, against the common assumption that umbrella searches peak in winter.
- [`D2-C802`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google warned that assumptions about when search interest peaks are sometimes wrong, and advised checking the pattern in Google Trends for your own target market.
- [`D2-C803`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Publish or refresh seasonal content a few weeks before the seasonal rise that Google Trends shows for each target country, so the pages are crawled and indexed before demand peaks.
- [`D2-C804`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: For ideation, Google recommended Google Trends' Trending now, where a real-world event shows up within about ten minutes as people hear the news and search for it.
- [`D2-C805`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google said journalists use Google Trends' Trending now every morning to find content gaps: topics people are searching for that their publication may need to cover.
- [`D2-C807`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends' Suggest search terms picks the search terms or topics to compare from a plain-language request, which helps in a field you know little about, for example the most popular jazz singers in Japan.
- [`D2-C808`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends' Suggest search terms combines Gemini's knowledge of the world with Google Trends data.
- [`D2-C809`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends' Suggest search terms compares up to eight search terms at once.
- [`D2-C810`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google said the search terms returned by Google Trends' Suggest search terms are ranked by search interest.
- [`D2-C812`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Clicking a Google Trends quick comparison chip overlays the search interest of the two time periods being compared.
- [`D2-C814`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Search Engine Roundtable reported on 19 August 2026 that Google Trends had added explore maps and a regional breakdown that morning, as announced by Google on LinkedIn.
- [`D2-C817`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: The regional search interest maps in Google Trends give a quick first check of demand by country or region before localising content for a new market.
- [`D2-C818`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Trends**: Trends TV, at trends.google.com/tv, is a little-known Google Trends dashboard of what is trending on Google right now, meant for an office screen or as a screensaver.
- [`D2-C819`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **Google Trends**: Google has published a YouTube series of about eight episodes on using Google Trends for research, journalism, marketing and SEO.
- [`D3-C015`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **Google Trends**: Google said the difference between words and entities can be seen in Google Trends, where a term can be searched as words or as an entity (Trends calls these a search term and a topic).
- [`D3-C104`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) **Google Trends**: To choose what to cover in depth, a community speaker's team used Google Trends to find what people in their market were interested in and then gave them that content.
- [`D3-C581`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) **Google Trends**: A Google slide showed nine Google Trends charts of trust-checking searches in several markets and languages (source line: Google Trends, January 2016 to March 2026, web search), all rising toward the end of the range: 'is [brand] legit?' (two panels), '[brand] è affidabile?', '[brand] jest bezpieczne?', 'Is [brand] betrouwbaar?', 'Ist [brand] seriös?', '[brand] est fiable?', '¿es [brand] falso?' and 'trustpilot'.
- [`D3-C582`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) **Google Trends**: Google Trends shows a rise since about 2020 in searches of the form 'is [brand] legit', in the UK and in most other countries Google looked at.
- [`D3-C594`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S16-mastering-the-messy-middle.md) **Google Trends**: Track trust queries about your brand, such as '[brand] legit', '[brand] reviews' or '[brand] seriös', in Search Console and Google Trends for each market, and answer them on the site, for example with a trust or about page, instead of leaving the answer to third-party review sites.

### Googlebot (`googlebot`): 68

- [`D1-C037`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Googlebot**: For classic Search, crawling means Googlebot, scheduling and robots.txt, with AI used in parts such as scheduling. Indexing is one big but not limitless index that calculates signals and understands more than words, with AI such as BERT. Serving uses hundreds of signals tailored to the moment, with AI such as RankBrain.
- [`D1-C203`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Googlebot**: A crawler is software that downloads pages, extracts their links and repeats the process on the links it extracted; Googlebot is the main crawler of Google Search.
- [`D1-C136`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Googlebot**: Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot currently fetches only the first 2MB of each URL, HTTP headers included (64MB for PDFs); bytes past that cutoff are not fetched, rendered or indexed, and each resource the page loads has its own separate limit.
- [`D1-C137`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Googlebot**: Google's Inside Googlebot post warns that bloated inline base64 images, large blocks of inline CSS or JavaScript, or megabytes of menus can push a page's text or structured data past Googlebot's 2MB cutoff, and advises moving heavy CSS and JavaScript to external files and placing meta tags, the title, the canonical and essential structured data high in the HTML.
- [`D1-C322`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Googlebot**: Googlebot is an ordinary HTTP client with nothing special about it: like a browser, it fetches a URL it was given and returns the fetched bytes to Google's servers.
- [`D1-C325`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Googlebot**: Googlebot is the crawler Google uses for web search, including Search's AI features.
- [`D1-C342`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Googlebot**: Google's Inside Googlebot post (March 2026) says Googlebot is today just one user of a centralized crawling platform, and that dozens of other clients, such as Google Shopping and AdSense, send their crawl requests through the same infrastructure under other crawler names, with only the larger ones documented.
- [`D1-C344`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **Googlebot**: On stage Google spoke of probably hundreds, if not thousands, of crawlers, while its Inside Googlebot post speaks of dozens of other clients; both agree that only the larger crawlers are documented, so a Google user agent missing from the public lists is not proof of a fake request, and reverse DNS or Google's published IP ranges are the test.
- [`D1-C078`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Googlebot**: For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent.
- [`D1-C138`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Googlebot**: Google's page on verifying its crawlers says Googlebot and Google's other common crawlers resolve to crawl-*.googlebot.com or geo-crawl-*.geo.googlebot.com host names, special-case crawlers to rate-limited-proxy-*.google.com and user-triggered fetchers to *.gae.googleusercontent.com or google-proxy-*.google.com, and it publishes each group's IP ranges as JSON files such as common-crawlers.json and special-crawlers.json.
- [`D1-C366`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Googlebot**: Google treats a 402 Payment Required response as a 404 Not Found, because Googlebot cannot pay for content.
- [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Googlebot**: CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D1-C372`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Googlebot**: Do not answer verified Googlebot with 401, 402 or 403, for example from a login wall, a paywall or a pay-per-crawl setup: Google treats them like 404 and drops the pages, and Google's status code page says not to use 401 or 403 to limit crawling; to slow crawling temporarily, return 429 or 503.
- [`D1-C079`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **googlebot**: The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.
- [`D1-C083`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Googlebot**: Under the example file, Googlebot may crawl /, /politics/eu-vote and /sports/live/, and is blocked from /?utm_source=x, /index.html, /politics (no trailing slash), /live/ and /sports/live-score. An 'allow: /$' rule does not cover the homepage with tracking parameters.
- [`D1-C087`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Googlebot**: Googlebot ignores an unknown line, such as a Content-signal line, placed between two user-agent lines and joins both user agents into one group, so the rules that follow apply to both; in the slide's example both are blocked.
- [`D1-C123`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Googlebot**: Bing closes the robots.txt group at an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines, so in the slide's example bingbot ends up not blocked while Googlebot is; the slide warned that different crawlers behave differently.
- [`D1-C519`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Googlebot**: A user-agent line with its allow and disallow rules forms a user-agent group, and one group can name several crawlers (the talk's example: Googlebot and Bingbot); give named crawlers their own group only when they need rules the * group should not grant to every crawler.
- [`D1-C531`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Googlebot**: In the talk's quiz, the answer for letting Googlebot crawl /staging/preview/ while keeping the rest of /staging/ closed to it was a user-agent: googlebot group with both rules, disallow /staging/ and allow /staging/preview/, rather than an allow in the * group or a Googlebot group with only the allow.
- [`D1-C533`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **googlebot**: Dave Smart said robots.txt groups are not additive: if a group matches a crawler's user agent, only that group's rules apply, so a googlebot group that blocks /dogs/ leaves Googlebot free to crawl the /goats/ and /cows/ that the * group blocks.
- [`D1-C536`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **Googlebot**: Dave Smart said this applies to all redirects, not only JavaScript ones; his examples: a redirect through an external authorisation service that is blocked by its own robots.txt, content that moved through several URLs over the years with one of them later blocked, and unexpected redirects, such as one served only to Googlebot's user agent.
- [`D1-C108`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Googlebot**: The non-standard crawl-delay rule is not processed by Googlebot, so it does not save any crawl budget.
- [`D1-C141`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Googlebot**: Google's guide to A/B testing says never to show one set of URLs to Googlebot and a different set to humans: that is cloaking, which is against Google's spam policies whether or not a test is running.
- [`D1-C375`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Googlebot**: Googlebot as a single standalone crawler is a historical idea: Google crawls through a centralised crawling infrastructure, so a request from a Google user agent in server logs is a request routed through that shared platform.
- [`D1-C387`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Googlebot**: An audience member asked, in questions submitted before the event, how often Googlebot should be expected to visit a site now that AI Mode has rolled out, and whether AI means more crawling.
- [`D1-C419`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **Googlebot**: A 404 fetch is still a fetch: Google's 2017 crawl budget post says generally any URL Googlebot crawls counts towards a site's crawl budget, so the stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget is best read as 'they do not slow crawling, and a 404 tells Google to crawl that URL less over time'.
- [`D1-C443`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: To judge crawl efficiency, check Search Console's Crawl Stats report: whether total crawling has plateaued over time, and whether the average response time shows the server is fast enough or is limiting Googlebot.
- [`D1-C467`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: To check that new content is crawled fast enough, Gary Illyes advised measuring the time between publishing a URL and Googlebot's first crawl of it: ideally it stays flat or falls, and only a rising trend calls for investigation.
- [`D1-C469`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site.
- [`D1-C473`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: Files such as cats.txt have no importance for Google Search: if a site links to one, Googlebot will find and crawl it, but it has no other effect.
- [`D1-C481`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: An audience member asked whether Google plans dedicated user agents for AI, as OpenAI has several, so that site owners can control AI access separately from Googlebot and analyse it in their logs.
- [`D1-C484`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: A Google panelist called blocking all AI crawlers while allowing search crawlers such as Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot a personal, philosophical decision that every site owner can make.
- [`D1-C486`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: The panel spoke of blocking Google's 'AI crawling or training' with Google-Extended, but Google documents Google-Extended as a usage token, not a crawler: disallowing it does not stop Googlebot fetching pages and only controls use for Gemini training and grounding.
- [`D1-C491`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot** (in the quote): If paginated pages are replaced by a load-more button or infinite scroll without crawlable links to them, Google will not see the further pages at all.
- [`D1-C494`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: To check whether Google lowered a site's crawl capacity limit, look at the number of connections Googlebot opens to the site: if it has dropped, the capacity limit changed.
- [`D1-C114`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: A Google panelist called pagination one of the trickiest things in web development and said switching to infinite scroll or a load-more button is risky, depending on what you want to achieve, because Googlebot does not click buttons.
- [`D1-C543`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: Gary Illyes said that if the time from publishing to Googlebot's first crawl starts rising, how much it rises matters: for the crawling of fresh stories, something like two hours is probably not great (a smaller example figure is unclear in the recording).
- [`D1-C546`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: A Google panelist illustrated a crawl capacity limit drop as a step down in the site's hostload, for example from 10 to 5, which the panelist said means Googlebot then makes up to five requests per second (the recording adds 'per connection', which is unclear).
- [`D1-C547`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **Googlebot**: Google's crawl budget guide does not express the crawl capacity limit in requests per second: it limits the total time a server spends holding connections open for Google, counting both the number of parallel connections and their duration. That fits the panel's advice to watch how many connections Googlebot opens (D1-C494): fewer connections is the documented form of a lower capacity limit.
- [`D1-C075`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **Googlebot**: Googlebot does not support HTTP/3 today.
- [`D2-C001`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **Googlebot**: An audience member asked whether HTML sitemaps still matter for large sites, whether they improve Googlebot's crawl discovery and whether they pass link equity to deeper pages.
- [`D2-C839`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **Googlebot**: An audience member asked how several sloppy migrations on the same domain can affect Googlebot's crawling.
- [`D2-C040`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **Googlebot**: Google cannot extract a link from an a element that only has an onclick handler, because Googlebot does not click, so the JavaScript is never triggered.
- [`D2-C057`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **googlebot**: The robots meta tag is written as `<meta name="robots" content="rule1,rule2">`, or with the name googlebot instead of robots, with several rules separated by commas.
- [`D2-C095`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **googlebot**: Google's Search documentation gives notranslate as a rule for a robots or googlebot meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header, and says the rule opts a page out of all translation features in Google Search.
- [`D2-C098`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **googlebot**: International sites should remove notranslate from their templates unless translation must be prevented: the robots or googlebot form switches off Google Search's translation features, and John Mueller said the form named google also blocks Chrome's translation for visitors who do not read the language.
- [`D2-C101`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **Googlebot**: Google's robots meta tag specification says Googlebot considerably decreases the crawl rate of a URL after the date and time set in its unavailable_after rule.
- [`D2-C131`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.
- [`D2-C164`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: Google says Googlebot and its Web Rendering Service identify resources that do not contribute to essential page content, such as reporting and error requests, and may not fetch them, so client-side analytics may not give a full or accurate picture of their activity.
- [`D2-C169`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says Googlebot extracts links twice, from the HTML response before rendering and again from the rendered HTML, so links injected with JavaScript can be found if they use crawlable `<a href>` markup.
- [`D2-C197`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: Lazy loading triggered by a scroll event listener, such as window.addEventListener('scroll', loadMoreProducts), never runs for Googlebot because Googlebot does not scroll.
- [`D2-C206`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: Google says its Web Rendering Service fetches the resources a page references through Googlebot, including JavaScript, CSS and XHR requests to APIs, but not images or videos.
- [`D2-C266`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: Google named three causes of content missing from the rendered HTML: JavaScript inaccessible to Googlebot, JavaScript DOM event triggers and disabled browser APIs.
- [`D2-C267`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: When the JavaScript is not accessible to Googlebot, Google cannot render the client-side DOM that the page builds asynchronously, so parts of the page may be present while the main content is absent.
- [`D2-C278`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Googlebot**: For effects that need WebGL, which Googlebot does not support, Google's guide to fixing JavaScript problems suggests skipping the effect or prerendering it with server-side rendering so that the content is accessible to Googlebot.
- [`D2-C374`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **Googlebot**: A growing cause of wrong clustering is bot protection: when a CDN or another protection system shows Googlebot the same 'you look like a bot, solve this puzzle' page on many unrelated URLs or domains, Google can cluster those pages as duplicates.
- [`D2-C375`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **Googlebot**: Google's systems find it very hard to recognise a bot-challenge page as an error page, and Googlebot cannot solve the puzzles, such as selecting all the cats, that those pages ask for.
- [`D2-C378`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **Googlebot**: Check what your CDN or bot protection serves to verified Googlebot and to the AI agents you want to allow; if crawlers must get a challenge page, return it with a 503 status as Google recommends, never as a 200 page across many URLs, which Google may cluster as duplicates.
- [`D2-C561`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **Googlebot**: Google's documentation says Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses and sends no Accept-Language header, so pages that change content or redirect by the visitor's perceived country or language may not have every version crawled, indexed or ranked; it recommends separate URLs annotated with hreflang.
- [`D3-C097`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) **Googlebot**: In Lightning session K (Facets of quality), a community speaker argued that SEO is for humans: write for people and the problems they have, rather than to please Googlebot.
- [`D3-C107`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) **Googlebot**: Because Googlebot is not a human, the speaker's team at the time thought more about Googlebot than about human readers, a community speaker said.
- [`D3-C108`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) **Googlebot**: A community speaker compared Googlebot to an inspector who cannot enter the shop and only looks through the window, seeing the page as ones and zeros, which the speaker linked to tokenization.
- [`D3-C109`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) **Googlebot**: The inspector metaphor blends two steps: Googlebot fetches pages during crawling, while tokenization happens later when the page is processed for the index, as Google explained on Day 2.
- [`D3-C116`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S04-lightning-session-k-facets-of-quality.md) **Googlebot**: Google's long-standing advice to write for people and give them what they want has become true in practice because Googlebot has become more and more human, a community speaker argued.
- [`D3-C301`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **Googlebot**: For developers, Google's five listed spam types map to concrete checks: serve Googlebot the same content as users (cloaking), avoid near-identical location or keyword pages (doorways), add value to reused content (scraped content), and patch and monitor the CMS against injected pages and links (hacked content).
- [`D3-C385`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Googlebot**: Google Shopping uses its own crawler, Storebot (Storebot-Google), instead of Googlebot because it needs fresh product information, prices, availability and shipping details and therefore crawls much more often.
- [`D3-C387`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Googlebot**: Storebot-Google also does deep crawls, for example of checkout pages, which do not belong in the search index; this is another reason it is kept separate from Googlebot.
- [`D3-C390`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Googlebot**: Treat Storebot-Google separately from Googlebot in robots.txt and bot protection: a shop that blocks it on product, cart or checkout paths can undermine Shopping price and availability checks, even when Googlebot is allowed.

### Grounding (`grounding`): 11

- [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **grounding**: AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D1-C308`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **grounding**: A community speaker said Microsoft is ahead of Google in giving site owners the grounding queries its AI uses.
- [`D1-C309`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **grounding**: A community speaker described the retrieval stage as whether an AI requests a site's pages when grounding its answer; if it does not, the cause may be a crawling or an indexing issue.
- [`D1-C486`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **grounding**: The panel spoke of blocking Google's 'AI crawling or training' with Google-Extended, but Google documents Google-Extended as a usage token, not a crawler: disallowing it does not stop Googlebot fetching pages and only controls use for Gemini training and grounding.
- [`D2-C067`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **grounding**: nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D2-C121`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **grounding**: Google's crawler documentation defines grounding in Gemini Apps and in Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI as providing content from the Google Search index to the model at prompt time, and sites manage whether their content is used for it with the Google-Extended robots.txt token.
- [`D2-C123`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **grounding**: Google documents Gemini grounding only as content from the Search index at prompt time; the live read of a specific page at a user's request, described on stage, is not documented, so it is unclear whether it works like a user-triggered fetcher, which generally ignores robots.txt, or follows Google-Extended.
- [`D2-C477`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **grounding**: As far as the speaker knows, in most of Google's main AI uses a page's schema.org markup is not turned into text and put directly into the model's context; the data is first sorted out, checked for quality and indexed before it is passed on as grounding context.
- [`D3-C057`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **grounding**: Google's slide on how LLM features with grounding generally work showed a query going to both the search engine and an LLM, the search engine's results going to the LLM, the LLM generating fan-out queries that go back to the search engine, and the LLM returning answers with links.
- [`D3-C094`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **grounding**: Google's Gemini API documentation on grounding with Google Search says the model automatically generates and runs one or more search queries when needed, and the response lists the search queries it executed.
- [`D3-C687`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **grounding**: Adding grounding or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) on top of a model reduces hallucinations but cannot eliminate them.

### hreflang (`hreflang-annotation`): 49

- [`D2-C033`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **hreflang**: Google extracts hreflang annotations, through which site owners specify the language variants of their content, to know whether a page has an equivalent with similar content in another language.
- [`D2-C034`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **hreflang**: The speaker said that knowing a page's other-language versions from hreflang is useful in ranking.
- [`D2-C035`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **hreflang**: Put rel=canonical and hreflang link elements in the head of the HTML the server sends, not only in JavaScript-rendered HTML, so Google can read them during HTML parsing without depending on rendering.
- [`D2-C353`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **hreflang**: Alternate names also serve localization: if Google knows that country versions such as you.de and you.at are equivalent, it can pick the right version to show using hreflang.
- [`D2-C382`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **hreflang**: When localized pages are clustered, Google tries to use hreflang alternates; the speaker's short version of the advice was to use hreflang, which he called really helpful for same-language, different-country content.
- [`D2-C384`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **hreflang**: For German-language sites serving Germany, Austria and Switzerland, add hreflang with region codes (de-DE, de-AT, de-CH) and make the country pages differ in more than boilerplate (prices, shipping, legal details), or expect Google to cluster them and show one.
- [`D2-C385`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **hreflang**: Google's canonical guide says that for canonicalization Google prefers URLs that are part of hreflang clusters: if German pages for Germany and Switzerland point to each other with hreflang but not to the Austrian page, the German and Swiss pages are preferred as canonicals.
- [`D2-C396`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **hreflang**: Google's closing suggestions on duplication: use redirects for site migrations, use HTTP result codes, don't block agents, check your rel=canonical links, use hreflang links to help Google localize, report weird canonicals in the forums, make secure pages that work, and keep canonical signals clear.
- [`D2-C400`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **hreflang**: Before a migration or template change, align every canonical signal for the preferred URL (redirects, rel=canonical, internal links, sitemap entries, hreflang and working HTTPS); Google says it follows the site owner only when the signals agree.
- [`D2-C434`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **hreflang**: Language versions of a page should be connected with hreflang annotations instead of canonical links.
- [`D2-C435`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **hreflang**: Google's guide to specifying canonical URLs says that on pages using hreflang, the canonical should be a page in the same language, or the best possible substitute language if no canonical page exists in the same language.
- [`D2-C436`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **hreflang**: Check that every canonical group contains a single document language: a group spanning languages means canonicals are joining versions that hreflang should connect, and each language version should keep its own self-referencing canonical.
- [`D2-C561`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's documentation says Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses and sends no Accept-Language header, so pages that change content or redirect by the visitor's perceived country or language may not have every version crawled, indexed or ranked; it recommends separate URLs annotated with hreflang.
- [`D2-C563`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's hreflang guide says language-specific subdomains such as en, en-gb or de in a URL are not used to determine a page's target audience; site owners must map the audience explicitly, for example with hreflang.
- [`D2-C564`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's hreflang example lists every language version in the page's HTML head as a link element with rel=alternate, the version's full URL and its hreflang code (en, en-gb, es), including the page's own URL.
- [`D2-C565`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Missing return links are a common hreflang mistake: if page X names page Y as a language version, page Y must link back to page X.
- [`D2-C566`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Each page in an hreflang set must also list its own URL, and a missing self-reference is a common mistake Google sees.
- [`D2-C567`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: When the HTML head is not suitable for a page, hreflang can be given by other methods instead, such as listing the language versions in a sitemap.
- [`D2-C568`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Any one hreflang method is fine, but a site should use only one: Google often sees sites using two or three methods at the same time, with annotations that conflict.
- [`D2-C569`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's hreflang guide says its three methods (link elements in the HTML head, an HTTP Link header, which suits non-HTML files such as PDFs, and an XML sitemap) are equivalent; using several at once is allowed but brings no benefit in Search and is harder to manage.
- [`D2-C570`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google ignores hreflang annotations that point only one way, where page A names page B as a language version but page B does not name page A back.
- [`D2-C571`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's hreflang guide says a site that finds it hard to keep every language pair bidirectional may omit some languages on some pages, because Google still processes the pairs that point to each other; new language versions should at least link both ways with the original or dominant language.
- [`D2-C572`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google requires hreflang return links because an alternate URL is a full URL that can be on any domain, so without them any site could declare itself a language version of someone else's website.
- [`D2-C573`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's hreflang guide says alternate URLs must be fully qualified, including the protocol (https://example.com/foo, not //example.com/foo or /foo), and need not be on the same domain.
- [`D2-C574`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Audit hreflang per cluster rather than per page: check that every page lists itself and all its alternates, that every alternate links back, and that only one method (HTML head, HTTP header or sitemap) supplies the annotations.
- [`D2-C575`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: hreflang language codes must be ISO 639-1 codes: Google's list of common mistakes marked se, dk and cz (the country codes of Sweden, Denmark and Czechia) as wrong and sv, da and cs (Swedish, Danish, Czech) as right.
- [`D2-C577`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Site owners do not need to memorise hreflang language and region codes, but should double-check every code when implementing hreflang.
- [`D2-C578`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Czech is a frequent hreflang error: CZ is the country code and ccTLD of Czechia, but the language code for Czech is cs.
- [`D2-C579`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: hreflang region codes must be ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 country codes; frequent mistakes are UK instead of GB for the United Kingdom, SW instead of CH for Switzerland and GE instead of DE for Germany.
- [`D2-C580`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: EU is not a valid hreflang region code: sites use it hoping to target the European Union, but hreflang targeting works only by country.
- [`D2-C581`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google also flagged LA used as a region code for Los Angeles (a city, not a country) and SA used for South Africa as wrong hreflang region codes.
- [`D2-C582`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: A region code cannot be used on its own in hreflang: en and en-GB are valid values, but GB alone is not, because the value must name a language.
- [`D2-C583`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Validate hreflang values against the ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 lists in a crawler rule or build check rather than by eye: reserved codes such as UK and EU are simply ignored, but some plausible mistakes are valid codes for something else (se is Northern Sami, GE Georgia, LA Laos, SA Saudi Arabia) and silently point the annotation at the wrong audience.
- [`D2-C584`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google does not use hreflang to determine a page's language when indexing the page.
- [`D2-C589`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's hreflang guide says pages that translate only the template (navigation, footer) around main content in one language still count as duplicates, because localized versions are duplicates only if the main content stays untranslated; it recommends hreflang for such pages.
- [`D2-C830`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's hreflang guide says the ISO 639-1 language code can be followed by a script in ISO 15924 format, such as zh-Hant or zh-Hans, and by an optional ISO 3166-1 Alpha-2 region code, as in zh-Hans-US.
- [`D2-C962`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **hreflang**: Google said incorrect hreflang language or region codes are a mistake it finds very often, with the same wrong codes coming up again and again, especially in Europe, because site owners assume the codes are easy.
- [`D2-C618`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: In a community speaker's audit case, a premium multifunctional-furniture maker about to be acquired had multilingual sites with clean translations by native speakers and hreflang tags that were in fairly good shape.
- [`D2-C625`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: When translations and hreflang are clean but one country version converts far worse, compare that market's product range, photography and delivery or installation constraints with local competitors before changing anything technical.
- [`D2-C626`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: A community speaker framed international SEO around three signals to settle before working on hreflang: language (what people can read), region (who the content is for) and authority (why local people should trust the site).
- [`D2-C628`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's documentation recommends hreflang annotations even when a site's versions differ only by small regional variations within one language, for example English-language content targeted to the US, GB and Ireland.
- [`D2-C631`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: A community speaker stressed that an hreflang annotation for a country (her example was German for Austria, de-AT) does not by itself make a site established or trusted in that country; local authority has to be worked for.
- [`D2-C632`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: Google's documentation lists the signals it uses to decide which locale a page targets: ccTLDs, hreflang statements, server location, and other signals such as local addresses and phone numbers, local language and currency, links from other local sites and Business Profile signals.
- [`D2-C633`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: A community speaker cited a Semrush study that found at least one hreflang error on 75% of multilingual websites; the study, reported in February 2017, audited 20,000 sites with several language versions (the speaker recalled it as about five years old).
- [`D2-C634`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: A community speaker said the SEO industry has treated hreflang as the hard part of international SEO; hreflang is complicated, but the real hard part is the homework of understanding consumers in each market.
- [`D2-C641`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **hreflang**: Treat hreflang as a way to show the right language version, not as a market-entry signal: before launching a country version, make sure local publications, partners or directories already mention the brand, and localise pricing and payment options.
- [`D2-C655`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **hreflang**: A site serving a smaller country in a big language, such as British English or Swiss German, should make that country unmistakable (country-code domain or region-specific hreflang, local address, prices and currency) so its pages can benefit from index selection's country balancing instead of competing with the much larger US or German content pool.
- [`D3-C010`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **hreflang**: Sites with several language versions should not leave brand searches to chance: annotate the versions with hreflang and offer a visible language switcher, because Google may have only the user's location and browser settings to choose a version.
- [`D3-C086`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **hreflang**: Make each page's language and target country unambiguous (one main language per page, hreflang between versions, local prices, addresses and shipping details), because Google applies language and country already at retrieval, before ranking.

### 200 (`http-200`): 23

- [`D1-C320`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **HTTP 200**: An HTTP 200 OK status only means that the server believes it managed to do what the client asked for.
- [`D1-C078`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **200**: For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent.
