- [`D1-C347`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **200**: When a crawler's request returns 200, the page, file or other resource that comes back is eligible for indexing.
- [`D1-C355`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **200**: A soft 404 is a 404 in disguise: the page returns 200 but its content says something like 'page not found', information the site should have sent as the HTTP status.
- [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **HTTP 200**: CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D1-C371`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **HTTP 200**: Day 1 said a CDN captcha page served with HTTP 200 becomes a soft 404, while Day 2 (D2-C374, D2-C375) said such challenge pages are hard to recognise as errors and can be clustered as duplicates; Google's CDN post describes both outcomes, and in both the real pages drop out of Search.
- [`D2-C009`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **200**: An audience member asked whether a product detail page that is out of stock for two to three months should keep returning 200 with links to similar products, or be 302-redirected to a similar product or to its parent product listing page.
- [`D2-C014`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **200**: Keep a product page that is out of stock for a few months live with a 200 status, show its availability on the page and in Product structured data, and offer pre-ordering where possible when users would wait for the product. Redirect it only when users would rather switch to a similar product than wait.
- [`D2-C131`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **200**: Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.
- [`D2-C132`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **200**: The stage remark that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering does not mean such pages skip rendering, because Google's guide queues every 200 page for rendering; read it as: content already in the raw HTML does not depend on the slower rendering pass.
- [`D2-C183`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **HTTP 200**: A community speaker listed four common but often overlooked JavaScript rendering mistakes: non-crawlable link markup, error pages that return HTTP 200 in single-page apps, content behind user interaction, and JavaScript or API resources blocked in robots.txt.
- [`D2-C190`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **HTTP 200**: In single-page apps, a missing page often shows a custom 404 page while the server returns HTTP 200, because the front-end router, not the server, handles the 404.
- [`D2-C191`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **200**: The fix for a client-side soft 404 is to make a missing page end with a real HTTP 404 status code instead of 200.
- [`D2-C257`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **200**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics says every page with a 200 status code is queued for rendering, whether or not it uses JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header says not to index it; for non-200 pages such as 404 error pages, rendering might be skipped.
- [`D2-C264`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **200**: Google's slide defined a soft 404 in a JavaScript application as a page that serves a 'Not Found' message but returns a 200 HTTP status code.
- [`D2-C291`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **200**: In JavaScript single-page apps, soft 404s typically arise because the server returns the app with a 200 status for every URL, so when the app shows a 'not found' message for a URL that does not exist, no error is reported.
- [`D2-C295`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **200**: After moving to real paths, set the server or hosting rewrite rules so a direct request to every valid path returns 200 with the content (ideally server-rendered) and an unknown path returns a 404 status, which removes client-side soft 404s at the source.
- [`D2-C334`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **HTTP 200**: A soft 404 is a page that should return an error status code but returns HTTP 200; from a crawling point of view it looks indexable, but because it has no real content Google throws it out of the index.
- [`D2-C342`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **200**: Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.
- [`D2-C376`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **200**: Google's Search Central post on CDNs says that if Google cannot recognise an error message served with a 200 status as an error, all pages showing the same message may be dropped from the index as duplicates, and recovery can be slow because Google has little incentive to recrawl duplicates. For bot-verification interstitials it recommends sending crawlers a 503 status.
- [`D2-C378`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **200**: Check what your CDN or bot protection serves to verified Googlebot and to the AI agents you want to allow; if crawlers must get a challenge page, return it with a 503 status as Google recommends, never as a 200 page across many URLs, which Google may cluster as duplicates.
- [`D2-C903`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **HTTP 200**: A community speaker warned that HTTP 200 responses across a new domain show only that the URLs work, not that the content users came for is still there, so after launch the redirect map becomes the test.
- [`D3-C676`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **200**: The stage doubt that every URL gets rendered sits beside Google's JavaScript guide, which says every page with a 200 status is queued for rendering unless a robots rule blocks indexing: queued is not the same as rendered, so do not rely on rendering for critical content.

### 403 (`http-403`): 4

- [`D1-C352`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **403**: A 403 response tells Google's crawler it has no permission to see the requested content, so there is nothing for Google to index.
- [`D1-C365`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **403**: Google has recently seen more 403 responses to its crawlers (described on stage as 'authentication required'); it treats them as client errors, technically equivalent to 404 or 410, and drops those pages from Search and its AI features.
- [`D1-C372`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **403**: Do not answer verified Googlebot with 401, 402 or 403, for example from a login wall, a paywall or a pay-per-crawl setup: Google treats them like 404 and drops the pages, and Google's status code page says not to use 401 or 403 to limit crawling; to slow crawling temporarily, return 429 or 503.
- [`D1-C509`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **403**: Google has seen an uptick in 402 Payment Required responses to its crawlers, an even more recent trend than the rise in 403 responses.

### 404 (`http-404`): 24

- [`D1-C351`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **404 Not Found**: 404 Not Found and 410 Gone both tell Google there is nothing at the URL, so the URL is not indexable.
- [`D1-C355`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **404**: A soft 404 is a 404 in disguise: the page returns 200 but its content says something like 'page not found', information the site should have sent as the HTTP status.
- [`D1-C365`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **404**: Google has recently seen more 403 responses to its crawlers (described on stage as 'authentication required'); it treats them as client errors, technically equivalent to 404 or 410, and drops those pages from Search and its AI features.
- [`D1-C366`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **404 Not Found**: Google treats a 402 Payment Required response as a 404 Not Found, because Googlebot cannot pay for content.
- [`D1-C372`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **404**: Do not answer verified Googlebot with 401, 402 or 403, for example from a login wall, a paywall or a pay-per-crawl setup: Google treats them like 404 and drops the pages, and Google's status code page says not to use 401 or 403 to limit crawling; to slow crawling temporarily, return 429 or 503.
- [`D1-C102`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **404**: If faceted URLs must be crawled, use the standard & separator, keep filters in a consistent order, and return a 404 when a filter combination has no results.
- [`D1-C109`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **404**: Google advises against using noindex to save crawl budget and against using robots.txt to temporarily reallocate budget. Use robots.txt only for pages you never want crawled, and 404 or 410 for removed pages.
- [`D1-C419`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **404**: A 404 fetch is still a fetch: Google's 2017 crawl budget post says generally any URL Googlebot crawls counts towards a site's crawl budget, so the stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget is best read as 'they do not slow crawling, and a 404 tells Google to crawl that URL less over time'.
- [`D2-C190`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **404**: In single-page apps, a missing page often shows a custom 404 page while the server returns HTTP 200, because the front-end router, not the server, handles the 404.
- [`D2-C191`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **404**: The fix for a client-side soft 404 is to make a missing page end with a real HTTP 404 status code instead of 200.
- [`D2-C192`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **404**: Google's JavaScript guides say that when client-side routing makes a real 404 status impractical, a single-page app can avoid soft 404s by redirecting with JavaScript to a URL whose server returns 404, or by adding a robots noindex meta tag with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C193`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **404**: In a single-page app, let the server return 404 for unknown routes where possible; otherwise use one of the two client-side fixes Google documents for error views: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns 404, or a robots noindex added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C257`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **404**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics says every page with a 200 status code is queued for rendering, whether or not it uses JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header says not to index it; for non-200 pages such as 404 error pages, rendering might be skipped.
- [`D2-C292`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **404**: The fix for a client-side soft 404 is to serve a real 404 error page where appropriate; how to detect URLs that do not exist depends on how the app works and where it is hosted.
- [`D2-C293`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **404**: In an app routed with the History API, when a user reaches a page that does not exist, Erin Sparling suggested asking how they got there and redirecting to a real 404 page.
- [`D2-C294`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **404**: For client-side rendered single-page apps, where meaningful status codes can be impossible or impractical, Google's documentation gives two ways to avoid soft 404s: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns a 404 status, or a noindex robots meta tag added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C295`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **404**: After moving to real paths, set the server or hosting rewrite rules so a direct request to every valid path returns 200 with the content (ideally server-rendered) and an unknown path returns a 404 status, which removes client-side soft 404s at the source.
- [`D2-C342`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **404**: Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.
- [`D2-C372`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **404**: Make location and variant pages differ in their main content (local stock, staff, prices, addresses) and return 404 for empty or invalid combinations; otherwise every URL that fits the pattern can be folded into one canonical.
- [`D2-C911`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **404**: Google's site move guide says not to redirect many old URLs to one irrelevant destination such as the new site's home page, which can confuse users and might be treated as a soft 404, and to return a 404 or 410 for deleted or merged content that is not moved to the new site.
- [`D2-C913`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **404**: For URLs removed in a consolidation, return 404 or 410: Google's site move guide names those two codes, and Google's crawlers treat every 4xx code except 429 the same way, as content that does not exist, so the choice between them matters less than not redirecting to an unrelated page.
- [`D3-C639`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **404**: After Google processes a page that now returns a 404 or a noindex, it usually removes the page from its serving index within one to three weeks, sometimes much sooner.
- [`D3-C653`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **404**: To hide a URL from Google Search urgently, use the Removals tool in Search Console (about 2 hours) and also add a noindex or a 404, which takes one to three weeks to drop the page from the index.
- [`D3-C673`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **404**: Google's Removals tool help says a temporary removal request usually takes up to a day to process and lasts only about six months, so the content must also be removed permanently, for example with a 404 or 410, a noindex or a password.

### 410 (`http-410`): 7

- [`D1-C351`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **410 Gone**: 404 Not Found and 410 Gone both tell Google there is nothing at the URL, so the URL is not indexable.
- [`D1-C365`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **410**: Google has recently seen more 403 responses to its crawlers (described on stage as 'authentication required'); it treats them as client errors, technically equivalent to 404 or 410, and drops those pages from Search and its AI features.
- [`D1-C109`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **410**: Google advises against using noindex to save crawl budget and against using robots.txt to temporarily reallocate budget. Use robots.txt only for pages you never want crawled, and 404 or 410 for removed pages.
- [`D2-C342`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **410**: Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.
- [`D2-C911`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **410**: Google's site move guide says not to redirect many old URLs to one irrelevant destination such as the new site's home page, which can confuse users and might be treated as a soft 404, and to return a 404 or 410 for deleted or merged content that is not moved to the new site.
- [`D2-C913`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **410**: For URLs removed in a consolidation, return 404 or 410: Google's site move guide names those two codes, and Google's crawlers treat every 4xx code except 429 the same way, as content that does not exist, so the choice between them matters less than not redirecting to an unrelated page.
- [`D3-C673`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **410**: Google's Removals tool help says a temporary removal request usually takes up to a day to process and lasts only about six months, so the content must also be removed permanently, for example with a 404 or 410, a noindex or a password.

### 429 (`http-429`): 10

- [`D1-C071`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **429**: 5xx and 429 responses prompt Google's crawlers to slow down temporarily. Already indexed URLs are preserved in the index for a while but eventually dropped.
- [`D1-C072`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **429**: 4xx status codes other than 429 have no effect on crawl rate.
- [`D1-C078`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **429**: For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent.
- [`D1-C353`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **429 Too Many Requests**: 429 Too Many Requests is the exception among 4xx codes: instead of meaning there is nothing at the URL, it tells Google's crawler to slow down, and Google slows its crawling.
- [`D1-C364`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **429**: A rise in HTTP errors in crawl reports can come from a CDN throttling crawlers by injecting 429 or 503 responses on the network path between Google's crawler and the site.
- [`D1-C372`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **429**: Do not answer verified Googlebot with 401, 402 or 403, for example from a login wall, a paywall or a pay-per-crawl setup: Google treats them like 404 and drops the pages, and Google's status code page says not to use 401 or 403 to limit crawling; to slow crawling temporarily, return 429 or 503.
- [`D1-C092`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **429**: Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down.
- [`D1-C386`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **429 Too Many Requests**: The stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget matches Google's documentation that 4xx codes have no effect on crawl rate (D1-C072), with one exception: 429 Too Many Requests counts as a server error and slows crawling like a 5xx (D1-C071, D1-C092).
- [`D2-C913`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **429**: For URLs removed in a consolidation, return 404 or 410: Google's site move guide names those two codes, and Google's crawlers treat every 4xx code except 429 the same way, as content that does not exist, so the choice between them matters less than not redirecting to an unrelated page.
- [`D3-C668`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **429**: Google's crawl rate guide says that when a significant number of URLs return 500, 503 or 429, Google reduces the site's crawl rate, which starts increasing again automatically once the errors drop; it warns against doing this for longer than 1-2 days.

- [`D1-C365`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **client errors**: Google has recently seen more 403 responses to its crawlers (described on stage as 'authentication required'); it treats them as client errors, technically equivalent to 404 or 410, and drops those pages from Search and its AI features.
- [`D1-C385`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **4xx**: 4xx responses do not affect a site's crawl budget, because Google expects pages, content and products to come and go as a natural part of the web.
- [`D1-C386`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **4xx**: The stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget matches Google's documentation that 4xx codes have no effect on crawl rate (D1-C072), with one exception: 429 Too Many Requests counts as a server error and slows crawling like a 5xx (D1-C071, D1-C092).
- [`D1-C419`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **4xx**: A 404 fetch is still a fetch: Google's 2017 crawl budget post says generally any URL Googlebot crawls counts towards a site's crawl budget, so the stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget is best read as 'they do not slow crawling, and a 404 tells Google to crawl that URL less over time'.
- [`D2-C913`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **4xx**: For URLs removed in a consolidation, return 404 or 410: Google's site move guide names those two codes, and Google's crawlers treat every 4xx code except 429 the same way, as content that does not exist, so the choice between them matters less than not redirecting to an unrelated page.

- [`D1-C364`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **503**: A rise in HTTP errors in crawl reports can come from a CDN throttling crawlers by injecting 429 or 503 responses on the network path between Google's crawler and the site.
- [`D1-C372`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **503**: Do not answer verified Googlebot with 401, 402 or 403, for example from a login wall, a paywall or a pay-per-crawl setup: Google treats them like 404 and drops the pages, and Google's status code page says not to use 401 or 403 to limit crawling; to slow crawling temporarily, return 429 or 503.
- [`D2-C342`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **503**: Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.

For bot-verification interstitials it recommends sending crawlers a 503 status.
