### 5xx (`http-5xx`): 12

- [`D1-C126`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **5xx**: Google treats network timeouts, connection resets and DNS errors like 5xx server errors: crawling slows down immediately, and already indexed URLs that stay unreachable are removed from Google's index within days.
- [`D1-C071`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **5xx**: 5xx and 429 responses prompt Google's crawlers to slow down temporarily. Already indexed URLs are preserved in the index for a while but eventually dropped.
- [`D1-C074`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **5xx**: If robots.txt returns a 5xx error, Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours, then uses the cached copy for up to 30 days.
- [`D1-C345`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **5xx**: HTTP status codes fall into five classes, 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and each class affects crawling differently.
- [`D1-C354`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **5xx errors**: Google slows crawling when a site returns 5xx errors, because a 5xx usually means the server, and often the whole site, cannot serve requests, and Google does not want to break the site.
- [`D1-C092`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **5xx**: Hostload is driven by changes in connect time, changes in time to first byte, and HTTP 429 or 5xx status codes. If these increase, hostload is adjusted and crawling slows down.
- [`D1-C099`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **server errors**: Three things burn crawl budget: server errors unrelated to server load, useless pages and resources, and infinite URL spaces.
- [`D1-C386`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **server error**: The stage point that 4xx responses do not affect crawl budget matches Google's documentation that 4xx codes have no effect on crawl rate (D1-C072), with one exception: 429 Too Many Requests counts as a server error and slows crawling like a 5xx (D1-C071, D1-C092).
- [`D1-C460`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **server error**: Chrome's Lighthouse documentation lists an llms.txt audit among its agentic browsing audits: it flags a server error when llms.txt is fetched and marks the audit not applicable when the file is missing, because providing the file is optional for now.
- [`D2-C210`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **5xx errors**: An API or CDN on its own host needs its own robots.txt check: a blanket Disallow there, or a robots.txt that returns 5xx errors, can stop Google fetching the data a page renders from.
- [`D2-C708`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **server errors**: The help page explains 'Discovered – currently not indexed' by expected server overload (capacity), while on stage it was explained as Google not wanting the URL yet (demand); the crawl budget guide covers both, so first rule out slow responses and server errors, then treat the status as a quality and demand problem.
- [`D3-C621`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **5xx errors**: Spoken and slide figures for capacity increases differ (one to three weeks, up to a month, versus 1-2 weeks typical and 1-3 weeks in recovery), but the lesson is the same: a burst of 5xx errors cuts crawling within hours and recovery takes weeks, so keep servers stable before launches and migrations.

### Index selection (`index-selection-concept`): 30

- [`D1-C211`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Index selection**: Index selection runs after signals are collected and duplicates are dropped, and decides what goes into Google's index, which is big but not limitless.
- [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **index selection**: A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.
- [`D2-C651`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **index selection**: Google detects the language of each document and weights language in index selection so that the index is not dominated by one or two languages.
- [`D2-C652`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **index selection**: Without language or country input to index selection, Google's index would become an English index, because so many documents on the web are in English.
- [`D2-C653`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **index selection**: Google also takes country into account in index selection, so that countries producing less content in a shared language, such as the UK for English or Switzerland for German, are not disadvantaged against the US or Germany, which produce most of it.
- [`D2-C655`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **index selection**: A site serving a smaller country in a big language, such as British English or Swiss German, should make that country unmistakable (country-code domain or region-specific hreflang, local address, prices and currency) so its pages can benefit from index selection's country balancing instead of competing with the much larger US or German content pool.
- [`D2-C658`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **index selection**: Freshness plays no big role in index selection: whether a page was published 30 years ago or today makes no difference to its chance of being indexed.
- [`D2-C659`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **index selection**: Changing a page's date or making cosmetic edits will not help an old page get indexed, because freshness plays no big role in index selection; freshness pays off only when ranking for queries that deserve fresh results.
- [`D2-C682`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: Google's index selection system calculates thresholds and decides which documents are kept and which are thrown out; a URL that does not meet the thresholds is not indexed.
- [`D2-C683`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection aims to index only documents that are useful to users now or potentially in the future.
- [`D2-C684`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection is a predictive AI system that relies heavily on machine learning.
- [`D2-C685`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection uses what Google already knows about a site: if the site, or even a section of it, satisfies users' needs well, new URLs from it are treated more forgivingly.
- [`D2-C686`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: Launch new pages under sections that Google already indexes well, and improve or remove weak sections, because index selection judges new URLs partly by what it knows about the site and the section they sit in.
- [`D2-C687`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection uses the signals calculated earlier in indexing for each document it has to select or discard.
- [`D2-C688`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection is the last step before documents enter Google's index.
- [`D2-C689`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: When Google's coverage of a country is limited, index selection becomes more likely to select documents relevant to that country, even if other signals would suggest otherwise.
- [`D2-C690`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: When Google lacks content in a language, such as Basque, index selection becomes more likely to select lower-quality documents in that language.
- [`D2-C692`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: The lower selection bar in under-served languages is an opening for content written for that market, not for machine translation at scale: index selection also applies spam signals, and Google's spam policies count generating many pages from scraped content through automated transformations such as translating, with little value for users, as scaled content abuse.
- [`D2-C693`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: The overall importance of a document or site plays a significant role in index selection.
- [`D2-C694`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: News sites were given as the example of importance at work in index selection: they are generally very important on the web and their pages usually get indexed very fast ('indexed' is a likely but not certain reading of the recording).
- [`D2-C696`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection applies the negative signals that immediately block indexing: noindex (the likely reading of one unclear word), expired unavailable_after dates, soft 404s, non-canonical duplicates, spam signals and other policies.
- [`D2-C697`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection drops a document carrying a noindex rule if it was not already dropped earlier in processing (noindex is a likely but not certain reading of the transcript, supported by the later mention of noindex among the Page indexing report reasons).
- [`D2-C698`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection checks for the robots unavailable_after rule and its date, and drops a page from the index once that date is reached.
- [`D2-C699`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: Use the unavailable_after robots rule on pages with a known end date, such as event pages, time-limited offers or job ads, so that index selection drops them automatically when the date passes instead of leaving expired pages in search results.
- [`D2-C700`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection drops soft 404 pages that were not dropped earlier, for example when a document is reprocessed.
- [`D2-C701`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: When Google already has duplicate information for a document, for example when reprocessing it, index selection uses it to drop non-canonical duplicates from further processing, so that, as the speaker put it, only canonicals end up in search results (a simplification; see D2-C703).
- [`D2-C704`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection loads most of Google's spam signals and acts as a gatekeeper so that no spam enters search results.
- [`D2-C705`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **Index selection**: Index selection also applies other policies, covering egregious violations and, in a less certain reading of the transcript, content Google is legally not allowed to index.
- [`D2-C711`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: 'Crawled – currently not indexed' in Search Console is an index selection decision: Google crawled and processed the page but decided not to keep it in the index.
- [`D2-C717`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **index selection**: Search Console's Page indexing report is the place to check for index selection issues, and its not-indexed reasons are useful when testing changes on a site.

### JavaScript (`javascript`): 89

- [`D1-C206`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **JavaScript**: Google renders JavaScript-heavy pages from their HTML, CSS and JavaScript as a browser would, using the latest version of Chromium.
- [`D1-C272`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **JavaScript**: A community speaker advised against publishing markdown copies of HTML pages for AI agents: the copy is a duplicate (which the speaker also called a possible source of cloaking, an uncertain word in the recordings), and the models are trained to read HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
- [`D1-C274`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **JavaScript**: A community speaker said AI agents understand a page through a combination of three inputs: a screenshot, the DOM (the HTML plus the changes rendered by JavaScript) and the accessibility tree.
- [`D1-C137`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **JavaScript**: Google's Inside Googlebot post warns that bloated inline base64 images, large blocks of inline CSS or JavaScript, or megabytes of menus can push a page's text or structured data past Googlebot's 2MB cutoff, and advises moving heavy CSS and JavaScript to external files and placing meta tags, the title, the canonical and essential structured data high in the HTML.
- [`D1-C534`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **JavaScript**: Dave Smart said robots.txt is checked for every URL in a redirect chain and crawling stops at the first blocked one; in his example a site redirected through /cart/ with JavaScript to set the local currency and back, and because /cart/ was disallowed the page was reported as blocked.
- [`D1-C536`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **JavaScript**: Dave Smart said this applies to all redirects, not only JavaScript ones; his examples: a redirect through an external authorisation service that is blocked by its own robots.txt, content that moved through several URLs over the years with one of them later blocked, and unexpected redirects, such as one served only to Googlebot's user agent.
- [`D1-C490`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **JavaScript**: An audience member asked what happens to thousands of crawled and indexed paginated category and tag pages if they are replaced by a single page with a JavaScript load-more button, and whether the old pages should then redirect to the canonical first page.
- [`D1-C541`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **JavaScript**: A Google panelist said, as a fun fact, that JavaScript was used for the language-consolidation redirects in Google's own site migration, because it was the only option available to the person doing it (the recording does not make fully clear whether the JavaScript performed the redirects or built the mapping).
- [`D1-C542`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **JavaScript**: Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript location redirects only after rendering, may never see one if rendering fails, and should be used only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible; its site move guide asks for server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) where technically possible. The JavaScript in Google's own migration was a fallback ('my only option'), not a pattern to copy.
- [`D2-C040`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **JavaScript**: Google cannot extract a link from an a element that only has an onclick handler, because Googlebot does not click, so the JavaScript is never triggered.
- [`D2-C045`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **JavaScript**: Audit every template and JavaScript component that outputs links, such as navigation, pagination, filters and product tiles: each needs a real a element with an href, because onclick handlers, routerLink without href, href on a span and javascript: URLs leave the target pages without a link Google can reliably extract.
- [`D2-C079`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: Google's robots meta tag specification says data-nosnippet may be extracted both before and after rendering, so the attribute should not be added to or removed from existing elements with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C106`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: A slide said robots meta rules can be added to a page's HTML with JavaScript, but doing so takes more time.
- [`D2-C107`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: Google's meta tags documentation recommends avoiding JavaScript to inject or change meta tags whenever possible and testing the implementation thoroughly when it must be used.
- [`D2-C108`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: Removing a robots restriction such as noindex with JavaScript does not work, a slide said.
- [`D2-C109`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: Ship robots rules in the HTML the server sends and never rely on JavaScript to lift a noindex: Google may skip rendering a page that arrives with noindex, so the page can stay out of the index even if a script removes the tag later.
- [`D2-C852`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: When Google finds a noindex rule in a page's HTML, it drops the page without even processing its JavaScript, so a script cannot switch the page back to indexable, John Mueller said.
- [`D2-C853`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: John Mueller recommended putting robots meta tags directly in a page's HTML exactly as intended, and adding them with JavaScript only where that is not possible, as in a JavaScript web app.
- [`D2-C854`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says that when Google encounters a noindex rule it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution, so using JavaScript to change or remove a noindex robots meta tag may not work as expected.
- [`D2-C855`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **JavaScript**: On stage the rule was absolute (Google won't even process the JavaScript of a page served with noindex), while Google's guide says only that it may skip rendering; either way, a noindex in the served HTML must never be one that JavaScript is expected to lift.
- [`D2-C110`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google framed rendering historically: when Google started, most of the web was plain, semantic HTML it could extract directly, but the modern web is built with JavaScript and much content is generated by JavaScript, so Google had to adapt.
- [`D2-C111`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Without its ability to render JavaScript, Google says it would not be able to see most of what is on the web today.
- [`D2-C114`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Being able to render and read JavaScript matters whether the client fetching a page is a search crawler or an AI system, Google said.
- [`D2-C115`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google described the mission of its rendering as simply executing JavaScript, while the implementation is complex, expensive and difficult.
- [`D2-C125`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: For pages people are likely to ask an AI assistant about (product, pricing, documentation and policy pages), server-render the main content so a live, user-triggered read does not depend on client-side JavaScript finishing quickly.
- [`D2-C127`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: A Google pipeline diagram ran from the crawl queue to the crawler, then through HTML parsing to processing, which passes pages to rendering and gets them back, and then to the index; rendering fetches its JavaScript and CSS through the crawler.
- [`D2-C130`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google said its pipeline needs to ensure that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering, while content that appears only through JavaScript and CSS takes a longer rendering pass.
- [`D2-C131`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.
- [`D2-C132`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: The stage remark that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering does not mean such pages skip rendering, because Google's guide queues every 200 page for rendering; read it as: content already in the raw HTML does not depend on the slower rendering pass.
- [`D2-C133`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Put everything indexing depends on (title, meta description, canonical, robots meta tag, main text and links) in the raw HTML so it is available without rendering, let JavaScript add enhancements only, and check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection for the rest.
- [`D2-C134`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google urged sites to make sure their JavaScript content can be crawled, rendered and indexed, calling this important today and also tomorrow, as AI systems increasingly ground answers to user requests.
- [`D2-C135`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: After Google's opener, Lightning session D had three community talks: rendering and JavaScript execution blind spots (Sören Bendig), debugging JavaScript rendering for Search (Rebecca Yu) and virtualizing the browser (Natalia Venditto).
- [`D2-C138`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Switching JavaScript off and on in the browser gives a quick first impression of which content on a page depends on rendering.
- [`D2-C139`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: A community speaker strongly advised putting everything you want cited into the raw, server-side rendered HTML, especially for AI systems that cannot render JavaScript yet.
- [`D2-C140`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: In a navigation example, the main navigation was in the raw HTML and would survive a rendering failure, but the whole sub-navigation was built by JavaScript, so all of its links would be inaccessible to bots if rendering broke.
- [`D2-C158`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: When something is missing from a rendered page, check both robots.txt and the Content Security Policy: the URL Inspection live test shows the page resources, the JavaScript console output and a screenshot of the rendered page.
- [`D2-C161`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Because even established brands have these rendering problems and every modern website uses a lot of JavaScript, a community speaker argued that most sites probably have them too and that ignoring rendering is reckless.
- [`D2-C166`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: The second community lightning talk of the rendering block covered debugging JavaScript rendering for Search: how Google renders pages, a step-by-step check, four common mistakes and a worked product page example.
- [`D2-C167`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: The diagram from Google's JavaScript SEO basics page shows a URL going from the crawl queue to the crawler, the crawled HTML going to processing, then the render queue and the renderer, whose rendered HTML returns to processing before the page reaches the index.
- [`D2-C169`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says Googlebot extracts links twice, from the HTML response before rendering and again from the rendered HTML, so links injected with JavaScript can be found if they use crawlable `<a href>` markup.
- [`D2-C172`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says a page may wait in the render queue for a few seconds but that it can take longer, and it gives no upper limit.
- [`D2-C173`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's renderer is a headless Chromium that runs the page's JavaScript.
- [`D2-C176`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: To check whether JavaScript content is affected, open the URL Inspection tool in Search Console or the Rich Results Test and look for that content in the rendered HTML tab.
- [`D2-C182`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: If the cause of missing JavaScript content is still unclear after checking the network requests, search the source code for a string related to the missing content.
- [`D2-C183`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: A community speaker listed four common but often overlooked JavaScript rendering mistakes: non-crawlable link markup, error pages that return HTTP 200 in single-page apps, content behind user interaction, and JavaScript or API resources blocked in robots.txt.
- [`D2-C192`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's JavaScript guides say that when client-side routing makes a real 404 status impractical, a single-page app can avoid soft 404s by redirecting with JavaScript to a URL whose server returns 404, or by adding a robots noindex meta tag with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C193`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: In a single-page app, let the server return 404 for unknown routes where possible; otherwise use one of the two client-side fixes Google documents for error views: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns 404, or a robots noindex added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C194`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: A community speaker called not hiding content behind user interaction the most important of the four JavaScript rendering mistakes.
- [`D2-C204`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Blocking JavaScript or API resources in robots.txt is a classic rendering mistake: if Google's renderer cannot fetch a resource, it cannot run it.
- [`D2-C206`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google says its Web Rendering Service fetches the resources a page references through Googlebot, including JavaScript, CSS and XHR requests to APIs, but not images or videos.
- [`D2-C214`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: A community speaker summed up JavaScript rendering issues as cases where search engines cannot execute, access or trigger the code needed to display a page's core content.
- [`D2-C216`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Natalia Venditto, a Principal Software Engineer at Adobe, gave a seven-minute community lightning talk on JavaScript and web standards, built around the Web Fragments library.
- [`D2-C219`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Natalia Venditto named three typical failure modes by which an embedded app can break the application hosting it: collisions in the global JavaScript scope and module registry, CSS bleed, and fate sharing.
- [`D2-C222`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Pages that embed third-party or AI-generated apps can share their fate, since an unhandled exception in the embedded code can break the host page; check the rendered HTML and JavaScript console output of such pages in Google's testing tools to make sure the host's own content still renders.
- [`D2-C223`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: A slide titled Orchestration approaches compared four ways to combine micro-frontends in one page (iframe, Shadow DOM, rewriting everything, and reframing with Web Fragments) on three criteria (JavaScript isolated, styles isolated, part of the page) and named the catch of each.
- [`D2-C224`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: An iframe, the long-established way to embed an app, isolates both JavaScript and styles but is not part of the page: it is walled off from the host's DOM, navigation and layout, which Natalia Venditto said brings many problems with accessibility, layout and navigation.
- [`D2-C228`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Shadow DOM isolates styles and keeps the embedded content part of the page, but it does not isolate JavaScript: the embedded code still shares the host's JavaScript globals.
- [`D2-C229`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Rewriting everything into one application keeps the result part of the page, but JavaScript and style isolation then have to be done by hand.
- [`D2-C231`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Reframing with Web Fragments was the only approach on the comparison slide ticked for all three criteria (JavaScript isolated, styles isolated, part of the page); its stated catch is that it relies on browser patches today.
- [`D2-C232`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Web Fragments is a lightweight library that puts a hidden iframe in the host page and uses it as an isolated sandbox to run the embedded app's JavaScript, not to render the app.
- [`D2-C234`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Web Fragments reframes the embedded app's DOM by placing it inside a shadow DOM in the host page, while the app's JavaScript runs in the hidden iframe.
- [`D2-C245`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Make sure robots.txt does not block the URLs from which the browser loads a fragment's assets (the gateway paths on the host page's origin, or the endpoint's own host if assets load from there), because Google does not render JavaScript from blocked files and robots.txt rules apply per host.
- [`D2-C246`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Natalia Venditto said Web Fragments is framework-agnostic and vendor-agnostic and works the same whatever JavaScript framework the embedded app uses.
- [`D2-C253`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Natalia Venditto said ShadowRealm, a JavaScript standard proposal, was at stage 2.7 at the time of the talk, which she glossed as meaning that only implementation is missing.
- [`D2-C856`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Websites that rely heavily on JavaScript and rendering have common blind spots, because these features often break in subtle ways, a community speaker said.
- [`D2-C257`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics says every page with a 200 status code is queued for rendering, whether or not it uses JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header says not to index it; for non-200 pages such as 404 error pages, rendering might be skipped.
- [`D2-C258`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: If JavaScript rendering fails, what Google indexes for a page differs from what the page shows once it is rendered.
- [`D2-C259`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Erin Sparling named server-side or hybrid rendering, fallbacks and not leaving placeholders in the DOM, among other measures, as ways to guard against failed JavaScript rendering.
- [`D2-C260`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google listed four common JavaScript problems for indexing: content not present in the rendered HTML, using # in URLs for content changes, soft 404s and blocked resources.
- [`D2-C261`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's slide called content missing from the rendered HTML the most common JavaScript issue for indexing.
- [`D2-C264`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's slide defined a soft 404 in a JavaScript application as a page that serves a 'Not Found' message but returns a 200 HTTP status code.
- [`D2-C265`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Blocked resources, one of Google's four common JavaScript indexing problems, means robots.txt disallowing the crawling of critical JavaScript files or API endpoints.
- [`D2-C266`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google named three causes of content missing from the rendered HTML: JavaScript inaccessible to Googlebot, JavaScript DOM event triggers and disabled browser APIs.
- [`D2-C267`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: When the JavaScript is not accessible to Googlebot, Google cannot render the client-side DOM that the page builds asynchronously, so parts of the page may be present while the main content is absent.
- [`D2-C278`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: For effects that need WebGL, which Googlebot does not support, Google's guide to fixing JavaScript problems suggests skipping the effect or prerendering it with server-side rendering so that the content is accessible to Googlebot.
- [`D2-C280`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics recommends differential serving and polyfills when feature detection finds a missing browser API, and warns that some browser features cannot be polyfilled.
- [`D2-C283`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Erin Sparling called URL fragments (the part of a URL after #) the next most common JavaScript issue seen, after rendering problems and blocked rendering.
- [`D2-C291`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: In JavaScript single-page apps, soft 404s typically arise because the server returns the app with a 200 status for every URL, so when the app shows a 'not found' message for a URL that does not exist, no error is reported.
- [`D2-C294`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: For client-side rendered single-page apps, where meaningful status codes can be impossible or impractical, Google's documentation gives two ways to avoid soft 404s: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns a 404 status, or a noindex robots meta tag added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C296`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: If robots.txt blocks JavaScript that client-side code needs to render, Google cannot render the content that the JavaScript would produce.
- [`D2-C298`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
- [`D2-C828`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's guide to fixing Search-related JavaScript problems says its Web Rendering Service keeps no state across page loads: local storage, session storage and HTTP cookies are cleared.
- [`D2-C829`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **JavaScript**: Google's guide to fixing Search-related JavaScript problems says the Web Rendering Service may ignore caching headers and so use outdated JavaScript or CSS, and recommends content fingerprinting, which puts a hash of the content in the file name, as in main.2bb85551.js.
- [`D2-C389`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **JavaScript**: Whether a page can load is really important for canonical selection: a broken certificate, failing JavaScript or a page that cannot be loaded counts against a URL, and the slide also listed meta refresh and security.
- [`D2-C946`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S14-lightning-session-f-media.md) **JavaScript**: Version 20 of the Screaming Frog SEO Spider, released in May 2024, was the first that could connect the crawler to ChatGPT through custom JavaScript, which let SEOs rewrite image alt text at scale.
- [`D2-C949`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S14-lightning-session-f-media.md) **JavaScript**: To test LLM-generated alt text before a rollout, a community speaker recommended running the crawler's custom JavaScript in Screaming Frog's List mode on a few chosen URLs and reviewing the generated alt text, instead of crawling the whole site in Spider mode.
- [`D3-C627`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **JavaScript**: Content that JavaScript adds to a page is typically seen by Google's indexing system within a few hours, and at worst within weeks.
- [`D3-C630`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **JavaScript**: Put critical content, links and meta tags in the server HTML: content that needs JavaScript reaches indexing only after rendering, usually within hours but sometimes weeks, and even Google's own speaker doubted that every URL gets rendered.
- [`D3-C676`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **JavaScript**: The stage doubt that every URL gets rendered sits beside Google's JavaScript guide, which says every page with a 200 status is queued for rendering unless a robots rule blocks indexing: queued is not the same as rendered, so do not rely on rendering for critical content.

### JSON-LD (`json-ld`): 12

- [`D1-C250`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **JSON-LD**: In a community demo, a fix loop gave a large LLM (Claude Opus) the current markup, the errors Google's test reported and Google's documentation, had it write new JSON-LD and re-ran the test, with at most three attempts; the demo's page passed on the second.
- [`D1-C269`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **JSON-LD**: Author's view: an LLM fix loop that stops when Google's test passes proves only that the JSON-LD is valid, not that its values are true; Google's generative AI content guidance asks for AI-generated structured data to be fact-checked as well as validated.
- [`D1-C289`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **JSON-LD**: A community speaker said a third-party study from early 2026 found that websites with JSON-LD were shown much more often, and that the industry reacted by adding schema markup everywhere.
- [`D2-C446`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **JSON-LD**: The 'gold nuggets' that Google's feature extraction step pulls out of a page's HTML are structured data (such as JSON-LD), images and videos.
- [`D2-C494`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **JSON-LD**: Google accepts three structured data syntaxes, JSON-LD, microdata and RDFa, which are all valid and are extracted at the very start into the same pipelines, so they are interpreted identically downstream.
- [`D2-C495`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **JSON-LD**: Google recommends JSON-LD because it is one contiguous block that is easier to author, so people make fewer mistakes with it.
- [`D2-C496`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **JSON-LD**: Microdata has an advantage when payload size matters: embedded in the existing HTML, it avoids duplicating the page content in a separate JSON-LD block.
- [`D2-C497`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **JSON-LD**: Default to JSON-LD and switch to microdata only where page weight is critical, since Google interprets all three syntaxes identically and JSON-LD is the one people get wrong least often.
- [`D2-C551`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **JSON-LD**: Google strongly suggests describing a video's metadata with JSON-LD structured data, on top of placing the video in an HTML element on the page.
- [`D3-C324`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **JSON-LD**: Rich results differ from other search features because Google builds them from extra data that site owners provide, usually structured data and usually in JSON-LD format.
- [`D3-C334`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **JSON-LD**: Google's Article slide showed the NewsArticle JSON-LD example from Google's Article documentation: a block in the page head with headline, three image URLs (1x1, 4x3 and 16x9), datePublished and dateModified with time zone offsets, and an author list of Person objects with name and url.
- [`D3-C383`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **JSON-LD**: In product markup, an offer's shipping and return information can point through a JSON-LD identifier (@id) to shipping and return data defined elsewhere.

### Lazy loading (`lazy-loading-concept`): 6

- [`D2-C197`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Lazy loading**: Lazy loading triggered by a scroll event listener, such as window.addEventListener('scroll', loadMoreProducts), never runs for Googlebot because Googlebot does not scroll.
- [`D2-C198`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Lazy loading**: Lazy loading should be triggered by an Intersection Observer that watches a sentinel element instead of by a scroll event listener.
- [`D2-C199`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **lazy-loaded**: An Intersection Observer fires when the observed element enters the viewport, and the viewport Google renders with is tall, so content lazy-loaded this way can load during rendering.
- [`D2-C203`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **lazy loading**: Audit tabs, accordions and 'load more' lists for content fetched on click or scroll: put tab content in the initial DOM and hide it with CSS, trigger lazy loading with an Intersection Observer, and give long lists paginated URLs linked with `<a href>`.
- [`D2-C275`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **lazy loading**: Treat the 10,000-pixel viewport as a safety margin, not a target: load lazy content when it enters the viewport (Intersection Observer or native lazy loading, never scroll listeners), and give infinite-scroll content paginated URLs linked with `<a href>` so anything below the first rendered screen stays reachable.
- [`D2-C276`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **lazy-loading**: To make infinite scroll indexable, Google's lazy-loading guide says to support paginated loading: give each chunk its own persistent, unique URL, link sequentially to those URLs, and update the displayed URL with the History API when a new chunk becomes the main visible element.

### llms.txt (`llms-txt-file`): 14

- [`D1-C054`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **llms.txt**: Myth: optimise for AI over readers. Google's answer: optimise for people, with no need to obsess over precise keywords or AI phrasing, no need to chop content, and no need for llms.txt.
- [`D1-C271`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **llms.txt**: A community speaker said llms.txt files are not necessary, citing a third-party study from summer 2026 (heard as Ahrefs') that looked at almost 40,000 sites over one month: 97% had no AI agent hits on the file, and those that had any got about two hits a month.
- [`D1-C505`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **llms.txt**: The llms.txt study cited on stage matches Ahrefs' June 2026 study of 137,210 domains: 28% (about 38,000, the 'almost 40,000' sites heard on stage) published an llms.txt file and 97% of those files received no requests at all in May 2026; the files that were fetched got about 22,000 requests across some 1,100 domains, around 20 each, not the 'two hits a month' heard on stage.
- [`D1-C453`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: An audience member asked whether llms.txt matters, given that Google had said it does not while PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse advocate it and audit tools ask site owners to create the file.
- [`D1-C454`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: Gary Illyes said llms.txt does not matter for Google Search right now and that he does not expect it to, while adding that he had been wrong before.
- [`D1-C455`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: Gary Illyes said llms.txt matters to some people, which is why tools such as Lighthouse add checks for it, so both sides of the debate are right in their own context.
- [`D1-C456`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: A Google panelist said he knew of no plan for Google to use llms.txt, though it could happen, and that a possible future change is no reason to implement it now.
- [`D1-C457`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: A Google panelist said most llms.txt files he had seen are generated automatically by a setting in SEO plugins, so if Google Search ever made llms.txt matter, a site could add one by ticking a checkbox.
- [`D1-C458`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: A Google panelist objected that llms.txt is designed for supposedly intelligent systems that should be able to parse a website.
- [`D1-C459`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: A Google panelist compared llms.txt to the old meta keywords debate: an AI agent should not blindly trust what a site says about its own authority, just as a site calling itself the best car insurance site is no reason to stop looking at others.
- [`D1-C460`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: Chrome's Lighthouse documentation lists an llms.txt audit among its agentic browsing audits: it flags a server error when llms.txt is fetched and marks the audit not applicable when the file is missing, because providing the file is optional for now.
- [`D1-C471`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: An audience question noted that a cats.txt file received more crawler requests than llms.txt in the server logs and asked how important that is.
- [`D1-C472`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **llms.txt**: cats.txt was created by an SEO as a satirical take on llms.txt, to show that crawlers fetch whatever files they are given, so requests for llms.txt in server logs do not mean the file is important.
- [`D1-C060`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S00-day-1-session-not-recorded.md) **llms.txt**: Speakers at the event were openly dismissive of llms.txt.

### Main content (`main-content-concept`): 35

- [`D1-C277`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **main content**: A community speaker advised keeping headings inside the main content in a logical hierarchy (title, section subtitles, subsections) so agents can follow its structure, avoiding several H1 elements and skipped levels such as an H3 followed directly by an H5.
- [`D2-C833`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **main content**: Google's sitemap guide says Google uses lastmod only when it is consistently and verifiably accurate, and counts a change to the main content, the structured data or the links of a page as significant, but not a changed copyright date.
- [`D2-C028`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **main content**: Google extracts every element of a page so that it can tell the header, the navigation and the main content apart, and a slide labelled the main content as very important.
- [`D2-C029`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **main content**: Make the main content of every template easy to separate from the header, navigation and footer, for example as one clearly delimited main area, because Google identifies the main content and treats it as the most important part of the page.
- [`D2-C125`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **main content**: For pages people are likely to ask an AI assistant about (product, pricing, documentation and policy pages), server-render the main content so a live, user-triggered read does not depend on client-side JavaScript finishing quickly.
- [`D2-C179`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **main content**: Check rendering per template rather than per URL: inspect one URL of each page type (product, category, article) in URL Inspection and confirm that the main content, prices and internal links appear in the rendered HTML.
- [`D2-C267`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **main content**: When the JavaScript is not accessible to Googlebot, Google cannot render the client-side DOM that the page builds asynchronously, so parts of the page may be present while the main content is absent.
- [`D2-C282`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **main content**: Wrap permission-based features (location, payments, camera) and WebGL effects in feature detection with a fallback, so the main content renders when the API is missing or the permission is declined; never make indexable content wait for a permission prompt.
- [`D2-C298`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **main content**: Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
- [`D2-C305`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **main content**: With a headless CMS, choose the rendering per template before launch (server-rendered or pre-rendered for pages that must rank), and make any agent-built test suite assert that the main content and `<a href>` links are present in the rendered HTML.
- [`D2-C309`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: A Google slide labelled the parts of an example blog page, marking the header and the navigation as not so important and the main content as very important.
- [`D2-C310`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **centerpiece**: Google's canonicalization guide says that when Google indexes a page it determines the page's primary content, which it also calls the centerpiece, and clusters pages whose primary content is the same or very similar.
- [`D2-C311`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Gary Illyes pointed to Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines as the detailed source on how Google thinks about the main content of a page.
- [`D2-C314`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: On Google's example blog page, the post title and opening sentence counted as important because they sit in the main content, in front of the user, while the site tagline, the 'Categories' sidebar and category links such as 'Hugo (7)' counted as less important supplementary text.
- [`D2-C315`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: To make a word count for ranking a page, Gary Illyes said the simplest step is to move it into the main content, because where text sits on a page already contributes quite a bit to ranking.
- [`D2-C316`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Gary Illyes said not everything on a page can or should be important: if everything were placed in the main content, nothing would stand out as main content, which he called working as intended.
- [`D2-C317`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Put the terms a page should rank for in its main content (title, headings, opening paragraphs) rather than only in sidebars, tag lists or footers; footer keyword blocks are unlikely to add ranking value.
- [`D2-C323`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: When tokenizing for Search, Google attaches metadata to each token for use in ranking, such as whether the word appeared in the header or in the main content (tagged 'centerpiece' on the slide), in bold or in a heading; Gary Illyes said he was not showing all of the metadata.
- [`D2-C339`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: For soft 404 detection, the position of error text decides: an error in a less important part such as the navigation need not make a page a soft 404, but an error message alone in the main content, like 'Error establishing a database connection', does, much as a human would judge it.
- [`D2-C340`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Google's soft 404 detection tells the page chrome, such as navigation and footer, apart from the main content by analysing the page's visual hierarchy alongside its text.
- [`D2-C342`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.
- [`D2-C862`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Gary Illyes defined a page's main content as any part of the page that directly helps the page achieve its purpose, what it was built for.
- [`D2-C863`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Main content**: Main content is not only text: images, videos, a tool or anything else that helps a page achieve its purpose can be main content.
- [`D2-C864`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Content created by other users can be main content: on a user-generated content site, the user-generated content can be the page's main content.
- [`D2-C865`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: A comment section below a blog post can still be part of the page's main content and can contribute to Google's understanding of the page.
- [`D2-C866`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Content inside tabs, for example separate tabs for a product description and a manufacturer description, might be part of a page's main content.
- [`D2-C867`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: A page's main content includes all of its headings and its visible title.
- [`D2-C868`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Gary Illyes said the main content is what Google considers when ranking a page.
- [`D2-C870`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines define main content as any part of the page that directly helps it achieve its purpose, including text, images, videos, page features such as calculators and content created by users, and they count the title at the top of the page as part of it.
- [`D2-C871`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **main content**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines say navigation links are a common type of supplementary content, and that content behind tabs and user reviews or comments may count as main content on some pages and as supplementary content on others, depending on the page's purpose.
- [`D2-C366`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **main content**: Pages whose boilerplate, such as menu and footer, is translated while the main content is not are near matches: the main reason to visit is the same, so Google clusters them as duplicates.
- [`D2-C372`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **main content**: Make location and variant pages differ in their main content (local stock, staff, prices, addresses) and return 404 for empty or invalid combinations; otherwise every URL that fits the pattern can be folded into one canonical.
- [`D2-C474`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **main content**: Google's systems sometimes fail to determine a page's main content correctly, and structured data helps because site owners tend to mark up what is actually important rather than boilerplate or ads.
- [`D2-C557`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **main content**: Give each important video its own watch page where the video is the main content, add VideoObject markup and list the video in a video sitemap; a video buried in a long article lacks the dedicated watch page that Google listed as a key factor.
- [`D2-C589`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **main content**: Google's hreflang guide says pages that translate only the template (navigation, footer) around main content in one language still count as duplicates, because localized versions are duplicates only if the main content stays untranslated; it recommends hreflang for such pages.

### max-image-preview (`max-image-preview`): 7

- [`D2-C087`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-image-preview**: The max-image-preview rule sets the maximum size of a page's image previews: none shows no preview, standard a default-sized one and large the largest possible, for example in Discover.
- [`D2-C089`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-image-preview**: max-image-preview:large matters mainly in Discover, where it allows a large image that draws people's attention, so the rule can make a page more visible than leaving it out, John Mueller said.
- [`D2-C104`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-image-preview**: To be as visible as possible in Google, John Mueller's closing slide recommended the robots rules max-image-preview:large and max-snippet:-1.
- [`D2-C105`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-image-preview**: Set max-snippet:-1 and max-image-preview:large on every indexable template unless licensing requires otherwise, and check that no CMS, plug-in or CDN setting adds lower snippet or image preview limits by default.
- [`D2-C936`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **max-image-preview**: Setting the max-image-preview robots meta tag to large can make content perform surprisingly well in Discover, Gary Illyes said.
- [`D3-C224`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **max-image-preview**: Google's Discover slide recommended large images at least 1,200 px wide, with more than 300,000 total pixels and a 16x9 aspect ratio, enabled by the max-image-preview:large setting.
- [`D3-C230`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **max-image-preview**: For Discover, set max-image-preview:large on article templates, give every article a relevant image at least 1,200 px wide in og:image or schema.org markup that is neither the site logo nor text-heavy, and show clear bylines and dates.

### max-snippet (`max-snippet`): 10

- [`D2-C075`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: Before adding nosnippet or a low max-snippet value, weigh the cost in AI features: both limit how much of the page AI Overviews and AI Mode can use, and John Mueller described those answers as built from snippets.
- [`D2-C082`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: The max-snippet:[number] rule limits a page's search result snippet to that number of characters (100 characters, for example), and max-snippet:0 shows no snippet, the same as nosnippet.
- [`D2-C083`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: John Mueller said, hedging with 'I think', that the max-snippet limit also applies to AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D2-C084`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: A max-snippet value too short for a useful snippet may lead Google to show no snippet at all, John Mueller said.
- [`D2-C085`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: max-snippet:-1 removes the length limit and can produce a longer snippet than having no rule, because by default Google keeps snippets to a length it considers reasonable instead of quoting a page at length.
- [`D2-C086`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: Google's robots meta tag specification says Google chooses the snippet length when no max-snippet rule is set, and with max-snippet:-1 chooses the length it believes most effective; it does not say that -1 produces longer snippets.
- [`D2-C104`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: To be as visible as possible in Google, John Mueller's closing slide recommended the robots rules max-image-preview:large and max-snippet:-1.
- [`D2-C105`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **max-snippet**: Set max-snippet:-1 and max-image-preview:large on every indexable template unless licensing requires otherwise, and check that no CMS, plug-in or CDN setting adds lower snippet or image preview limits by default.
- [`D2-C728`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **max-snippet**: Google's robots meta tag specification says the nosnippet rule also prevents a page's content from being used as a direct input for AI Overviews and AI Mode, and max-snippet also limits how much of it may be used that way.
- [`D2-C731`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **max-snippet**: Treat nosnippet, data-nosnippet and max-snippet as AI visibility settings too: Google lists them as the controls for content in AI features, and if AI answers are built from index snippets, as Google said on stage, a blocked or shortened snippet leaves AI Overviews and AI Mode less to use.

### Merchant Center (`merchant-center`): 31

- [`D2-C005`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's ecommerce documentation recommends linking from menus to category pages, from category pages to sub-category pages and from sub-category pages to all product pages; where not every product can be linked, it recommends a sitemap or a Merchant Center feed.
- [`D2-C507`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's documentation updates log calls the July 2026 sale price change a clarification: a new Sale duration section of the merchant listing guide explains validFrom with validThrough or priceValidUntil, aligned with Merchant Center's sale_price_effective_date attribute.
- [`D2-C508`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Merchant Center**: For time-limited sales, give the sale price its validity dates in the product markup (Google's merchant listing documentation describes validFrom, validThrough and priceValidUntil) instead of editing markup by hand when the sale ends, and keep the dates aligned with the Merchant Center feed.
- [`D3-C343`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Google Merchant Center**: Google Search displays product rich results from product structured data; it may also use the product data a merchant provides in Google Merchant Center, but Merchant Center is not required for them.
- [`D3-C344`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's Product structured data introduction says that providing both on-page structured data and a Merchant Center feed maximizes eligibility for shopping experiences and helps Google understand and verify the data; product snippets may take pricing from the feed when the markup lacks it.
- [`D3-C345`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Google Merchant Center**: Product annotations on Google Images results also come from product structured data and do not need Google Merchant Center.
- [`D3-C346`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Google Merchant Center**: To appear in the Shopping tab of Google Search, a product must be submitted in Google Merchant Center; product structured data alone is not enough.
- [`D3-C347`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's Merchant Center help says products and details crawled from an online store can show up on Google even when they are not marked up with schema.org or added in Merchant Center, and lists the Shopping tab among the places Merchant Center free listings appear.
- [`D3-C348`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's free listings help says crawled store products can appear on Google without markup or Merchant Center but does not say whether that includes the Shopping tab; for a shop that wants Shopping tab visibility, the stage rule that Merchant Center is required is the safe working assumption.
- [`D3-C349`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Merchant Center**: Product structured data can help Merchant Center in some cases, for example during data validation, but Merchant Center does not require it.
- [`D3-C350`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Merchant Center**: Merchant Center's automatic item updates use structured data and other product data found on landing pages to fix price, sale price, availability and condition mismatches in a merchant's product data; Google says they do not replace regular feed updates.
- [`D3-C351`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **Merchant Center**: For an online shop, Product structured data is enough for product rich results and Google Images product annotations, but the Shopping tab needs a Merchant Center feed too; keep feed and markup values identical, since Google can use the markup to validate the feed.
- [`D3-C352`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's Merchant Center feed specification is how millions of merchants send Google billions of product offers, which are used in Shopping ads, Search ads and organic search results.
- [`D3-C359`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: In 2026, a few months before the October event, Google added new Merchant Center feed attributes to help AI systems understand product nuances, prompted by feedback since 2025 from merchants worried whether AI experiences represented them correctly.
- [`D3-C361`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: On 11 January 2026 Google announced 'dozens of new data attributes' in Merchant Center for conversational commerce on AI Mode, Gemini and Business Agent, to roll out first with a small group of retailers.
- [`D3-C362`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: At Google Marketing Live on 20 May 2026 Google said retailers globally can now use conversational attributes in Merchant Center to reflect the more conversational way people search.
- [`D3-C365`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Google added six Merchant Center feed attributes for AI shopping experiences: question and answer, documents, related products, item group title and variant option for variants, and popularity rank.
- [`D3-C366`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's January 2026 announcement spoke of 'dozens' of new Merchant Center attributes, while the Day 3 talk counted six; all six named on stage (question_and_answer, document_link, related_product, item_group_title, variant_option, popularity_rank) are in the Merchant Center product data specification as of 3 October 2026.
- [`D3-C367`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's Merchant Center help marks the question_and_answer, document_link, related_product and popularity_rank attributes as primarily intended for conversational experiences such as AI Mode in Google Search.
- [`D3-C369`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Merchant Center's question_and_answer attribute takes up to 30 question-and-answer pairs per product, each question and answer up to 1,000 characters and 10,000 characters in total, and must not contain prices, shipping, dates or the company name.
- [`D3-C371`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Merchant Center's document_link attribute takes up to five URLs of PDF documents about a product, such as manuals, user guides or assembly instructions, and the merchant must own the content licensing rights.
- [`D3-C375`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Merchant Center's popularity_rank is a 0-100 value the merchant assigns to rank a product's popularity, based on its recent sales, against the rest of its own inventory; it does not reflect user ratings.
- [`D3-C381`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: As of 3 October 2026 Google's Merchant Center help lists no schema.org property for question_and_answer, document_link, related_product, popularity_rank, variant_option or product_detail (only item_group_title maps, to ProductGroup.name), and Search Central does not document such markup: reading these attributes from schema.org is a stage statement, the feed is the documented route.
- [`D3-C388`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Google's Merchant Center help says the StoreBot crawler goes through product detail, cart and checkout pages, can fill in checkout forms, and records price, shipping, availability, coupons and payment methods to verify the data merchants share in Merchant Center.
- [`D3-C392`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Google now emphasises two existing Merchant Center attributes for AI, product highlights (a short bulleted list) and product detail (detailed specifications), and updated its Help Center guidance to say they help AI systems.
- [`D3-C393`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Merchant Center's product_highlight attribute takes 2 to 100 highlights of up to 150 characters each that describe only the product itself, without promotional text, keywords or search terms.
- [`D3-C395`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Merchant Center**: Merchant Center's product_detail attribute takes up to 100 specifications, each a section name, attribute name and attribute value, and Google's help says clean key-value specifications improve product details on Google Shopping and AI-driven surfaces.

- [`D2-C056`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tag**: The primary function of the robots meta tag is to control how a page is indexed and shown in search results.

- [`D2-C058`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tags**: John Mueller said robots.txt does not control indexing, so robots meta tags are what site owners have to use to control it.
- [`D2-C059`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tag**: The robots meta rule all is the default value and does nothing: it places no restrictions on indexing the page or following its links, the same as having no robots meta tag, and it is not an instruction that search engines must index the page.
- [`D2-C821`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tags**: John Mueller suspected that if robots meta tags were reinvented today, the page-level nofollow rule would probably not be part of them.
- [`D2-C065`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tags**: Audit robots meta tags set by templates and plug-ins: an explicit all rule does nothing and can go, while a page-level nofollow strips link signals from every link on the page and is better replaced by qualifying only the specific links that need it.
- [`D2-C069`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tag**: Google's robots meta tag specification says robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers are found only when a URL is crawled, so the rules on a URL disallowed in robots.txt are never seen and are ignored.

- [`D2-C086`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tag**: Google's robots meta tag specification says Google chooses the snippet length when no max-snippet rule is set, and with max-snippet:-1 chooses the length it believes most effective; it does not say that -1 produces longer snippets.
- [`D2-C101`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots meta tag**: Google's robots meta tag specification says Googlebot considerably decreases the crawl rate of a URL after the date and time set in its unavailable_after rule.

- [`D2-C257`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **robots meta tag**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics says every page with a 200 status code is queued for rendering, whether or not it uses JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header says not to index it; for non-200 pages such as 404 error pages, rendering might be skipped.

### nofollow (`nofollow`): 10

- [`D1-C101`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **nofollow**: Google's faceted navigation guide prefers prevention: disallow filter URLs in robots.txt and keep crawlable only item pages plus one unfiltered listing page, or use URL fragments, which Google generally does not crawl. rel=canonical and nofollow are weaker, slower options.
- [`D1-C107`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **nofollow**: The nofollow rule can still consume crawl budget: Google does not crawl through the nofollow link itself, but it still crawls the linked page when it finds that page through other links.
- [`D1-C127`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **nofollow**: Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling, not a block: nofollow links will generally not be followed, but the linked pages may still be crawled if Google finds them through sitemaps or other links. To stop Google fetching URLs on your own site, use a robots.txt disallow rule.
- [`D2-C063`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **nofollow**: The page-level nofollow robots rule tells search engines not to pass signals to any of the links on the page, which John Mueller called a weird and very broad rule that makes the page stand on its own.
- [`D2-C064`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **rel=nofollow**: John Mueller recommends rel=nofollow on individual links instead of the page-level nofollow robots rule, so a site can choose which links are useful and which are not.
- [`D2-C821`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **nofollow**: John Mueller suspected that if robots meta tags were reinvented today, the page-level nofollow rule would probably not be part of them.
- [`D2-C065`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **nofollow**: Audit robots meta tags set by templates and plug-ins: an explicit all rule does nothing and can go, while a page-level nofollow strips link signals from every link on the page and is better replaced by qualifying only the specific links that need it.
- [`D2-C066`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **nofollow**: John Mueller said AI crawlers do not really know what to do with nofollow links, because they look at the content rather than building a link graph; he did not say whether he meant Google's AI systems, other AI crawlers or both.
- [`D2-C067`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **nofollow**: nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D2-C068`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **nofollow**: The robots rule none is equivalent to noindex plus nofollow, so a page that carries it will not show up in Search, provided Google can see the tag.
