- [`D1-C172`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **query fan-out**: Google said the Gemini model lets Search understand the user's intent, and query fan-out then adds further queries to the first one to enrich the quality of the answer.
- [`D1-C173`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S01-welcome-and-opening-keynotes.md) **fan-out**: Google's fan-out example: for a simple query about getting rid of weeds in a lawn, Search also looks for the best herbicide to use, the best non-chemical solution and how to prevent weeds.
- [`D1-C038`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **query fan-out**: AI Mode and AI Overviews use the same crawling and the same index as Search. At serving they add grounding on the Search index and query fan-out.
- [`D1-C051`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **query fan-out**: Three reasons were given: generative AI features are built directly on the core ranking systems, query fan-out expands the original query to find related information, and generative AI features highlight content indexed by Google Search.
- [`D1-C053`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **Query fan-out**: Query fan-out means running several related searches at once to gather more results; a question about lawn weeds may also search herbicides and weed prevention.
- [`D1-C129`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **fan-out queries**: Google's guide says creating separate content for every variation of how people might search, including fan-out queries, primarily to manipulate rankings or AI responses violates its scaled content abuse policy. It adds that its AI systems can understand a page's relevance even without an exact match to the query.
- [`D1-C225`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **query fan-out**: Google said query fan-out is nothing new: it fires, for example, ten different searches in the background, each a normal search on the same systems.
- [`D1-C292`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **fan-out queries**: A community speaker suggested that LLMs pick up some of Google's years of work on judging honesty and trust (E-E-A-T) by proxy, because they send many queries (probably fan-out queries) to search engines.
- [`D1-C294`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **fan-out queries**: A community speaker cited a third-party study (heard as Peec AI's) finding that 43% of prompts produced fan-out queries in a language other than the one the user searched in.
- [`D1-C295`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **fan-out queries**: A community speaker showed a Spanish-language AI prompt about places to eat in Barcelona whose fan-out queries were all in English, so the content used to answer may be written by and for a different audience than the one asking.
- [`D1-C307`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **fan-out queries**: A community speaker proposed a 'brand co-occurrence rate' for the search stage: the share of an AI's fan-out queries that contain the brand (one in three is 33%), which also hints at the associations the model already has; problems there are mostly relevance problems.
- [`D1-C504`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **fan-out**: The study cited on stage matches Peec AI's analysis (reported in February 2026) of over 10 million ChatGPT prompts and 20 million fan-outs: 43% of the fan-out searches for non-English prompts ran in English, and nearly 78% of non-English prompt runs had at least one English fan-out (from 66% for Spanish to 94% for Turkish), so the 43% is a share of fan-out searches, not of prompts.

- [`D3-C061`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **fan-out queries**: Google tries to make fan-out queries distinct from each other for better coverage, avoiding asking the same question several times, which would return the same answers.

- [`D3-C065`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **fan-out**: Because every system runs fan-out differently, Google advised understanding that fan-out happens but not overfocusing on individual fan-out queries or on how to rank for them.

- [`D3-C073`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **query understanding**: After query understanding and expansion, Google sends the queries to the index to look up pages, the retrieval step.
- [`D3-C075`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S03-making-sense-of-users-queries.md) **query understanding**: At retrieval, Google splits the query into words, applies query understanding and expansion, and matches the words and their expansions against the posting lists.
- [`D3-C304`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **query understanding**: Which kinds of results Google shows for a query is decided by query understanding, which tries to predict the intent behind the query.
- [`D3-C321`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **query understanding**: Google's serving diagram shows the query passing through query understanding and retrieval to the index, then back through ranking and search features to the user, with the Search Features step highlighted (example query 'Where to eat orange').
- [`D3-C356`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **query understanding**: Behind the visible attributes, small pieces of product data such as brand and UPC or other barcodes are very important for Google Shopping's query understanding, retrieval and ranking.

### Redirects (`redirects`): 61

- [`D1-C345`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **3xx**: HTTP status codes fall into five classes, 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error and 5xx server error, and each class affects crawling differently.
- [`D1-C349`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **3xx**: Google follows 3xx redirects, permanent (301, 308) and temporary (302, 307), to the new location, and whether content gets indexed depends on what the redirect target returns.
- [`D1-C370`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **redirect**: Google's crawlers follow up to 10 redirect hops by default (some products' crawlers have other limits); content served by the redirecting URL is ignored and the final target's content is processed instead.
- [`D1-C534`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **redirect**: Dave Smart said robots.txt is checked for every URL in a redirect chain and crawling stops at the first blocked one; in his example a site redirected through /cart/ with JavaScript to set the local currency and back, and because /cart/ was disallowed the page was reported as blocked.
- [`D1-C536`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **redirects**: Dave Smart said this applies to all redirects, not only JavaScript ones; his examples: a redirect through an external authorisation service that is blocked by its own robots.txt, content that moved through several URLs over the years with one of them later blocked, and unexpected redirects, such as one served only to Googlebot's user agent.
- [`D1-C537`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **redirects**: When Search Console says a URL is blocked by robots.txt but the file does not block it, check whether the URL redirects and test every URL in the chain.
- [`D1-C397`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) **redirects**: A community speaker said similar URLs are an indicator of duplicate content, broken links, unnecessary redirects and other technical issues.
- [`D1-C403`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) **redirect**: A community speaker advised that a web application compute the expected URL for every request, for example with reverse routing from the page type and ID, and redirect or return an error page when the requested URL differs.
- [`D1-C404`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) **redirecting**: For query parameters, a community speaker advised checking that every parameter in a request is actually used and in the expected order, and otherwise redirecting to the expected URL with only the used parameters in the correct order.
- [`D1-C421`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S11-lightning-session-c-crawling.md) **redirect**: Of the two answers a community speaker offered for a request to a URL variant (redirect, or an error page), Google's canonicalization guide favours the redirect: a redirect is a strong signal that its target should become canonical, while an error page throws away any links pointing at the variant.
- [`D1-C445`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **redirect**: One fix for parameter variants of a URL is to work out the normalised URL and redirect the variants to it: the redirects cost crawl budget at first, but leave the site with a clean slate.
- [`D1-C479`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **redirected**: Where content was duplicated across languages, Google's own site consolidation redirected two language versions into one, giving both old URLs one target path to redirect to.
- [`D1-C490`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **redirect**: An audience member asked what happens to thousands of crawled and indexed paginated category and tag pages if they are replaced by a single page with a JavaScript load-more button, and whether the old pages should then redirect to the canonical first page.
- [`D1-C541`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **redirects**: A Google panelist said, as a fun fact, that JavaScript was used for the language-consolidation redirects in Google's own site migration, because it was the only option available to the person doing it (the recording does not make fully clear whether the JavaScript performed the redirects or built the mapping).
- [`D1-C542`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **redirects**: Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript location redirects only after rendering, may never see one if rendering fails, and should be used only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible; its site move guide asks for server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) where technically possible. The JavaScript in Google's own migration was a fallback ('my only option'), not a pattern to copy.
- [`D2-C009`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) pinned: An audience member asked whether a product detail page that is out of stock for two to three months should keep returning 200 with links to similar products, or be 302-redirected to a similar product or to its parent product listing page.
- [`D2-C010`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **redirect**: Google answered on a Q&A slide that whether to keep a temporarily out-of-stock product page or redirect it depends on how important that product page is to users.
- [`D2-C013`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **redirect**: Google's redirect documentation says that with a temporary redirect, such as a 302, Google Search shows the source page in search results and does not use the redirect as a signal that the target should be canonical.
- [`D2-C014`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **Redirect**: Keep a product page that is out of stock for a few months live with a 200 status, show its availability on the page and in Product structured data, and offer pre-ordering where possible when users would wait for the product. Redirect it only when users would rather switch to a similar product than wait.
- [`D2-C192`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **redirecting**: Google's JavaScript guides say that when client-side routing makes a real 404 status impractical, a single-page app can avoid soft 404s by redirecting with JavaScript to a URL whose server returns 404, or by adding a robots noindex meta tag with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C193`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **redirect**: In a single-page app, let the server return 404 for unknown routes where possible; otherwise use one of the two client-side fixes Google documents for error views: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns 404, or a robots noindex added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C293`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **redirecting**: In an app routed with the History API, when a user reaches a page that does not exist, Erin Sparling suggested asking how they got there and redirecting to a real 404 page.
- [`D2-C294`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **redirect**: For client-side rendered single-page apps, where meaningful status codes can be impossible or impractical, Google's documentation gives two ways to avoid soft 404s: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns a 404 status, or a noindex robots meta tag added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C355`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirect**: When someone searches for an old domain after a migration, Google shows the old URL as an alternate version because that is what was searched for, and relies on the redirect to take the user to the new site.
- [`D2-C357`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Google's redirects guide says Google keeps track of both the source and the target of a redirect: one becomes the canonical, depending on signals such as whether the redirect is permanent or temporary, and the other becomes an alternate name that may appear in results when a query suggests the user trusts the old URL more. After a move to a new domain, old URLs may still show occasionally; the guide calls this normal.
- [`D2-C358`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: After a migration, judge success by the new domain's indexing and traffic in Search Console rather than by a site: query on the old domain, and keep the old domain's redirects in place long term so searches for the old brand still reach the new site.
- [`D2-C360`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Google builds duplicate clusters from four kinds of input: redirects, content, rel=canonical, and a 'magic bucket' of other things.
- [`D2-C361`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Google trusts redirects very much for clustering, because a redirect is a clear sign that there is one version of the content; Google keeps track of both URLs but stores only one copy of the content.
- [`D2-C362`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirect**: Whether a redirect is permanent or temporary matters only for choosing the canonical, not for clustering the URLs together.
- [`D2-C363`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **permanent redirects**: Use permanent redirects (301 or 308) for moves you want reflected in Search: a temporary redirect still groups the URLs, but it changes which URL Google is likely to pick as the canonical.
- [`D2-C387`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Google named three considerations when picking a representative URL: hijacking across pages or sites, user experience (the page can load, meta refresh, security) and site-owner signals (redirects, rel=canonical, sitemaps).
- [`D2-C390`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Clear site-owner signals about which URL should be canonical make a big difference to Google's choice; the speaker named redirects, listing only the preferred URL in sitemaps, and rel=canonical, which the speaker said also helps a bit.
- [`D2-C391`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Google's canonical guide ranks the ways to signal a preferred canonical by strength: redirects and rel=canonical annotations are strong signals, sitemap inclusion is a weak signal, and combining methods makes them more effective.
- [`D2-C392`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Google's duplication talk described rel=canonical as something that 'also helps a bit', while Google's canonical guide calls it a strong signal alongside redirects and calls sitemap inclusion weak; treat redirects and rel=canonical as the main levers and sitemaps as support.
- [`D2-C396`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Google's closing suggestions on duplication: use redirects for site migrations, use HTTP result codes, don't block agents, check your rel=canonical links, use hreflang links to help Google localize, report weird canonicals in the forums, make secure pages that work, and keep canonical signals clear.
- [`D2-C400`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **redirects**: Before a migration or template change, align every canonical signal for the preferred URL (redirects, rel=canonical, internal links, sitemap entries, hreflang and working HTTPS); Google says it follows the site owner only when the signals agree.
- [`D2-C409`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirects**: A community speaker said it helps to view small canonical groups as a graph that shows any redirects between members, together with the indexability of each member page.
- [`D2-C412`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: In the real-world canonical group shown on screen (a German-language travel magazine section, site not named), a feed URL's canonical pointed to a URL on another subdomain that 301-redirected to the leader, a canonical chain through a server-side redirect.

- [`D2-C414`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirects**: Google's 2009 Search Central blog post introducing rel=canonical says a canonical URL may be a URL that redirects: Google then processes the redirect as usual.
- [`D2-C416`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirects**: To audit canonicals at scale, resolve every crawled URL to the final URL its canonical links and redirects lead to, group URLs by that leader, and flag groups with more than one hop, a loop, several canonicals on one page, or a leader that is noindexed, blocked, non-200 or redirecting.
- [`D2-C421`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: Canonical chains can run through canonical links alone, through a server-side redirect between members, or through a client-side redirect between members.
- [`D2-C423`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirecting**: After a migration or a subdomain change, update rel=canonical tags to the new final URLs: canonicals still pointing at old, redirecting URLs create chains through server-side redirects like the one in the real-world example shown.
- [`D2-C425`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirects**: Canonical loops can also run through server-side or client-side redirects, not only through canonical tags.
- [`D2-C426`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirects**: A community speaker said that at best a search engine's heuristic would treat a canonical loop through redirects as self-referencing canonicals, and doubted that this is often done when the loop runs through a client-side redirect.
- [`D2-C431`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirects**: A leader reachable only through a canonical and a leader with weak link equity share one fix: point internal links, sitemap entries and redirects at the URL chosen as canonical, so the leader is both reachable for users and the strongest page in its group.
- [`D2-C439`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirecting**: The crawler report shown at the talk rated a redirecting canonical target as an error, while Google's 2009 guidance accepts a canonical URL that redirects and says Google can follow canonical chains; the gap is one of severity, since both recommend pointing every canonical link straight at the final URL.
- [`D2-C882`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **301**: In a community case study, an old URL got a 301 redirect only when a new page served the same intent; URLs with no same-intent match were removed with an error status instead of being redirected (the exact code is unclear in the recording).
- [`D2-C883`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirected**: A community speaker's team never redirected removed URLs to the homepage, even those that still brought traffic, because the aim was a clear signal about what the site is rather than keeping every visitor.
- [`D2-C884`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirects**: The technical steps of a community speaker's domain consolidation included submitting new sitemaps, filing a change of address in Search Console and updating internal links so the new pages did not rely on redirects alone.
- [`D2-C895`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: A community speaker said a migration should be run around one document, the redirect map, which gives every old URL an approved destination.
- [`D2-C901`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: For migrations with many URLs, a community speaker suggested letting a similarity score propose redirect destinations and having people review the critical pages.
- [`D2-C902`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: Before a migration launches, a community speaker advised freezing the inventory (CMS export, crawl, sitemap, search data and logs), saving all content and approving the redirect map.
- [`D2-C903`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: A community speaker warned that HTTP 200 responses across a new domain show only that the URLs work, not that the content users came for is still there, so after launch the redirect map becomes the test.
- [`D2-C907`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: A community speaker said a long expected recovery after a migration is no reason to wait: broken redirect routes and blocked pages need action immediately.
- [`D2-C911`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirect**: Google's site move guide says not to redirect many old URLs to one irrelevant destination such as the new site's home page, which can confuse users and might be treated as a soft 404, and to return a 404 or 410 for deleted or merged content that is not moved to the new site.
- [`D2-C913`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **redirecting**: For URLs removed in a consolidation, return 404 or 410: Google's site move guide names those two codes, and Google's crawlers treat every 4xx code except 429 the same way, as content that does not exist, so the choice between them matters less than not redirecting to an unrelated page.
- [`D2-C561`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **redirect**: Google's documentation says Googlebot mostly crawls from US IP addresses and sends no Accept-Language header, so pages that change content or redirect by the visitor's perceived country or language may not have every version crawled, indexed or ranked; it recommends separate URLs annotated with hreflang.
- [`D3-C489`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S13-lightning-session-l-understanding-serps-and-your-users.md) **redirect**: Nik Vujic said some keyword cannibalization is fine because it is logical, but for bad cannibalization his agency groups all of an article's Search Console queries and then decides whether to redirect the pages or rewrite and split the content.
- [`D3-C645`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **redirects**: Keep migration redirects in place for at least a year and judge a site move after one to three months, not days: Google's speaker said its slowest signal needs about a year to be recalculated (a partly uncertain passage of the recording), and Google's site move guide says to keep redirects generally at least one year.
- [`D3-C671`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **redirects**: Google's site move guide says to keep redirects for as long as possible, generally at least one year, so that Google can transfer all signals to the new URLs.

- [`D2-C414`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **rel=canonical**: Google's 2009 Search Central blog post introducing rel=canonical says a canonical URL may be a URL that redirects: Google then processes the redirect as usual.
- [`D2-C415`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical tag**: The crawler report shown on screen flagged a URL discovered only through a canonical tag, with no internal a href links leading to it, as a phantom document outside the visible site structure.
- [`D2-C416`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical links**: To audit canonicals at scale, resolve every crawled URL to the final URL its canonical links and redirects lead to, group URLs by that leader, and flag groups with more than one hop, a loop, several canonicals on one page, or a leader that is noindexed, blocked, non-200 or redirecting.
- [`D2-C418`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **rel=canonical**: Google's 2013 Search Central blog post on rel=canonical mistakes says to specify no more than one rel=canonical per page: when a page has more than one, Google will likely ignore all of them, and any benefit of a legitimate canonical is lost.
- [`D2-C419`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical link**: Canonical chains, where a page's canonical target leads on to yet another URL, are named as improper use in the canonical link specification, according to a community speaker.
- [`D2-C420`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **rel=canonical**: Google's 2009 Search Central blog post introducing rel=canonical says Google's algorithm is lenient and can follow canonical chains, but strongly recommends updating links to point to a single canonical page for optimal canonicalization.
- [`D2-C421`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical links**: Canonical chains can run through canonical links alone, through a server-side redirect between members, or through a client-side redirect between members.
- [`D2-C422`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical links**: The crawler report shown on screen flagged a canonical chain as a problem: canonical links that form a chain instead of all pointing directly to the group's canonical leader.
- [`D2-C423`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **rel=canonical**: After a migration or a subdomain change, update rel=canonical tags to the new final URLs: canonicals still pointing at old, redirecting URLs create chains through server-side redirects like the one in the real-world example shown.
- [`D2-C424`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical tags**: Canonical loops, such as two HTML pages whose canonical tags point to each other, are a structural conflict: the group has no canonical leader, so its canonical information cannot be used.
- [`D2-C425`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical tags**: Canonical loops can also run through server-side or client-side redirects, not only through canonical tags.
- [`D2-C427`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical link**: When internal links point only to page A and the canonical leader is reached only through A's canonical link, the leader is reachable by machines but not by human visitors, a signal conflict that asks the search engine to index a page users cannot reach.
- [`D2-C433`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **Canonical links**: Canonical links between different language versions of a page are a misuse: if a search engine accepted such a canonical group, only one language version would rank.
- [`D2-C434`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical links**: Language versions of a page should be connected with hreflang annotations instead of canonical links.
- [`D2-C438`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical link**: A community speaker advised fixing canonical chains by cleaning up the canonical graph so that every canonical link points directly to the canonical leader.
- [`D2-C439`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical link**: The crawler report shown at the talk rated a redirecting canonical target as an error, while Google's 2009 guidance accepts a canonical URL that redirects and says Google can follow canonical chains; the gap is one of severity, since both recommend pointing every canonical link straight at the final URL.
- [`D2-C440`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **rel=canonical**: Google says canonicalization consolidates link signals from duplicates into the chosen canonical, so a leader with few links of its own is not necessarily weaker once Google accepts it; the practical risk of a weakly linked leader is that Google, treating rel=canonical as a hint, picks a different page as canonical.
- [`D2-C873`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **canonical link**: A community speaker said that, under the canonical link specification, an improperly declared canonical tag can also be ignored completely by the application that processes it, not only replaced by that application's own heuristic.
- [`D2-C718`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **canonical tag**: Not-indexed reasons in the Page indexing report include pages excluded by a noindex rule and 'Alternate page with proper canonical tag'.

### Rendering (`rendering-concept`): 79

- [`D1-C542`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **rendering**: Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript location redirects only after rendering, may never see one if rendering fails, and should be used only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible; its site move guide asks for server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) where technically possible. The JavaScript in Google's own migration was a fallback ('my only option'), not a pattern to copy.
- [`D2-C026`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **rendering**: A Google pipeline slide placed processing between the crawler and the index and listed six processing steps: HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication, feature extraction, signal extraction and index selection.
- [`D2-C035`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S03-how-is-html-interpreted.md) **rendering**: Put rel=canonical and hreflang link elements in the head of the HTML the server sends, not only in JavaScript-rendered HTML, so Google can read them during HTML parsing without depending on rendering.
- [`D2-C079`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **rendering**: Google's robots meta tag specification says data-nosnippet may be extracted both before and after rendering, so the attribute should not be added to or removed from existing elements with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C109`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **rendering**: Ship robots rules in the HTML the server sends and never rely on JavaScript to lift a noindex: Google may skip rendering a page that arrives with noindex, so the page can stay out of the index even if a script removes the tag later.
- [`D2-C854`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **rendering**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says that when Google encounters a noindex rule it may skip rendering and JavaScript execution, so using JavaScript to change or remove a noindex robots meta tag may not work as expected.
- [`D2-C855`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **rendering**: On stage the rule was absolute (Google won't even process the JavaScript of a page served with noindex), while Google's guide says only that it may skip rendering; either way, a noindex in the served HTML must never be one that JavaScript is expected to lift.
- [`D2-C110`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google framed rendering historically: when Google started, most of the web was plain, semantic HTML it could extract directly, but the modern web is built with JavaScript and much content is generated by JavaScript, so Google had to adapt.
- [`D2-C112`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Rendering** (in the quote): Google renders pages in order to index what users see: its commitment to reflecting the user experience means understanding what people see when a page loads in a browser and surfacing that in Search.
- [`D2-C115`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google described the mission of its rendering as simply executing JavaScript, while the implementation is complex, expensive and difficult.
- [`D2-C124`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google's simple solution for the extra time of live page reads is to make JavaScript-generated content render quickly and efficiently, or to use server-side rendering.
- [`D2-C127`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: A Google pipeline diagram ran from the crawl queue to the crawler, then through HTML parsing to processing, which passes pages to rendering and gets them back, and then to the index; rendering fetches its JavaScript and CSS through the crawler.
- [`D2-C128`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Although Google's pipeline diagram shows rendering as part of indexing, Google's rendering is a detached system, kept separate because rendering is time-consuming and computationally expensive.
- [`D2-C129`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: After the crawler has fetched a page, Google's rendering system executes it, checks that it loads properly and works out what it looks like at different sizes.
- [`D2-C130`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google said its pipeline needs to ensure that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering, while content that appears only through JavaScript and CSS takes a longer rendering pass.
- [`D2-C131`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google's JavaScript SEO guide says Googlebot sends every page with a 200 HTTP status code to the rendering queue, whether or not it contains JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header tells Google not to index it, and Google uses the rendered HTML to index the page.
- [`D2-C132`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: The stage remark that content indexable without JavaScript can pass through without rendering does not mean such pages skip rendering, because Google's guide queues every 200 page for rendering; read it as: content already in the raw HTML does not depend on the slower rendering pass.
- [`D2-C133`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Put everything indexing depends on (title, meta description, canonical, robots meta tag, main text and links) in the raw HTML so it is available without rendering, let JavaScript add enhancements only, and check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection for the rest.
- [`D2-C135`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: After Google's opener, Lightning session D had three community talks: rendering and JavaScript execution blind spots (Sören Bendig), debugging JavaScript rendering for Search (Rebecca Yu) and virtualizing the browser (Natalia Venditto).
- [`D2-C136`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Many SEOs still treat everything beyond the raw HTML as the developers' business, but developers often do not handle rendering problems, a community speaker warned.
- [`D2-C137`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: The first rendering blind spot a community speaker showed was content changes: text, images and recommendations that differ between the raw HTML and the rendered page, illustrated by a shop page whose rendered version had a whole extra section.
- [`D2-C138`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Switching JavaScript off and on in the browser gives a quick first impression of which content on a page depends on rendering.
- [`D2-C140`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: In a navigation example, the main navigation was in the raw HTML and would survive a rendering failure, but the whole sub-navigation was built by JavaScript, so all of its links would be inaccessible to bots if rendering broke.
- [`D2-C142`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: One site that builds its whole content by rendering also rendered its meta description with HTML tags inside it, which makes no sense and points to a flawed process.
- [`D2-C143`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Sites that create their content by rendering should have at least basic monitoring to check that the rendered pages come out right, a community speaker advised.
- [`D2-C151`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Unresolved placeholders caused by rendering timeouts are hard to catch because the problem moves around: it is not always the same page that is broken.
- [`D2-C153`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: To catch intermittent rendering problems, archive the full HTML and the resources of each page during a site audit and analyse them yourself, a community speaker advised.
- [`D2-C157`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Never block a resource that a page needs for rendering with robots.txt, a community speaker said, calling this common sense.
- [`D2-C160`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: A community speaker summarised five rendering blind spots to check: content and markup changes, invisible links, rendering timeouts, Content Security Policy and blocked resources.
- [`D2-C161`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Because even established brands have these rendering problems and every modern website uses a lot of JavaScript, a community speaker argued that most sites probably have them too and that ignoring rendering is reckless.
- [`D2-C164`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Web Rendering Service**: Google says Googlebot and its Web Rendering Service identify resources that do not contribute to essential page content, such as reporting and error requests, and may not fetch them, so client-side analytics may not give a full or accurate picture of their activity.
- [`D2-C166`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: The second community lightning talk of the rendering block covered debugging JavaScript rendering for Search: how Google renders pages, a step-by-step check, four common mistakes and a worked product page example.
- [`D2-C168`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: In Google's processing step, links are extracted from the HTML Google already has, before rendering, and the URLs found go back to the crawl queue.
- [`D2-C169`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics guide says Googlebot extracts links twice, from the HTML response before rendering and again from the rendered HTML, so links injected with JavaScript can be found if they use crawlable `<a href>` markup.
- [`D2-C170`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: After processing, an indexable page is placed in Google's render queue to wait for rendering.
- [`D2-C174`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Whatever is in the DOM at the moment Google's rendering finishes is what likely gets indexed.
- [`D2-C175`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: If a page keeps loading content indefinitely, not all of that content will be indexed, because Google's rendering does not go on forever (this passage of the recording is partly unclear).
- [`D2-C179`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Check rendering per template rather than per URL: inspect one URL of each page type (product, category, article) in URL Inspection and confirm that the main content, prices and internal links appear in the rendered HTML.
- [`D2-C183`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: A community speaker listed four common but often overlooked JavaScript rendering mistakes: non-crawlable link markup, error pages that return HTTP 200 in single-page apps, content behind user interaction, and JavaScript or API resources blocked in robots.txt.
- [`D2-C194`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: A community speaker called not hiding content behind user interaction the most important of the four JavaScript rendering mistakes.
- [`D2-C196`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: For rendering, what matters is whether content is present in the DOM, not whether it is visible on screen: hidden content can be indexed, absent content cannot.
- [`D2-C199`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: An Intersection Observer fires when the observed element enters the viewport, and the viewport Google renders with is tall, so content lazy-loaded this way can load during rendering.
- [`D2-C200`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: In Google's March 2023 SEO office hours, John Mueller said Google handles infinite scroll with viewport expansion, rendering a page like a very long phone, which is not very efficient and can miss content, so pagination links are strongly recommended.
- [`D2-C204`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Blocking JavaScript or API resources in robots.txt is a classic rendering mistake: if Google's renderer cannot fetch a resource, it cannot run it.
- [`D2-C205`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Disallowing a script folder such as /static/js/ or a generic /api/ folder in robots.txt can block the endpoints that supply a page's content, leaving blank modules and missing content after rendering.
- [`D2-C206`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **Web Rendering Service**: Google says its Web Rendering Service fetches the resources a page references through Googlebot, including JavaScript, CSS and XHR requests to APIs, but not images or videos.
- [`D2-C207`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: If an API folder must stay blocked in robots.txt, allow the endpoints that rendering needs, for example Disallow: /api/ together with Allow: /api/products/.
- [`D2-C211`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: On a product page whose data is fetched client-side, the rendering mistakes described can leave Google seeing no content at all while users still see the price and images.
- [`D2-C214`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: A community speaker summed up JavaScript rendering issues as cases where search engines cannot execute, access or trigger the code needed to display a page's core content.
- [`D2-C215`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: To find rendering issues, compare a page's raw source code with its rendered versions, including the rendered HTML that Google's testing tools show; the differences point to the problems.
- [`D2-C240`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Because Web Fragments monkey-patches core browser APIs such as document, history and location, test pages that use it in Google's rendering (the rendered HTML in Search Console's URL Inspection tool or the Rich Results Test), not only in a normal desktop browser.
- [`D2-C856`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Websites that rely heavily on JavaScript and rendering have common blind spots, because these features often break in subtle ways, a community speaker said.
- [`D2-C857`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: None of the rendering problems a community speaker showed from established brands' sites had been fixed promptly: some were fixed by the time of the talk and some were still live.
- [`D2-C859`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: A rendering failure such as a Content Security Policy blocking a video on a landing page that explains how to open a business account could have a drastic impact for a purely online business, a community speaker warned.
- [`D2-C860`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **rendering**: Besides using Chrome DevTools more often, a community speaker advised checking rendering at scale with a modern crawler.
- [`D2-C256`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google renders nearly all of the web by replicating what a browser does, using a real browser's rendering engine.
- [`D2-C257`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google's JavaScript SEO basics says every page with a 200 status code is queued for rendering, whether or not it uses JavaScript, unless a robots meta tag or header says not to index it; for non-200 pages such as 404 error pages, rendering might be skipped.
- [`D2-C258`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: If JavaScript rendering fails, what Google indexes for a page differs from what the page shows once it is rendered.
- [`D2-C259`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Erin Sparling named server-side or hybrid rendering, fallbacks and not leaving placeholders in the DOM, among other measures, as ways to guard against failed JavaScript rendering.
- [`D2-C262`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Content that is not in the final DOM after rendering cannot be seen by Google, so it cannot be indexed.
- [`D2-C273`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Google's March 2023 SEO office hours say Google sees infinite-scroll content through viewport expansion, rendering a page like a very long phone, which is not particularly efficient and can miss infinite content.
- [`D2-C274`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Content loaded as elements enter the viewport, for example with an Intersection Observer, does load when Google renders a page, because Google's rendering viewport is very tall.
- [`D2-C277`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: WebGL does not work well in Google's rendering: a WebGL shader that makes a page look like it is underwater will not be applied when Google renders the page.
- [`D2-C278`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: For effects that need WebGL, which Googlebot does not support, Google's guide to fixing JavaScript problems suggests skipping the effect or prerendering it with server-side rendering so that the content is accessible to Googlebot.
- [`D2-C279`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Erin Sparling recommended differential serving and polyfills to keep a site compatible with Google's rendering engine where it lacks a browser feature.
- [`D2-C283`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Erin Sparling called URL fragments (the part of a URL after #) the next most common JavaScript issue seen, after rendering problems and blocked rendering.
- [`D2-C298`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
- [`D2-C301`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: For headless CMS content, Erin Sparling presented rendering on the server, not only in the browser, as a way to avoid indexing issues.
- [`D2-C304`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: When Search Console reports that content is not rendering, Erin Sparling suggested putting AI agents on the problem, but only after doing your own due diligence.
- [`D2-C305`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **rendering**: With a headless CMS, choose the rendering per template before launch (server-rendered or pre-rendered for pages that must rank), and make any agent-built test suite assert that the main content and `<a href>` links are present in the rendered HTML.
- [`D2-C828`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Web Rendering Service**: Google's guide to fixing Search-related JavaScript problems says its Web Rendering Service keeps no state across page loads: local storage, session storage and HTTP cookies are cleared.
- [`D2-C829`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **Web Rendering Service**: Google's guide to fixing Search-related JavaScript problems says the Web Rendering Service may ignore caching headers and so use outdated JavaScript or CSS, and recommends content fingerprinting, which puts a hash of the content in the file name, as in main.2bb85551.js.
- [`D2-C441`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **rendering**: Google's indexing pipeline slide put a Processing stage between the crawler and the index and listed HTML parsing, rendering, deduplication and feature extraction above it, with feature extraction highlighted as the step of this talk.
- [`D2-C445`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S11-finding-the-gold-nuggets-structured-data-media-and-more.md) **rendering**: Google's guide to how Search works says rendering happens during the crawl, and describes indexing as analysing a page's text, key tags and attributes such as title elements and alt attributes, images and videos, and deciding whether the page is a duplicate or the canonical.
- [`D3-C625`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **rendering**: Google estimated that rendering takes seconds when done right away and hours when the page waits in the queue, with an end point of days to weeks.
- [`D3-C628`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **rendering**: Gary Illyes said Google keeps saying it renders every URL on the internet and that he would say this is not true, though it is what he was told; he went on to say that Google's logs show the rendering queue cleared within weeks.
- [`D3-C629`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **rendering**: According to Google's logs, everything in the rendering queue gets rendered within weeks.
- [`D3-C630`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **rendering**: Put critical content, links and meta tags in the server HTML: content that needs JavaScript reaches indexing only after rendering, usually within hours but sometimes weeks, and even Google's own speaker doubted that every URL gets rendered.
- [`D3-C676`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **rendering**: The stage doubt that every URL gets rendered sits beside Google's JavaScript guide, which says every page with a 200 status is queued for rendering unless a robots rule blocks indexing: queued is not the same as rendered, so do not rely on rendering for critical content.
