### robots.txt (`robots-txt-file`): 113

- [`D1-C037`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **robots.txt**: For classic Search, crawling means Googlebot, scheduling and robots.txt, with AI used in parts such as scheduling. Indexing is one big but not limitless index that calculates signals and understands more than words, with AI such as BERT. Serving uses hundreds of signals tailored to the moment, with AI such as RankBrain.
- [`D1-C273`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **robots.txt**: A community speaker pointed out that, according to Google's documentation, user-triggered fetchers, which fetch a page because a user asked for it, generally ignore robots.txt rules.
- [`D1-C064`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **robots.txt**: The crawler has multiple tasks: fetch from the internet, ensure it doesn't break the internet, and enforce robots.txt policies. Fetched data is sent for indexing.
- [`D1-C329`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **robots.txt**: Apart from contractual crawlers, all of Google's automated crawlers obey robots.txt, which Google treats as the way site owners opt out of its crawling.
- [`D1-C330`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **robots.txt**: The only Google-owned crawlers that do not obey robots.txt are contractual crawlers, which crawl a site whose owner has agreed that Google may crawl it however it likes.
- [`D1-C343`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **robots.txt**: Google's crawler documentation says special-case crawlers serve specific Google products where the crawled site and the product have an agreement about the crawl process, so they may ignore robots.txt rules; AdsBot, for example, ignores the global (*) user agent with the ad publisher's permission.
- [`D1-C074`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **robots.txt**: If robots.txt returns a 5xx error, Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours, then uses the cached copy for up to 30 days.
- [`D1-C079`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: The robots.txt session worked through an example file with three groups: a default group that disallows everything except the bare homepage, a shared bingbot and googlebot group that also allows /politics/ and /*/live/, and a google-extended group that disallows /subscriptions/.
- [`D1-C082`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: In robots.txt, * matches zero or more of any character and $ marks the end of the URL.
- [`D1-C084`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
- [`D1-C085`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Google generally caches robots.txt for up to 24 hours and reads only the first 500 KiB of the file.
- [`D1-C123`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Bing closes the robots.txt group at an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines, so in the slide's example bingbot ends up not blocked while Googlebot is; the slide warned that different crawlers behave differently.
- [`D1-C088`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Content-Signal lines are now common because a large CDN provider adds them to its managed robots.txt files. Never place any non-standard directive between user-agent lines; put it after a group's rules and test the file with each search engine's tools, such as Bing's robots.txt tester and Google's open-source robots.txt parser.
- [`D1-C089`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: The robots.txt talk pointed to the robots.txt file of thebestfriedchickenever.com to show why comments in robots.txt are useful; the live file is mostly a large ASCII-art drawing written as # comment lines, followed by a single user-agent group (checked 2026-10-04).
- [`D1-C140`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
- [`D1-C510`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Google's robots.txt talk recalled that robots.txt began in 1994, when bots were crashing servers: Martijn Koster proposed a text file in the root of a site with rules for how automated clients may access it.
- [`D1-C511`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Google said it already supported robots.txt when it started crawling in 1996 as a Stanford PhD project, and has supported it ever since.
- [`D1-C512`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Robots.txt**: Robots.txt is now an IETF standard, RFC 9309, supported by basically all major crawlers; Google said it follows it because it is the right thing to do: anyone who wants to opt out of crawling should be able to.
- [`D1-C513`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Robots Exclusion Protocol**: The standard's official name is the Robots Exclusion Protocol (REP). Google stressed that it was designed in 1994 only to control which automated clients may access what on a site, and has nothing to do with how the content is used.
- [`D1-C514`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Robots.txt**: Robots.txt is not a security measure: the file sits at a predictable public address, so anyone can read the paths it disallows. Protect a secret folder with authentication, or do not put it on the internet.
- [`D1-C515`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: The robots.txt file always sits in the root of the host; it cannot be placed anywhere else.
- [`D1-C516`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **Robots.txt**: Robots.txt was made extremely simple by design so that anyone could implement and understand it; it was extended as websites grew more complex, but it still has only three rules: user-agent (a named crawler, or * for every crawler), disallow and allow.
- [`D1-C518`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Comments in robots.txt start with #, and a line without the # that a parser cannot read is ignored anyway, because the standard requires parsers to skip lines they cannot parse, so it acts like a comment.
- [`D1-C522`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Google said a site can keep a directory or the whole site out of Gemini model training by disallowing it for the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, and that Google respects that policy; the speaker believed Google was the first to offer such an opt-out from model training.
- [`D1-C523`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: The 'first' needs care: OpenAI documented how to block its GPTBot crawler in robots.txt in August 2023, before Google announced Google-Extended on 28 September 2023. What Google-Extended added was a token that controls AI-training use of pages fetched by Google's existing crawlers, separately from Search; Apple later introduced a similar token, Applebot-Extended.
- [`D1-C524`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Other companies have similar 'extended' robots.txt tokens; Google named Apple's Applebot-Extended.
- [`D1-C525`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Google called robots.txt extremely forgiving: a typo in a path only blocks the wrong path, a typo in a rule name such as disallow makes Google ignore that line, and the rest of the file is still used.
- [`D1-C526`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **RFC 9309**: The real trouble is an unknown line placed between two user-agent lines: while writing RFC 9309, Google asked people whether the first crawler should then inherit the rules that follow, and opinions split roughly 50-50 (how the talk said the question was settled is unclear in the recording).
- [`D1-C528`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch.
- [`D1-C529`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Google said the robots.txt report helps catch CDNs that update a site's robots.txt without the owner's knowledge, and hosts that cloak the robots.txt file, which happens more often than people think.
- [`D1-C532`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: A typo in a rule name is not always ignored by Google: its open-source robots.txt parser deliberately accepts common misspellings of disallow (such as dissallow, dissalow and disalow) and of user-agent (useragent, user agent), but not of allow. Google's spec page does not mention typos, and other crawlers may be stricter, so spell rule names correctly.
- [`D1-C533`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Dave Smart said robots.txt groups are not additive: if a group matches a crawler's user agent, only that group's rules apply, so a googlebot group that blocks /dogs/ leaves Googlebot free to crawl the /goats/ and /cows/ that the * group blocks.
- [`D1-C534`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Dave Smart said robots.txt is checked for every URL in a redirect chain and crawling stops at the first blocked one; in his example a site redirected through /cart/ with JavaScript to set the local currency and back, and because /cart/ was disallowed the page was reported as blocked.
- [`D1-C535`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Dave Smart said Search Console reports such a block only on the first URL of the chain, which is confusing: the URL shown as blocked by robots.txt is not itself disallowed.
- [`D1-C536`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: Dave Smart said this applies to all redirects, not only JavaScript ones; his examples: a redirect through an external authorisation service that is blocked by its own robots.txt, content that moved through several URLs over the years with one of them later blocked, and unexpected redirects, such as one served only to Googlebot's user agent.
- [`D1-C537`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S08-lightning-session-b-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt**: When Search Console says a URL is blocked by robots.txt but the file does not block it, check whether the URL redirects and test every URL in the chain.
- [`D1-C101`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **robots.txt**: Google's faceted navigation guide prefers prevention: disallow filter URLs in robots.txt and keep crawlable only item pages plus one unfiltered listing page, or use URL fragments, which Google generally does not crawl. rel=canonical and nofollow are weaker, slower options.
- [`D1-C105`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **robots.txt**: URLs disallowed through robots.txt do not affect crawl budget, because they are not fetched.
- [`D1-C127`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **robots.txt**: Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling, not a block: nofollow links will generally not be followed, but the linked pages may still be crawled if Google finds them through sitemaps or other links. To stop Google fetching URLs on your own site, use a robots.txt disallow rule.
- [`D1-C109`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **robots.txt**: Google advises against using noindex to save crawl budget and against using robots.txt to temporarily reallocate budget. Use robots.txt only for pages you never want crawled, and 404 or 410 for removed pages.
- [`D1-C110`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **robots.txt**: A URL blocked in robots.txt can still be indexed without its content if other pages link to it, and Google cannot see a noindex on a page it is not allowed to fetch.
- [`D1-C427`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: An audience question asked how to make sure bots behave well beyond robots.txt.
- [`D1-C428`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: Mainstream crawlers from Google, other large search engines and AI companies try to follow robots.txt, so implementing robots.txt correctly is the way to stop them doing something specific on a site.
- [`D1-C429`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: A Google panelist said crawlers that ignore robots.txt and cause a nuisance are better treated as a scraping problem than as a crawling problem.
- [`D1-C430`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: Google follows robots.txt partly in its own interest: crawling an infinite URL space such as a calendar that robots.txt blocks would waste Google's crawling time as well as the site's resources.
- [`D1-C432`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: A Google panelist said they were working on a set of crawler best practices and offering research, malware-scanning and privacy crawlers an exemption from following them, apparently because such crawlers sometimes need to ignore robots.txt or probe URLs that other crawlers would not touch (the reason is a best reading: the audio has 'don't need', which would not explain an exemption).
- [`D1-C434`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: User-initiated fetchers, such as a translation service fetching a page a user asked to translate, are a different category from crawlers and generally do not check robots.txt, because a user asked for the fetch.
- [`D1-C435`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: AI agents acting on a user's request fall into the same category as user-initiated fetchers: an agent told to look at a site reads the page without checking robots.txt.
- [`D1-C436`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: A Google panelist argued that it makes business sense for agents not to follow robots.txt: an agent sent to buy something that obeyed a robots.txt block could not complete the purchase, a bad experience for the user and lost revenue for the shop.
- [`D1-C437`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: A Google panelist said much of robots.txt is written with search engines in mind: a search engine should never add items to a cart or check out, but an agent acting for a user probably should be able to.
- [`D1-C469`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: Gary Illyes said disallowing a section that should not be crawled, such as /ads, in a Googlebot group in robots.txt shifts crawl budget to the rest of the site.
- [`D1-C470`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: Google's crawl budget guide says crawl budget freed by robots.txt blocks is not shifted to other pages unless the site already hits its crawl capacity limit, and advises against robots.txt for temporary reallocation; so block only sections you never want crawled, and expect a shift only on capacity-limited sites.
- [`D1-C482`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: Nearly all mainstream AI crawlers and AI systems use their own user agents, so robots.txt can set a separate policy for each; at the event OpenAI was said to have three or four, Anthropic a few and Microsoft some.
- [`D1-C483`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: A Google panelist doubted that setting different robots.txt policies per AI crawler makes practical sense yet, because nobody knows how these systems will develop.
- [`D1-C485`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: To opt out of Google's AI training, a site can use the Google-Extended token in robots.txt.
- [`D1-C487`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: A Google panelist said Apple offers a robots.txt control for Applebot similar to Google-Extended, so a site can allow Applebot for search while opting out of Apple's AI use.
- [`D1-C488`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: When logs show an unknown crawler fetching a lot, search for its user agent online to find the robots.txt token that controls it; the mainstream crawlers that send the most traffic can all be controlled this way.
- [`D1-C489`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **robots.txt**: A Google panelist called a default-deny robots.txt, which blocks every crawler and allows only chosen ones, a bad pattern because the site owner does not know what is being blocked.
- [`D2-C015`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.
- [`D2-C017`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google answered on a Q&A slide that a sitemap listed in the robots.txt file can be picked up by any crawler, not only by Google's.
- [`D2-C018`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google's Q&A slide said that a sitemap not listed in robots.txt has to be submitted instead, for example in Search Console.
- [`D2-C019`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: An audience member noted that a robots.txt block does not mean noindex and that explaining this to developers is a constant struggle, and asked why Google does not treat a robots.txt block as a noindex.
- [`D2-C020`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google answered on a Q&A slide that it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as a noindex because some extremely important sites disallow their most important pages, by accident or out of ignorance.
- [`D2-C021`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google's Q&A slide said Google does not index the content of pages disallowed in robots.txt, but users will still find the URLs of those pages in Search.
- [`D2-C022`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google's noindex documentation says the noindex rule works only if the page is not blocked by robots.txt: a crawler that cannot fetch the page never sees the rule, and the page can still appear in search results, for example if other pages link to it.
- [`D2-C023`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Explain robots.txt and noindex to developers as two separate controls: robots.txt controls crawling, noindex controls indexing. To keep a page out of Search, let Google crawl it and serve noindex; a robots.txt disallow alone can leave the bare URL in results.
- [`D2-C842`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google said listing the sitemap in robots.txt is fine, as many websites do.
- [`D2-C843`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google pointed out the trade-off of listing a sitemap in robots.txt: anyone can then see the sitemap, which a site may not want.
- [`D2-C844`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google illustrated why it does not treat a robots.txt disallow as noindex with an extremely important site, such as a national tax authority, that blocks very important PDF files with robots.txt: Google cannot index the PDFs' content but can at least show their URLs in search results.
- [`D2-C845`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google said very few URLs disallowed by robots.txt are in its index, compared with the index as a whole (no figure given).
- [`D2-C846`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google said a URL disallowed by robots.txt might still be indexed if the URL is important, in which case the URL is indexed but not its content.
- [`D2-C849`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **robots.txt**: Google's robots.txt introduction names links from elsewhere on the web as the reason a disallowed URL can still be indexed, while on stage Google spoke of the URL's importance; either way, well-linked important URLs are the disallowed ones most likely to appear in results, so keep such pages crawlable with noindex if they must stay out of Search.
- [`D2-C050`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots.txt**: John Mueller noted that robots.txt is defined by an internet standard, RFC 9309, which Google's Gary Illyes co-authored.
- [`D2-C051`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots.txt**: John Mueller said there is currently no RFC that standardises robots meta tags, unlike robots.txt.
- [`D2-C058`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots.txt**: John Mueller said robots.txt does not control indexing, so robots meta tags are what site owners have to use to control it.
- [`D2-C067`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots.txt**: nofollow is a link-graph hint for search engines, not an access control: to keep AI crawlers away from content, use robots.txt rules for the specific crawlers; at Google, Google-Extended covers Gemini training and grounding, and the Search generative AI control covers AI Overviews and AI Mode.
- [`D2-C069`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots.txt**: Google's robots meta tag specification says robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers are found only when a URL is crawled, so the rules on a URL disallowed in robots.txt are never seen and are ignored.
- [`D2-C850`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots.txt**: John Mueller said robots meta rules only work if robots.txt allows Google to fetch the page.
- [`D2-C851`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **robots.txt**: When robots.txt blocks a page, the page's content is not indexable but Google can still index its URL, John Mueller said.
- [`D2-C119`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: If Gemini training reuses the rendering done for Search, a site needs no separate rendering work for Gemini; whether its rendered content is used for training is decided with the Google-Extended token in robots.txt, not by rendering choices.
- [`D2-C121`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Google's crawler documentation defines grounding in Gemini Apps and in Grounding with Google Search on Vertex AI as providing content from the Google Search index to the model at prompt time, and sites manage whether their content is used for it with the Google-Extended robots.txt token.
- [`D2-C122`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Google says user-triggered fetchers, which fetch a URL because a user asked for it in a Google product (for example Gemini Notebook fetching URLs users add as sources, or Google-Agent acting on a user's request), generally ignore robots.txt rules.
- [`D2-C123`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Google documents Gemini grounding only as content from the Search index at prompt time; the live read of a specific page at a user's request, described on stage, is not documented, so it is unclear whether it works like a user-triggered fetcher, which generally ignores robots.txt, or follows Google-Extended.
- [`D2-C157`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Never block a resource that a page needs for rendering with robots.txt, a community speaker said, calling this common sense.
- [`D2-C158`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: When something is missing from a rendered page, check both robots.txt and the Content Security Policy: the URL Inspection live test shows the page resources, the JavaScript console output and a screenshot of the rendered page.
- [`D2-C181`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: For each suspect script or API request in Chrome DevTools, check whether it runs, whether something blocks it and whether robots.txt disallows it.
- [`D2-C183`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: A community speaker listed four common but often overlooked JavaScript rendering mistakes: non-crawlable link markup, error pages that return HTTP 200 in single-page apps, content behind user interaction, and JavaScript or API resources blocked in robots.txt.
- [`D2-C204`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Blocking JavaScript or API resources in robots.txt is a classic rendering mistake: if Google's renderer cannot fetch a resource, it cannot run it.
- [`D2-C205`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Disallowing a script folder such as /static/js/ or a generic /api/ folder in robots.txt can block the endpoints that supply a page's content, leaving blank modules and missing content after rendering.
- [`D2-C207`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: If an API folder must stay blocked in robots.txt, allow the endpoints that rendering needs, for example Disallow: /api/ together with Allow: /api/products/.
- [`D2-C208`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: A robots.txt carve-out works because Google applies the most specific matching rule, so Allow: /api/products/ beats Disallow: /api/ for product endpoints only; re-test a rendered page after every robots.txt change to script or API paths.
- [`D2-C209`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: robots.txt rules apply per host, so the rules in example.com/robots.txt do not apply at all to an API served from api.example.com.
- [`D2-C210`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: An API or CDN on its own host needs its own robots.txt check: a blanket Disallow there, or a robots.txt that returns 5xx errors, can stop Google fetching the data a page renders from.
- [`D2-C212`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: In the speaker's product page example, three of the mistakes combine: product links behind onclick handlers keep the product detail pages hidden, the product API is blocked in robots.txt, and some content waits for a user interaction.
- [`D2-C245`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Make sure robots.txt does not block the URLs from which the browser loads a fragment's assets (the gateway paths on the host page's origin, or the endpoint's own host if assets load from there), because Google does not render JavaScript from blocked files and robots.txt rules apply per host.
- [`D2-C265`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Blocked resources, one of Google's four common JavaScript indexing problems, means robots.txt disallowing the crawling of critical JavaScript files or API endpoints.
- [`D2-C296`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: If robots.txt blocks JavaScript that client-side code needs to render, Google cannot render the content that the JavaScript would produce.
- [`D2-C297`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Google's introduction to robots.txt says unimportant image, script or style files may be blocked, but resources whose absence makes a page harder for Google to understand should not be blocked.
- [`D2-C298`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **robots.txt**: Check robots.txt for Disallow rules covering JavaScript bundles, build folders or API endpoints the page calls while rendering, including on separate API or CDN hostnames with their own robots.txt, then confirm in URL Inspection's live test that the rendered HTML contains the main content.
- [`D2-C328`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **robots.txt**: Google's two tokenization slides showed the difference on the same sentence: the Search tokenizer kept 'robots.txt' and 'tl;dr' as single tokens, while the AI-model tokenizer split them into pieces such as 'tl' and 'dr' or 'robots' and 'txt', with the punctuation as separate tokens.
- [`D2-C432`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **robots.txt**: The canonical leader of a group should be indexable: it should carry no noindex robots directive, return no error status code and not be blocked in robots.txt.
- [`D2-C529`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **robots.txt**: Google's documented ways to keep a site's images out of search results are a robots.txt disallow rule (for example for Googlebot-Image) or a noindex X-Robots-Tag HTTP header, with the Removals tool for emergencies.
- [`D2-C530`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **robots.txt**: Hiding an image as a CSS background is a fragile way to keep it out of Google: it only stops extraction from that page, so the same image URL used in an img element elsewhere or listed in a sitemap can still be indexed; the documented robots.txt or noindex X-Robots-Tag methods are the reliable route.
- [`D2-C931`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **robots.txt**: Googlebot-Image and Googlebot-Video are the Google crawlers that fetch images and videos, and robots.txt rules addressed to their user agent tokens control how Google indexes a site's images and videos.
- [`D2-C932`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **robots.txt**: If robots.txt disallows the location of an image or video file, Google does not index that image or video.
- [`D2-C933`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **robots.txt**: Unlike a disallowed web page, whose bare URL can still appear in web results, a video blocked by robots.txt is not shown by its URL, because Google sees no good reason to show a video URL alone.
- [`D3-C389`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **robots.txt**: Google's crawler list says robots.txt rules addressed to the Storebot-Google user agent affect all surfaces of Google Shopping, such as the Shopping tab in Google Search.
- [`D3-C390`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **robots.txt**: Treat Storebot-Google separately from Googlebot in robots.txt and bot protection: a shop that blocks it on product, cart or checkout paths can undermine Shopping price and availability checks, even when Googlebot is allowed.
- [`D3-C613`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **robots.txt**: Google estimated that a robots.txt update is picked up in about 24 hours, with a minimum of seconds and an end point of 25 hours on the slide.
- [`D3-C614`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **robots.txt**: Google said its service level objective is to refresh robots.txt every 24 hours, as RFC 9309 calls for, though delays happen now and then.
- [`D3-C615`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **robots.txt**: A site owner can submit robots.txt in Search Console to force Google to refresh it sooner.
- [`D3-C616`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **robots.txt**: Plan robots.txt changes a day ahead, because Google may use the old file for about 24 hours; for an urgent change, request a refresh in Search Console instead of waiting.
- [`D3-C667`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **robots.txt**: Google's robots.txt guide says its crawlers update their cached copy of a site's robots.txt every 24 hours, and that the Request a recrawl option in Search Console's robots.txt report refreshes it faster.

### robots.txt report (`robots-txt-report`): 5

- [`D1-C140`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt report**: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt files Google found for the top 20 hosts of a Domain property, with their fetch status, warnings and errors; to test whether a specific URL is blocked, Google's help page points to the URL Inspection tool and to Google's open-source robots.txt library.
- [`D1-C528`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt report**: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the robots.txt file as Google last fetched it, with a version history and the errors and successes of each fetch.
- [`D1-C529`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt report**: Google said the robots.txt report helps catch CDNs that update a site's robots.txt without the owner's knowledge, and hosts that cloak the robots.txt file, which happens more often than people think.
- [`D1-C530`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **robots.txt report**: Google said the robots.txt report uses the parser Google open-sourced at github.com/google/robotstxt.
- [`D3-C667`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **robots.txt report**: Google's robots.txt guide says its crawlers update their cached copy of a site's robots.txt every 24 hours, and that the Request a recrawl option in Search Console's robots.txt report refreshes it faster.

### Scaled content abuse (`scaled-content-abuse`): 10

- [`D1-C048`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **scaled content abuse**: The answer is not a claim that Google detects AI text. It says ranking favours text that reads as natural to people. The risk with AI content is scale without value, which falls under Google's scaled content abuse policy, not the tool itself.
- [`D1-C129`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S03-how-search-works-and-where-s-ai.md) **scaled content abuse**: Google's guide says creating separate content for every variation of how people might search, including fan-out queries, primarily to manipulate rankings or AI responses violates its scaled content abuse policy. It adds that its AI systems can understand a page's relevance even without an exact match to the query.
- [`D2-C611`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **scaled content abuse**: Google's spam policies define scaled content abuse as generating many pages mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value to users, no matter how they are created, and list automated translating of scraped content among the examples.
- [`D2-C612`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **scaled content abuse**: Treat machine translation as a first draft: have a native speaker review it and adapt dates, calendars and units before publishing, because unreviewed bulk translation that adds little value can also fall under Google's scaled content abuse policy.
- [`D2-C692`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **scaled content abuse**: The lower selection bar in under-served languages is an opening for content written for that market, not for machine translation at scale: index selection also applies spam signals, and Google's spam policies count generating many pages from scraped content through automated transformations such as translating, with little value for users, as scaled content abuse.
- [`D3-C207`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **scaled content abuse**: Google's quality talk listed recent updates to Google's spam policies: back button hijacking, scaled content abuse and manipulating AI responses.
- [`D3-C284`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **scaled content abuse**: Reviewing the spam slide, the speaker said link spam would probably be replaced with scaled content abuse as the spam type worth talking about today.
- [`D3-C300`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **scaled content abuse**: Weight spam audits toward scaled content abuse: a Googler said that type would replace link spam on the slide, so review mass-produced pages, including AI-generated ones, before older link-building patterns.
- [`D3-C694`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **Scaled content abuse**: Scaled content abuse is becoming a problem again: in the early 2000s pages were churned out with Perl or PHP scripts, and now the same is done with LLMs.
- [`D3-C695`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **scaled content abuse**: The cheaper tokens become, the more AI slop is created, and Google counts AI slop as scaled content abuse.

### Schema.org (`schema-org-vocabulary`): 30

- [`D1-C315`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S04-lightning-session-a-automation-and-ai.md) **schema.org**: Google's AI optimisation guide says structured data is not required for generative AI search and needs no special schema.org markup, and on Day 2 Google said raw schema.org is generally not put into model context (D2-C477); use markup for rich-result eligibility and clear data, not as an AI-visibility lever.
- [`D2-C460`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: In the speaker's own tests, even the latest LLMs asked to generate schema.org markup for a page often invent properties that do not exist, get deeply nested schemas such as complex pricing models wrong, and duplicate content across several fields.
- [`D2-C477`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: As far as the speaker knows, in most of Google's main AI uses a page's schema.org markup is not turned into text and put directly into the model's context; the data is first sorted out, checked for quality and indexed before it is passed on as grounding context.
- [`D2-C478`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: The speaker said there are concerns that feeding raw schema.org markup straight into an AI model's context would be a big abuse vector, one reason Google does not do so.
- [`D2-C479`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: There is no separate markup for AI features: by Google's account the same processed markup feeds classic results and AI answers, and raw schema.org is generally not passed into model context, so invest in the types Google documents for its features rather than in extra markup written for AI.
- [`D2-C480`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: Google's guide to optimizing for generative AI features lists 'overfocusing on structured data' among the things site owners don't need to do: structured data is not required for generative AI search and no special schema.org markup is needed, though it remains worth using because it helps pages become eligible for rich results.
- [`D2-C484`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Schema.org**: Schema.org is a common vocabulary that several major search engines started together so that site owners can mark up pages and every consumer interprets the markup the same way; the speaker put its start 15 to 20 years ago (Google, Bing and Yahoo! announced it in June 2011).
- [`D2-C485`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Schema.org**: Schema.org is an open public collaboration, and the speaker invited people who enjoy ontologies and data to join it.
- [`D2-C486`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: Marking something up with only a very generic schema.org type says little about it and is very hard for Google to use.
- [`D2-C487`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: Google uses schema.org as its markup vocabulary but mostly consumes only the subsets that its developer documentation declares, for the features it builds.
- [`D2-C510`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Schema.org**: Schema.org, in which Google is a major participant, began publishing usage statistics for all its types and properties in 2026, showing in buckets how many domains use each one; the data is also in schema.org's GitHub repository.
- [`D2-C511`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: Google often needs to see a markup type adopted on websites before it invests in a feature that uses it, a chicken-and-egg problem that the schema.org usage statistics are meant to help break.
- [`D2-C512`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **Schema.org**: Schema.org added support for RDF lists and sets, which give a way to express ordered values, because RDF triples are not ordered by nature.
- [`D2-C513`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S12-what-is-structured-data-and-why-we-need-it-on-the-internet.md) **schema.org**: Markup for schema.org types that Google does not use yet is a bet on future features; check a type's usage bucket on schema.org before investing, since adoption is what Google says it watches before building a feature.
- [`D3-C227`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **schema.org**: Google's Discover documentation says to specify the large image with schema.org markup or the og:image meta tag, which can influence the thumbnail Discover chooses, and that a vertical image cropped to 16x9 must keep its important details.
- [`D3-C230`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S06-uncovering-trustworthy-experiences-on-discover.md) **schema.org**: For Discover, set max-image-preview:large on article templates, give every article a relevant image at least 1,200 px wide in og:image or schema.org markup that is neither the site logo nor text-heavy, and show clear bylines and dates.
- [`D3-C326`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **schema.org**: Google's AI features guide says there are no additional requirements, and no special schema.org structured data, needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode; a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet.
- [`D3-C347`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **schema.org**: Google's Merchant Center help says products and details crawled from an online store can show up on Google even when they are not marked up with schema.org or added in Merchant Center, and lists the Shopping tab among the places Merchant Center free listings appear.
- [`D3-C353`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S11-shopping-on-search-beyond-the-blue-links.md) **Schema.org**: Schema.org product markup on websites is another source of billions of product offers for Google Shopping, next to merchant feeds.

- [`D2-C773`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: After the Nano Banana surge faded, worldwide baseline search interest in Gemini stayed much higher than before, which Google read as a sustained gain in brand recognition.

- [`D2-C776`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: A Google Trends chart of worldwide search interest in AI from 2004 to mid-2025 showed a huge rise in the two to three years before mid-2025.
- [`D2-C827`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: Google said worldwide search interest in AI has climbed far higher since mid-2025, beyond the range of the 2004 to mid-2025 chart shown in the talk.

- [`D2-C780`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: Google's Trends FAQ says Google Trends adds statistical noise to protect privacy, so one-off spikes on queries with low or no search interest may be noise rather than real search activity.
- [`D2-C782`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: Worldwide Google Trends search interest for ski since 2004 shows strong seasonality, peaking every winter.

- [`D2-C784`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: Google Trends shows search interest, not search volume: each point on its 0 to 100 scale represents the share of searches for the term out of all searches.
- [`D2-C785`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: Because total Google searches were far fewer in 2004 than today, a falling search interest share in Google Trends can hide a rising number of searches.

- [`D2-C795`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: Google Trends' commonly searched queries come as top queries, with the highest search interest or volume, and rising queries, with the largest increase from the previous time frame to the current one.

- [`D2-C800`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: A Google Trends chart of US search interest over five years showed umbrella and sunscreen correlated, both peaking in June, against the common assumption that umbrella searches peak in winter.
