- [`D2-C813`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: Google said colour maps of the geographic breakdown of search interest (regions within a country, or countries worldwide) had launched in the new Google Trends Explore page about a month before the October 2026 talk.
- [`D2-C817`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S24-google-trends.md) **search interest**: The regional search interest maps in Google Trends give a quick first check of demand by country or region before localising content for a new market.

### Search profiles (`search-profile`): 7

- [`D1-C023`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Search profiles**: Google listed eight ways AI Search helps users find and visit websites: preferred sources expansion, fresh perspectives and prominent links, subscription content, in-line quotes in AI Mode and AI Overviews, rich linking and embedded web, context on content sources, 'Highly Cited' labels and Search profiles.
- [`D1-C025`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Search profile**: Publishers and creators can claim a dedicated Search profile with a name, profile photo, cover image, bio, connected social and website accounts, pinned posts and links, and users can follow it.
- [`D1-C026`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Search profiles**: Search profiles launched on 4 June 2026, in the US first, for creators and publishers with a sizable following on at least one major social or video platform. They appear in knowledge panels and Discover.
- [`D1-C125`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Search profile**: Since 16 September 2026, US publishers and creators qualify for a Search profile with 10,000 followers across YouTube, Instagram, X or TikTok, and media organisations can claim and manage profiles for all their sub-brands from one login.
- [`D1-C028`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **Search profiles**: Preferred sources, linked subscriptions and Search profiles all depend on users acting on a brand's behalf. They reward brands with a loyal audience and do little for anonymous lead-generation sites.
- [`D3-C453`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search profile**: Media teams that publish on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok or X should add each account as a Search Console platform property and compare formats by URL pattern; Google's July 2026 post says an account already used for a Search profile should already give access to its data.
- [`D3-C468`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S12-inside-search-console-what-s-new-how-to-use-it.md) **Search profile**: Google's social and video performance guide says that if you already claimed your Search profile, all of its verified accounts are added automatically as platform properties in Search Console.

### Search quality raters (`search-quality-raters`): 25

- [`D2-C311`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Gary Illyes pointed to Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines as the detailed source on how Google thinks about the main content of a page.
- [`D2-C870`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines define main content as any part of the page that directly helps it achieve its purpose, including text, images, videos, page features such as calculators and content created by users, and they count the title at the top of the page as part of it.
- [`D2-C871`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines say navigation links are a common type of supplementary content, and that content behind tabs and user reviews or comments may count as main content on some pages and as supplementary content on others, depending on the page's purpose.
- [`D3-C156`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **search quality raters**: Google's How Search Works page says that in a side-by-side experiment search quality raters see two sets of results, one with the proposed change and one without, and are asked which they prefer and why.
- [`D3-C158`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's slide pointed to the Search Quality Rater Guidelines at goo.gle/raters-guidelines, with a QR code to the guidelines PDF, and the speaker said this is the exact document Google's raters use.
- [`D3-C159`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **search quality raters**: Google's slide said search quality raters are independent reviewers who help Google decide whether a change it is about to launch is good for users.
- [`D3-C160`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **search quality raters**: Google's slide said search quality raters cannot affect the rankings of individual sites.
- [`D3-C161`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **search quality raters**: Google's slide said Google gives its search quality raters guidelines that describe how Google thinks about quality.
- [`D3-C162`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **rater guidelines**: The rater guidelines' table of contents shown on Google's slide covers page quality rating, YMYL topics, main and supplementary content, website and creator reputation, E-E-A-T and lowest quality pages.
- [`D3-C163`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **search quality raters**: Google's quality talk said search quality raters are external to Google, not Google employees.
- [`D3-C164`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **search quality raters**: Google's quality talk said search quality raters can be employed by other search engines too, not just by Google.
- [`D3-C168`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's quality talk stressed that nothing in the Search Quality Rater Guidelines is itself a ranking factor; the guidelines explain how Google thinks about quality.
- [`D3-C169`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **rater guidelines**: Use the rater guidelines as a description of what Google's ranking systems aim to reward, not as a checklist of ranking factors: rater scores evaluate Google's changes and are not used to rank any particular site.
- [`D3-C170`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's quality talk pointed to page 21 of the Search Quality Rater Guidelines for its definition of content quality by effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy, noting that the document is updated from time to time.
- [`D3-C171`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **rater guidelines**: Google's quality talk said effort, in the rater guidelines, is the extent to which a human being actively worked to create satisfying content, and that effort can be direct or indirect.
- [`D3-C173`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **rater guidelines**: The talk's originality test ('are you adding more value') matches Google's helpful-content question on content that draws on other sources, while the rater guidelines ask raters, where other websites have similar content, to consider whether the page is the original source; aim to be the original source, and add substantial value where you build on others.
- [`D3-C176`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **search quality raters**: Google's helpful-content guidance lists effort, originality, talent or skill and accuracy as the main-content attributes search quality raters are trained to evaluate, and says using generative AI to produce large amounts of text without manual oversight or curation represents little to no effort.
- [`D3-C265`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google sometimes couples a core update with an update to its Search Quality Rater Guidelines.
- [`D3-C266`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **search quality raters**: Google's 2019 post on core updates says Google tests any broad core update before it goes live, including feedback from its search quality raters, whose data is not used directly in ranking.
- [`D3-C689`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines tell raters that any form of deception makes a page untrustworthy and earns it the lowest rating.
- [`D3-C690`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **Quality raters**: Quality raters cannot give a site a penalty or a manual action; their ratings are converted into labels that Google uses to improve its algorithms.
- [`D3-C697`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines point out that the tool used to create content is not the problem, but how it was used and what for.
- [`D3-C710`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines (September 2025) list fake owner or content creator profiles, such as made-up author profiles with AI-generated images, as deception, and say pages using deception of any type should be rated Lowest.
- [`D3-C711`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines say no single rating can directly change how a page appears in Google Search; ratings measure how well search works and give examples of helpful and unhelpful results to improve it.
- [`D3-C713`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S18-wrapping-all-up-ai-search-and-making-sense-of-everything.md) **Search Quality Rater Guidelines**: Google updated its generative AI content guidance on 1 October 2026 with information from the Search Quality Rater Guidelines, to keep its documentation in sync with the presentations used at its developer events.

### Single-page app (`single-page-app`): 12

- [`D2-C183`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **single-page apps**: A community speaker listed four common but often overlooked JavaScript rendering mistakes: non-crawlable link markup, error pages that return HTTP 200 in single-page apps, content behind user interaction, and JavaScript or API resources blocked in robots.txt.
- [`D2-C185`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **single-page app**: The crawlable pattern for single-page app navigation is a real URL in the href, such as `<a href=/products>`, combined with History API routing (window.history.pushState) instead of hash routes.
- [`D2-C190`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **single-page apps**: In single-page apps, a missing page often shows a custom 404 page while the server returns HTTP 200, because the front-end router, not the server, handles the 404.
- [`D2-C192`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **single-page app**: Google's JavaScript guides say that when client-side routing makes a real 404 status impractical, a single-page app can avoid soft 404s by redirecting with JavaScript to a URL whose server returns 404, or by adding a robots noindex meta tag with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C193`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **single-page app**: In a single-page app, let the server return 404 for unknown routes where possible; otherwise use one of the two client-side fixes Google documents for error views: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns 404, or a robots noindex added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C285`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **single-page apps**: Google recommends the History API to give single-page apps clean URLs instead of fragment-based routes.
- [`D2-C286`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **single-page app**: Moving a single-page app from fragment-based routes to real paths with the History API keeps the same client-side behaviour and was described as not free but relatively straightforward.
- [`D2-C288`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **single-page app**: With the History API, a single-page app can use real links and attach event listeners that intercept the click, rewrite the URL with pushState and load the new content, so Google can follow the links while users avoid full page reloads.
- [`D2-C290`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **single-page app**: Audit a single-page app by searching both the templates and the rendered HTML for href="#..." routes, `<a>` elements without href and onclick navigation; every view that should rank needs an `<a href>` link to a real path.
- [`D2-C291`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **single-page apps**: In JavaScript single-page apps, soft 404s typically arise because the server returns the app with a 200 status for every URL, so when the app shows a 'not found' message for a URL that does not exist, no error is reported.
- [`D2-C294`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **single-page apps**: For client-side rendered single-page apps, where meaningful status codes can be impossible or impractical, Google's documentation gives two ways to avoid soft 404s: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns a 404 status, or a noindex robots meta tag added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C342`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **single-page apps**: Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.

### Site move (`site-move`): 11

- [`D1-C542`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **site move**: Google's redirects guide says Google Search follows JavaScript location redirects only after rendering, may never see one if rendering fails, and should be used only when server-side or meta refresh redirects are impossible; its site move guide asks for server-side permanent redirects (301 or 308) where technically possible. The JavaScript in Google's own migration was a fallback ('my only option'), not a pattern to copy.
- [`D2-C911`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **site move**: Google's site move guide says not to redirect many old URLs to one irrelevant destination such as the new site's home page, which can confuse users and might be treated as a soft 404, and to return a 404 or 410 for deleted or merged content that is not moved to the new site.
- [`D2-C912`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **site move**: Google's site move guide says to submit a Change of Address in Search Console when moving from one domain or subdomain to another, to submit the new sitemap, and to change internal links on the new site from the old URLs to the new ones.
- [`D2-C913`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **site move**: For URLs removed in a consolidation, return 404 or 410: Google's site move guide names those two codes, and Google's crawlers treat every 4xx code except 429 the same way, as content that does not exist, so the choice between them matters less than not redirecting to an unrelated page.
- [`D2-C915`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **site move**: The 304-day median recovery a community speaker cited from an unnamed study and Google's site move guide (a few weeks or more for a medium-sized site until Google shows the new URLs, longer for larger sites) measure different things: indexing can switch within weeks while traffic recovery can take far longer, so plan and report on both.
- [`D3-C642`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **site move**: Google treats a site move as a complex canonicalization process in which every signal of the old site is recalculated and moved to the new one, and every indexing process has to run.
- [`D3-C643`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **site move**: A site move can finish within a few weeks for a small site, takes one to three months on average, and in the worst case about a year.
- [`D3-C644`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **site move**: Gary Illyes said a site move can take up to about a year in the worst case, because Google's slowest signal is recalculated only about once a year (some words of this passage are uncertain readings).
- [`D3-C645`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **site move**: Keep migration redirects in place for at least a year and judge a site move after one to three months, not days: Google's speaker said its slowest signal needs about a year to be recalculated (a partly uncertain passage of the recording), and Google's site move guide says to keep redirects generally at least one year.
- [`D3-C671`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **site move**: Google's site move guide says to keep redirects for as long as possible, generally at least one year, so that Google can transfer all signals to the new URLs.
- [`D3-C672`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **site move**: Google's site move guide says that, as a general rule, a small to medium-sized site can take a few weeks for most pages to move and larger sites take longer, depending on the number of URLs and server speed.

### Sitemaps (`sitemap-file`): 41

- [`D1-C067`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **sitemaps**: A page with no internal links depends on sitemaps alone to be found, so it is discovered slowly and attracts little crawl demand.
- [`D1-C336`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **sitemaps**: Google finds what to crawl mainly by extracting URLs from previously crawled pages, and additionally from sitemaps.
- [`D1-C337`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S05-how-crawling-works.md) **XML sitemap**: An XML sitemap, a format from around 2005, gives Google, other search engines and potentially AI systems a list of the URLs a site wants crawled; Google called it nothing fancy but said it still uses sitemaps.
- [`D1-C084`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S07-how-google-interprets-robots-txt.md) **sitemap**: Google supports only the user-agent, allow, disallow and sitemap fields in robots.txt. Other fields such as crawl-delay are not supported.
- [`D1-C127`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S10-how-google-thinks-about-crawl-budget.md) **sitemaps**: Google treats nofollow as a hint for crawling, not a block: nofollow links will generally not be followed, but the linked pages may still be crawled if Google finds them through sitemaps or other links. To stop Google fetching URLs on your own site, use a robots.txt disallow rule.
- [`D1-C474`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **sitemap**: An audience member asked where the sweet spot is for a sitemap that misses nothing but does not overflow Search Console.
- [`D1-C475`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **sitemap**: There is no sweet spot to find for a sitemap: technically it should list every URL you want indexed, so that Google can find each of them.
- [`D1-C540`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S12-q-a.md) **sitemaps**: Asked how to plan a migration that does not leave many URLs unindexed, a Google panelist said the answer is probably not sitemaps: decide what matters from the business's perspective (for example whether to consolidate languages); listing the new URLs in a sitemap is probably a good idea and cannot hurt, but it is not the main tool.
- [`D2-C005`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemap**: Google's ecommerce documentation recommends linking from menus to category pages, from category pages to sub-category pages and from sub-category pages to all product pages; where not every product can be linked, it recommends a sitemap or a Merchant Center feed.
- [`D2-C008`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemaps**: Google's view of HTML sitemaps has moved: a 2005 blog post encouraged them, the current sitemap and ecommerce documentation does not mention them, and the 2026 Q&A slide pointed large sites to category hub pages instead.
- [`D2-C015`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemap**: An audience member asked whether the sitemap link should be included in robots.txt, noting that many websites include it but that it was missing from an earlier robots.txt slide by a Google speaker, which the question called 'Gary's slide'.
- [`D2-C017`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemap**: Google answered on a Q&A slide that a sitemap listed in the robots.txt file can be picked up by any crawler, not only by Google's.
- [`D2-C018`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemap**: Google's Q&A slide said that a sitemap not listed in robots.txt has to be submitted instead, for example in Search Console.
- [`D2-C833`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemap**: Google's sitemap guide says Google uses lastmod only when it is consistently and verifiably accurate, and counts a change to the main content, the structured data or the links of a page as significant, but not a changed copyright date.
- [`D2-C842`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemap**: Google said listing the sitemap in robots.txt is fine, as many websites do.
- [`D2-C843`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S02-welcome-to-indexing-day.md) **sitemap**: Google pointed out the trade-off of listing a sitemap in robots.txt: anyone can then see the sitemap, which a site may not want.
- [`D2-C189`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **sitemaps**: Build market and language selectors as plain `<a href>` links to each alternate URL, not buttons or script handlers; otherwise the language versions have no internal links and depend on sitemaps to be found, which is slow.
- [`D2-C387`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **sitemaps**: Google named three considerations when picking a representative URL: hijacking across pages or sites, user experience (the page can load, meta refresh, security) and site-owner signals (redirects, rel=canonical, sitemaps).
- [`D2-C390`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **sitemaps**: Clear site-owner signals about which URL should be canonical make a big difference to Google's choice; the speaker named redirects, listing only the preferred URL in sitemaps, and rel=canonical, which the speaker said also helps a bit.
- [`D2-C391`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **sitemap**: Google's canonical guide ranks the ways to signal a preferred canonical by strength: redirects and rel=canonical annotations are strong signals, sitemap inclusion is a weak signal, and combining methods makes them more effective.
- [`D2-C392`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **sitemap**: Google's duplication talk described rel=canonical as something that 'also helps a bit', while Google's canonical guide calls it a strong signal alongside redirects and calls sitemap inclusion weak; treat redirects and rel=canonical as the main levers and sitemaps as support.
- [`D2-C400`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **sitemap**: Before a migration or template change, align every canonical signal for the preferred URL (redirects, rel=canonical, internal links, sitemap entries, hreflang and working HTTPS); Google says it follows the site owner only when the signals agree.
- [`D2-C431`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **sitemap**: A leader reachable only through a canonical and a leader with weak link equity share one fix: point internal links, sitemap entries and redirects at the URL chosen as canonical, so the leader is both reachable for users and the strongest page in its group.
- [`D2-C884`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **sitemaps**: The technical steps of a community speaker's domain consolidation included submitting new sitemaps, filing a change of address in Search Console and updating internal links so the new pages did not rely on redirects alone.
- [`D2-C902`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **sitemap**: Before a migration launches, a community speaker advised freezing the inventory (CMS export, crawl, sitemap, search data and logs), saving all content and approving the redirect map.
- [`D2-C912`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **sitemap**: Google's site move guide says to submit a Change of Address in Search Console when moving from one domain or subdomain to another, to submit the new sitemap, and to change internal links on the new site from the old URLs to the new ones.
- [`D2-C527`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemaps**: One of the most reliable ways to make sure Google finds an image is to include it in an img element in the HTML; Gary Illyes named image sitemaps as the other method.
- [`D2-C530`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemap**: Hiding an image as a CSS background is a fragile way to keep it out of Google: it only stops extraction from that page, so the same image URL used in an img element elsewhere or listed in a sitemap can still be indexed; the documented robots.txt or noindex X-Robots-Tag methods are the reliable route.
- [`D2-C540`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemaps**: Besides img elements, image sitemaps tell Google about images: they are XML sitemaps that list, under a page's loc entry, the locations of the images on that page.
- [`D2-C552`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemap**: Google's slide listed seven key factors for video SEO success: high-quality video content, a dedicated watch page, compelling titles and descriptions, relevant thumbnails, video markup, fast-loading pages and sitemap inclusion.
- [`D2-C556`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemap**: Including videos in a sitemap helps Google discover all of a site's video content.
- [`D2-C557`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemap**: Give each important video its own watch page where the video is the main content, add VideoObject markup and list the video in a video sitemap; a video buried in a long article lacks the dedicated watch page that Google listed as a key factor.
- [`D2-C925`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemaps**: Video sitemaps are not critical but good to have, because Google ingests video sitemaps much more often than it can process HTML pages.
- [`D2-C926`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S13-using-images-to-your-advantage-and-engaging-search-users-with-videos.md) **sitemap**: A video sitemap or video feed tells Google which URLs carry videos so it can visit those URLs to double-check; without one, Google has to check every page individually.
- [`D2-C567`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **sitemap**: When the HTML head is not suitable for a page, hreflang can be given by other methods instead, such as listing the language versions in a sitemap.
- [`D2-C569`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **XML sitemap**: Google's hreflang guide says its three methods (link elements in the HTML head, an HTTP Link header, which suits non-HTML files such as PDFs, and an XML sitemap) are equivalent; using several at once is allowed but brings no benefit in Search and is harder to manage.
- [`D2-C574`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S15-focusing-on-internationalisation-and-localisation.md) **sitemap**: Audit hreflang per cluster rather than per page: check that every page lists itself and all its alternates, that every alternate links back, and that only one method (HTML head, HTTP header or sitemap) supplies the annotations.
- [`D3-C610`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **sitemap**: Google estimated that processing a sitemap takes about 24 hours on average, with a minimum of minutes.
- [`D3-C611`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **sitemap**: If a sitemap is useful to Google and the site is of high quality, Google tries to refetch the sitemap within 14 days at most.
- [`D3-C612`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **sitemap**: Google may never fetch a lower-quality site's sitemap again: once it figures out the site is of lower quality, it no longer wants to fetch the sitemap.
- [`D3-C638`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **sitemaps**: By Google's own averages, getting found and crawled takes far longer than indexing (about 20 hours to discover a URL and 30 days to refresh one, against 1.5 hours to index), so for faster results work on discovery: internal links from often-crawled pages and accurate sitemaps.

### Snippets (`snippets`): 27

- [`D1-C034`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S02-what-s-new-in-the-world-of-search.md) **snippets**: Lead-generation, local-service and e-commerce sites should normally stay included, because AI answers cite and link sources. Sites selling paywalled or licensed content should test exclusion on a child property first. Use nosnippet only if you also want out of regular snippets.
- [`D2-C070`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **text snippet**: The nosnippet rule stops Google from showing a text snippet or video preview for a page in search results, while the page's title is still shown.
- [`D2-C073`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: John Mueller said Google uses the snippet as a way of building AI Overviews and AI Mode answers, so if a page forbids a snippet, Google cannot use that snippet for them.
- [`D2-C074`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: Google's AI features guide says a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet to appear as a supporting link in AI Overviews or AI Mode, with no additional technical requirements.
- [`D2-C075`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippets**: Before adding nosnippet or a low max-snippet value, weigh the cost in AI features: both limit how much of the page AI Overviews and AI Mode can use, and John Mueller described those answers as built from snippets.
- [`D2-C076`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: John Mueller said data-nosnippet is rarely needed but lets a site keep a specific piece of text, such as a business phone number, out of the snippet, so the page can still be found for it while searchers have to visit the page to see it.
- [`D2-C078`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: Broken HTML can widen data-nosnippet: if a div marked data-nosnippet is not closed properly, the rest of the page can be blocked from the snippet as well.
- [`D2-C081`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: To hide one detail, such as a phone number, a price or a direct answer, instead of the whole snippet, wrap it in data-nosnippet on a span, div or section in the server HTML and validate the HTML so that an unclosed element cannot hide the rest of the page from snippets.
- [`D2-C082`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: The max-snippet:[number] rule limits a page's search result snippet to that number of characters (100 characters, for example), and max-snippet:0 shows no snippet, the same as nosnippet.
- [`D2-C084`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: A max-snippet value too short for a useful snippet may lead Google to show no snippet at all, John Mueller said.
- [`D2-C085`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: max-snippet:-1 removes the length limit and can produce a longer snippet than having no rule, because by default Google keeps snippets to a length it considers reasonable instead of quoting a page at length.
- [`D2-C086`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: Google's robots meta tag specification says Google chooses the snippet length when no max-snippet rule is set, and with max-snippet:-1 chooses the length it believes most effective; it does not say that -1 produces longer snippets.
- [`D2-C105`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S04-controlling-indexing.md) **snippet**: Set max-snippet:-1 and max-image-preview:large on every indexable template unless licensing requires otherwise, and check that no CMS, plug-in or CDN setting adds lower snippet or image preview limits by default.
- [`D2-C152`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **snippets**: Broken titles and snippets caused by unresolved placeholders may hurt business, especially for e-commerce shops and affiliate-heavy sites, a community speaker warned.
- [`D2-C724`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **snippet**: The snippet shown for a web result is reconstructed from the tokens stored in Google's index: Google knows the position of each token in the document and rebuilds the snippet from those positions.
- [`D2-C725`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **snippet**: Google's snippet documentation says snippets are created automatically, primarily from the page content, to preview the part that best relates to the user's specific search, so one page can get different snippets for different searches; sometimes the meta description is used instead.
- [`D2-C726`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **snippets**: AI Overviews and AI Mode use the same index structures and token-based snippets as classic web results, a point Google called important but not obvious.
- [`D2-C727`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **snippets**: Google said that when AI Overviews or AI Mode run a query fan-out, the generated queries are sent to Google's Search index and documents come back with their snippets, which then feed the AI-generated answer (part of this passage is unclear in the recording).
- [`D2-C730`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **snippet**: There is no separate AI index to optimise for: when a page never shows up as a source in AI Overviews or AI Mode, first check that it is indexed, that no nosnippet rule blocks its snippet and that the site is not excluded in Search Console's generative AI setting, the eligibility conditions Google lists.
- [`D2-C731`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S23-how-does-the-index-look-like.md) **snippets**: Treat nosnippet, data-nosnippet and max-snippet as AI visibility settings too: Google lists them as the controls for content in AI features, and if AI answers are built from index snippets, as Google said on stage, a blocked or shortened snippet leaves AI Overviews and AI Mode less to use.
- [`D3-C314`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **snippet**: A text result on Google's results page is made of parts such as the attribution, the title link, the snippet and the site name.
- [`D3-C315`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **snippet**: Google's Visual Elements gallery describes a text result as based on the page's textual content, with attribution, title link and snippet; attribution can include the site name, favicon and visible URL, and a rich result typically relies on structured data.
- [`D3-C316`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **snippet**: Google generates the parts of a text result, such as title link and snippet, from its understanding of the underlying web page, even when the site owner provides nothing extra.
- [`D3-C326`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S10-how-search-results-are-born.md) **snippet**: Google's AI features guide says there are no additional requirements, and no special schema.org structured data, needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode; a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown with a snippet.
- [`D3-C654`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **snippet**: Google estimated that a snippet update takes 1-2 days on average and up to several weeks to months, because the page has to be reprocessed to extract the new text.
- [`D3-C657`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **snippet**: Google estimated that a title update takes as long as a snippet update: 1-2 days on average, up to several weeks to months.
- [`D3-C658`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **snippets**: After changing a title or meta description, wait at least a few days before judging the result in Search; if nothing changes after several weeks, check that the page was recrawled, since snippets and titles are only re-extracted from a reprocessed page.

### Soft 404 (`soft-404-error`): 34

- [`D1-C070`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Soft 404s**: Soft 404s were named as a crawl problem alongside DNS and firewall issues, and described as one of the biggest problems on the internet right now for crawling and showing up in Search.
- [`D1-C073`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **soft 404**: A soft 404 is a page that returns a success code while its content looks like an error or an empty page. It is kept out of the index but continues to be crawled, wasting crawl budget.
- [`D1-C078`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **soft 404**: For temporary blocks return 503 or 429, never a 200 page with a captcha or error message, which becomes a soft 404 and can replace real content in the index. Verify Googlebot by reverse DNS, not by user agent.
- [`D1-C355`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **soft 404**: A soft 404 is a 404 in disguise: the page returns 200 but its content says something like 'page not found', information the site should have sent as the HTTP status.
- [`D1-C356`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **Soft 404**: Soft 404 pages are still crawled like normal pages; their bigger consequences are for indexing, and they also affect crawling.
- [`D1-C367`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **soft 404**: CDN captcha challenges often return HTTP 200; Googlebot does not solve them and sees only content with a 200 status, which indexing then classifies as a soft 404, reported as an error in Search Console.
- [`D1-C369`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **soft 404**: Google's status code page says that with a 204 No Content response Google receives no content and cannot process it, and that a 2xx page whose content is empty or an error message shows as a soft 404 in Search Console.
- [`D1-C371`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **soft 404**: Day 1 said a CDN captcha page served with HTTP 200 becomes a soft 404, while Day 2 (D2-C374, D2-C375) said such challenge pages are hard to recognise as errors and can be clustered as duplicates; Google's CDN post describes both outcomes, and in both the real pages drop out of Search.
- [`D1-C508`](../40-sessions/day1/D1-S06-how-crawling-errors-affect-search.md) **soft 404s**: Google said soft 404s, like some other problem categories, are looked up in Search Console's page indexing report, while other crawl issues are debugged in the Crawl Stats report.
- [`D2-C191`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **soft 404**: The fix for a client-side soft 404 is to make a missing page end with a real HTTP 404 status code instead of 200.
- [`D2-C192`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **soft 404s**: Google's JavaScript guides say that when client-side routing makes a real 404 status impractical, a single-page app can avoid soft 404s by redirecting with JavaScript to a URL whose server returns 404, or by adding a robots noindex meta tag with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C213`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S05-lightning-session-d-rendering-and-javascript.md) **soft 404**: A page that renders empty for Google, such as a client-side product page hit by these mistakes, is seen as thin content and ends up treated as a soft 404 even though users see a full page.
- [`D2-C260`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **soft 404s**: Google listed four common JavaScript problems for indexing: content not present in the rendered HTML, using # in URLs for content changes, soft 404s and blocked resources.
- [`D2-C264`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **soft 404**: Google's slide defined a soft 404 in a JavaScript application as a page that serves a 'Not Found' message but returns a 200 HTTP status code.
- [`D2-C291`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **soft 404s**: In JavaScript single-page apps, soft 404s typically arise because the server returns the app with a 200 status for every URL, so when the app shows a 'not found' message for a URL that does not exist, no error is reported.
- [`D2-C292`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **soft 404**: The fix for a client-side soft 404 is to serve a real 404 error page where appropriate; how to detect URLs that do not exist depends on how the app works and where it is hosted.
- [`D2-C294`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **soft 404s**: For client-side rendered single-page apps, where meaningful status codes can be impossible or impractical, Google's documentation gives two ways to avoid soft 404s: a JavaScript redirect to a URL that returns a 404 status, or a noindex robots meta tag added with JavaScript.
- [`D2-C295`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S06-what-is-google-friendly-javascript.md) **soft 404s**: After moving to real paths, set the server or hosting rewrite rules so a direct request to every valid path returns 200 with the content (ideally server-rendered) and an unknown path returns a 404 status, which removes client-side soft 404s at the source.
- [`D2-C334`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404**: A soft 404 is a page that should return an error status code but returns HTTP 200; from a crawling point of view it looks indexable, but because it has no real content Google throws it out of the index.
- [`D2-C335`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404s**: Because error pages are worded in endless variations, of which 'page not found' is only the classic one, Google cannot detect soft 404s with simple error, word or keyword matching.
- [`D2-C336`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404s**: Google listed four common causes of soft 404s: pages that look like errors but are not, thin or empty content, server or CMS misconfigurations, and JavaScript-dependent content that fails to load.
- [`D2-C337`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404s**: Mistakes in Google's own systems are a further cause of soft 404s, and Gary Illyes asked site owners to report such mistakes in Google's forums.
- [`D2-C338`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404s**: Google detects soft 404s with a language model, described as something like BERT, that is trained to understand the structure and layout of a page as well as its language, instead of reading the page as one flat wall of text.
- [`D2-C339`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404**: For soft 404 detection, the position of error text decides: an error in a less important part such as the navigation need not make a page a soft 404, but an error message alone in the main content, like 'Error establishing a database connection', does, much as a human would judge it.
- [`D2-C340`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404**: Google's soft 404 detection tells the page chrome, such as navigation and footer, apart from the main content by analysing the page's visual hierarchy alongside its text.
- [`D2-C341`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404**: Gary Illyes said soft 404 detection keeps searchers from clicking into dead ends and avoids wasting site owners' resources on visitors sent to error pages.
- [`D2-C342`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S07-understanding-what-s-on-a-page.md) **soft 404**: Return real error status codes for error states, 404 or 410 for missing content and 503 for outages such as a failed database connection, also in single-page apps; a 200 page whose main content is only an error message is treated as a soft 404 even when header and navigation look normal.
- [`D2-C364`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **soft 404s**: Google clusters duplicate pages by content in four ways: exact matches, near matches, structurally similar content, and soft 404s.
- [`D2-C367`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S08-handling-web-duplication.md) **Soft 404**: Soft 404 pages are another reason Google clusters pages together, an outcome site owners usually do not want.
- [`D2-C911`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S09-lightning-session-e-managing-duplicates-and-site-moves.md) **soft 404**: Google's site move guide says not to redirect many old URLs to one irrelevant destination such as the new site's home page, which can confuse users and might be treated as a soft 404, and to return a 404 or 410 for deleted or merged content that is not moved to the new site.
- [`D2-C696`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **soft 404s**: Index selection applies the negative signals that immediately block indexing: noindex (the likely reading of one unclear word), expired unavailable_after dates, soft 404s, non-canonical duplicates, spam signals and other policies.
- [`D2-C700`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **soft 404**: Index selection drops soft 404 pages that were not dropped earlier, for example when a document is reprocessed.
- [`D2-C714`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S20-deciding-what-goes-in-the-index.md) **soft 404s**: 'Crawled – currently not indexed' is most of the time a quality issue rather than a technical one: the pages are usually low quality or useless for the index, for example duplicates or soft 404s.
- [`D3-C607`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **soft 404s**: An audience member reported recrawl intervals on one very large, popular client site: the homepage about 5 times a day, first-level pages about every 1.5 days (uncertain reading), and pages clustered as soft 404s every 160 to 190 days, adding that other sites will differ.

### Spam updates (`spam-updates`): 18

- [`D2-C978`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **spam update**: Google's October 2023 spam update post (4 October 2023) says the update improved coverage in many languages and spam types, cleaning up spam reported in Turkish, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Hindi, Chinese and other languages, particularly cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam.
- [`D2-C979`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S16-lightning-session-g-internationalisation.md) **spam update**: The October 2023 spam update cited in the non-Latin-script talk names neither Persian nor Arabic (only 'other languages') and lists cloaking, hacked, auto-generated and scraped spam, not link spam, so it does not show that the bought links the presenter saw working in Persian or Arabic search were addressed.
- [`D3-C157`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **spam updates**: Google made 4,781 launches to Search in 2023 while its status dashboard lists nine named ranking updates that year, so almost every change to Search goes unannounced; monitor rankings and traffic continuously, not only around announced core or spam updates.
- [`D3-C201`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **spam updates**: Google's quality talk said Google had released four spam updates in 2026 by the time of the talk on 2 October, with one still rolling out.
- [`D3-C202`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **spam update**: Google's Search Status Dashboard says the September 2026 spam update began on 24 September 2026, applies globally to all languages and may take up to two weeks to roll out.
- [`D3-C203`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **spam updates**: Google's quality talk said its spam updates mostly target spam pages, so most site owners in the audience were probably not affected.
- [`D3-C205`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S05-how-google-thinks-about-quality.md) **spam updates**: Google's quality talk said AI has fundamentally changed how Google builds spam updates, letting it evaluate many more candidates and drastically increasing its velocity, so it launches faster with more impact.
- [`D3-C250`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam update**: Every kind of Search update, whether a feature launch, a core update or a spam update, has the same goal: satisfying users' information needs with better results.
- [`D3-C261`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam updates**: As of 3 October 2026, the Ranking history of Google's Search Status Dashboard lists two core updates in 2026 (March and May) and four spam updates (March, June, August and September).
- [`D3-C286`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam updates**: When spammers find loopholes that Google's systems miss, Google releases spam updates that change its systems to catch them.
- [`D3-C287`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam updates**: Google's spam updates page says its automated spam detection systems run constantly, and a notable improvement to them, such as to the AI-based SpamBrain system, is called a spam update and listed with Google's ranking updates.
- [`D3-C288`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **Spam updates**: Spam updates target only spam: they go after sites that churn out millions of low-quality pages to make money, very likely not the site owners and SEOs in the audience.
- [`D3-C289`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam update**: Google's 'Recoveries' slide said that to recover from a spam update a site should remove the kind of spam Google described in its blog announcements of the update.
- [`D3-C290`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam update**: The speaker declined to give a timeline for recovering from a spam update, saying the update had targeted spam.
- [`D3-C291`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam updates**: Google's spam updates page says that after a spam update, changes may help a site improve if Google's automated systems learn over a period of months that the site complies with its spam policies.
- [`D3-C292`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam updates**: Google's spam updates page says that after a link spam update, fixing the site might not bring an improvement, because any ranking benefit the spammy links had generated is lost and cannot be regained.
- [`D3-C293`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S07-what-are-quality-updates.md) **spam update**: A ranking drop after a core update is not a penalty, so technically there is no recovery from a core update in the way there is after a spam update.
- [`D3-C663`](../40-sessions/day3/D3-S17-how-long-does-it-take-to.md) **spam update**: Google estimated that a spam update affects sites within 1-2 days of the rollout, 1-2 weeks for continuous processing (said on stage as 2 weeks on average) and months for batch refreshes.

- [`D2-C671`](../40-sessions/day2/D2-S19-calculating-some-signals.md) **SpamBrain**: Google's 2021 webspam report says SpamBrain, its AI-based spam-prevention system, was launched in 2018 and has been continuously improved since.
